Cpt_816.c: Parchment codex with a modern green leather binding preserving a lectionary (Katameros) written in Coptic and Arabic in the 16th century in Egypt. A lectionary is a book of biblical readings organised according to the liturgical year. The decorated frontispiece is a stepped-cross with interlace ornament flanked by four birds. The Alpha (Α) and Omega (Ω), or beginning and end, are written above and below the cross. The letters in the arms of the cross—ΙΗΣ ΠΧΣ ΧΣ ΘΣ—are abbreviations for the Coptic phrase Ⲓⲏⲥⲟⲩⲥ Ⲡⲓⲭ̀ⲣⲓⲥⲧⲟⲥ Ⲡ̀ϣⲏⲣⲓ ⲙ̀Ⲫ̀ⲛⲟⲩϯ (Iêsous Piekhristos Epshêri Emefnouti) or Jesus Christ, Son of God.

Cpt_818.c: Ostraca (broken piece of pottery) written in Coptic in the 7th or 8th century in Egypt. The text is an exhortatory tag probably written as a student exercise. ‘Blame no man, except that you have prayed... Be at peace with everyone in order that you might pray in Paradise (?). This is the Law of the Prophets.’ The staurogram became a standard opening to Christian documentary texts written in Coptic. A staurogram ⳨ is a Christian symbol derived from a ligature, the combination of two or more letters into a single glyph, in this case Tau (Τ) and Rho (Ρ).

Cpt_823.t: Folio of two angels from a Coptic manuscript
Cpt_823.c: Folio from a Coptic manuscript, illuminated between the 3rd and 7th century AD in Egypt. Decorative border probably made with a compass. The descriptions of angels in biblical texts, however, are vague; they are described only as brilliant, fiery and shining. As a result, the appearance of angels in art had to be invented. The earliest representations of angels in Christian art show wingless figures. Winged angels only appear in the fourth century, their images derived from Roman Victories or winged genii (protective spirits).

Cpt_829_1.t: An unidentified legend and the Legend of Apa Jeremias and Apa Johannes (pp.35–36)
Cpt_829_1.c: Fragmentary folio (pp.35–36) from a parchment codex preserving part of an unidentified legend (pp.1–8) and part of the Legend of Apa Jeremias and Apa Johannes (pp.9–40) in Coptic, copied in the 9th or 10th century in Egypt. All folios have suffered from historic fire damage: shrinkage, curling and charring. These pages contain part of chapters eleven, twelve and thirteen from the legend of Apa Jeremias: the First encounter with the luxuries of King John, and Jeremias' perplexity (chapters 9–11) and King John's secret revealed to Jeremias (chapters 12–13). For the Coptic transcription and French translation see: Esbroeck, Michel van, 'La légende d'Apa Jeremias et Apa Johannes et les fragments Chester Beatty Copte 829,' Orientalia, 67.1 (1998): 1–63.

For the Coptic transcription and French translation see: Esbroeck, Michel van, 'La légende d'Apa Jeremias et Apa Johannes et les fragments Chester Beatty Copte 829,' Orientalia, 67.1 (1998): 1–63.

Cpt_1494_1.c: Small papyrus scroll containing an archival copy of a homiletic letter from Horsiesios addressed to the brothers of the Pachomian monastic community in Egypt, written in Sahidic Coptic and probably copied in the seventh century. Horsiesios (d. 387) was successor to Pachomius, founder of Christian cenobitic (communal) monasticism, as head of the Pachomian Koinonia. This manuscript is associated with a collection of material from the Pachomian monastic library (also known as the Dishna Papers or Bodmer Papyri), a portion of which was purchased by Beatty in 1956.

Cpt_1494_2.c: 21 unplaced fragments from a small papyrus scroll containing an archival copy of a homiletic letter from Horsiesios addressed to the brothers of the Pachomian monastic community in Egypt, written in Sahidic Coptic and probably copied in the seventh century. Horsiesios (d. 387) was successor to Pachomius, founder of Christian cenobitic (communal) monasticism, as head of the Pachomian Koinonia. This manuscript is associated with a collection of material from the Pachomian monastic library (also known as the Dishna Papers or Bodmer Papyri), a portion of which was purchased by Beatty in 1956.

Cpt_2013.c: Small parchment scroll (rotuli) containing an archival copy made for the Pachomian monastic library, probably at Phbow (Pbau), Egypt, of Theodore's Letter 2, on the annual remission of debts, written in Sahidic Coptic in the 6th century. Theodore (c. 314-386) was an early successor of Pachomius, the founder of Christian communal monasticism, as head of the whole community, centred at Phbow (modern Faw Qibla). The letter, entitled 'This is the letter from our father Theodore for the Remission', is a call to the annual meeting at the end of the year. It is associated with a collection of material from the Pachomian monastic library (also known as the Dishna Papers or Bodmer Papyri), a portion of which was purchased by Beatty in 1956.

Cpt_2022_1.c: Papyrus fragments preserving the Martyrdom of St Cephalon, an unknown Coptic martyr, executed under the prefect of Egypt, Clodius Culcianus. Text written in Sahidic Coptic in Egypt and dated to the 6th or 7th century AD. Text on both sides (presumably continuous) suggests the fragment originally formed part of a codex. The text features the prefect presiding over the martyr's trial, Cephalon the martyr, and a third figure whose name is broken, perhaps Eusebios. (See also Cpt 2065)

Cpt_2025_1.c: One of two frames containing fragments of two papyrus bifolios which preserve passages from a Lectionary. The text was written in Sahidic Coptic in Egypt. This plate includes text from Psalms 50:14-15, Matthew 4:3, 1 John 4:11-12 and fragments of Acts 13:26+.

Cpt_2025_2.c: One of two frames containing fragments of two papyrus bifolios which preserve passages from a Lectionary. The text was written in Sahidic Coptic in Egypt. This plate includes text from 1 John 4:14-16, Acts 13:26, 27-29, 31-33, Psalms 96:3-4 and Psalm 31:1-4.

Cpt_2026.t: Fragments of a homily or exhortation from an Easter Lectionary
Cpt_2026.c: Four papyrus fragments from a single folio, part of the Crosby-Schoyen Codex Ms 193. Written in Sahidic Coptic in Egypt, and dated to the 4th or 5th century AD. The full codex contained Melito of Sardis' On the Passover, Jonah the Prophet, Jewish Martyrs, Epistle of Peter, and an unidentified homily or supplication for mercy. It has been suggested that the codex was an Easter lectionary composed at a Pachomian monastery. According to the editors, the codex originally contained 68 leaves (or 146 pages). These fragments are from the fifth and final text and are part of the same folio as Ms 193 p.127, containing text from the homily or exhortation. Both Moses and the Pharaoh figure prominently. This text may have been composed by Pachomius or one of his successors, Theodore or Horsiesius.

Cpt_2027.c: Papyrus fragment with non-biblical text about Pilate, written in Bohairic Coptic in Egypt.

Cpt_2028.c: Fragments of papyrus folios which preserves text from the Martyrdom of Herai of Tamma, a twelve-year-old martyr. The text was written in Sahidic Coptic in Egypt. During the prefecture of Clodius Culcianus (c. 301-307 AD) a ship of Christian prisoners on route to trial at Antinopolis, dock at Tamma (Memphite) where Herai, the daughter of a presbyter, demands to be included among the prisoners. The prefect unsuccessfully attempts to dissuade her due to her age.

Cpt_2029_1.c: One of two frames containing fragments of two papyrus folios which preserve text from the Martydrom of Phoebammon, probably Phoebammon of Ausim (Letopolis). The text was written in Sahidic Coptic in Egypt. Phoebammon was the grandson of Antichous, prefect of Egypt under Valerian. During the time of Maximian (r. 286-305 AD), after lengthy trials and tortures, Phoebammon was beheaded at Tam(m)a.

Cpt_2029_2.c: One of two frames containing fragments of two papyrus folios which preserve text from the Martydrom of Phoebammon, probably Phoebammon of Ausim (Letopolis). The text was written in Sahidic Coptic in Egypt. Phoebammon was the grandson of Antichous, prefect of Egypt under Valerian. During the time of Maximian (r. 286-305 AD), after lengthy trials and tortures, Phoebammon was beheaded at Tam(m)a.

Cpt_2030.c: Fragments of two papyrus folios containing passages from the Martyrdom of Hermauo. The text was written in Sahidic Coptic in Egypt.

Cpt_2033_1.c: One of two frames containing eleven papyrus fragments which preserve text about Apa Pshoi of (the monastery of) Jeremias, an associate of Paul of Tamma(h). Text was written in Sahidic Coptic in Egypt and dated to the 5th century AD, composed and/or copied by Ezekiel (perhaps the disciple of Paul of Tammah).

Cpt_2033_2.c: One of two frames containing eleven papyrus fragments which preserve text about Apa Pshoi of (the monastery of) Jeremias, an associate of Paul of Tamma(h). Cpt_2034.t: Homily on the weakness of the flesh
Cpt_2034.c: Papyrus fragment preserving a homily on the weakness of the flesh, written in Sahidic Coptic in Egypt.

Cpt_2036.c: Eleven papyrus fragments, some with Coptic text on both sides, some with text on one side only, and some blank, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 6th centuries in Egypt. The fragments were written by at least four different scribes. Many appear to be Christian; one fragment mentions Abraham and God and another mentions a priest.

Cpt_2037.c: Eleven papyrus fragments with Coptic texts on front and back, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 8th centuries in Egypt. At least three different scribes, and one fragment is written in a business hand.

Cpt_2038.c: Six papyrus fragments from two unrelated folios, with Coptic texts on front and back, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 8th centuries in Egypt. The upper fragment contains the words 'kingdom' and 'he blessed'.

Cpt_2040.c: Two unrelated papyrus fragments with Coptic texts on front and back, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 8th centuries in Egypt. One fragment mentions angel names and the other mentions the cross of Christ.

Cpt_2041.c: Two papyrus fragments from a literary codex with Coptic texts on front and back, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 6th centuries in Egypt (possibly Thebes). The larger fragment is paginated: Λ (30).

Cpt_2042.c: Sixteen papyrus fragments with Sahidic Coptic texts on the front only, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 6th centuries in Egypt. The fragments are probably all from the same papyrus manuscript or document.

Cpt_2043.c: Fifteen papyrus fragments with Coptic or Greek texts on one side only, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 8th centuries in Egypt.

Cpt_2044.t: Papyrus fragments from Athanasius' letter to Dracontius
Cpt_2044.c: Nine papyrus fragments from a roll, with Coptic texts on the front only. The fragments preserve a portion of Athanasius' Letter to Dracontius (see Cpt 2047), from a scroll in the Montserrat collection (P . Monts Roca inv. 14), written in Coptic in the 4th century in Egypt.

Cpt_2045.c: Nineteen papyrus fragments from a codex written in two columns, with Sahidic Coptic texts on front and back, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 6th centuries in Egypt. The fragments include portions of the Passion homily (Peri Pasha) of Melito of Sardis, from what is known as the 'Crosby-Schoyen codex' (MS 193) (see Cpt 2046).

Cpt_2046.c: Twenty-four papyrus fragments preserving unidentified literary texts (most blank on the reverse), written in Sahidic Coptic in Egypt.

Cpt_2047.c: Forty-seven papyrus fragments preserving some portions of Athanasius' Letter to Dracontius dated to the 4th century AD (see Cpt 2044) and other unidentified literary texts (many blank on the reverse), written in Sahidic Coptic in Egypt.

Cpt_2048.c: Fragment of a papyrus folio from a codex, with Fayyumic Coptic text on front and back in two columns, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 6th centuries in Egypt. The text contains authoritative pronouncements about Sunday.

Cpt_2049.t: Papyrus fragments possibly from a letter
Cpt_2049.c: Eight papyrus fragments written in Coptic cursive scribe on the front only, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 6th centuries in Egypt, possibly preserving portions of a private letter.

Cpt_2050.t: Papyrus fragments possibly from a homily
Cpt_2050.c: Twenty-five papyrus fragments from a roll with Coptic text on the recto only, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 6th centuries in Egypt. As Easter is mentioned the fragments may preserve part of a homily, perhaps Melito's Paschal Homily.

Cpt_2051.c: Two papyrus fragments with Greek and Coptic texts on front and back, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 8th centuries in Egypt. The upper fragment is written in Coptic and includes a gloss with 'faith, hope, charity' written in the upper margin and 'Moses, Solomon, David' in the left margin. The lower fragment is written in Greek, with different orientations on either side, 'Christ' is written on one and 'the kingdom of ... on earth' is written on the other side.

Cpt_2052.c: Papyrus fragments preserving an unidentified literary text, written in Sahidic Coptic in Egypt.

Cpt_2053.c: Four papyrus fragments from two different folios preserving an unidentified literary text, written in Sahidic Coptic in Egypt.

Cpt_2054.c: Four papyrus fragments with Coptic and Greek texts on front and back, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 6th centuries in Egypt. Three fragments are written in Coptic including one with text from Mark 1.21, and one which is paginated; one fragment is written in Greek and mentions bread.

Cpt_2055.t: Parchment fragments from a homily citing Revelation 4
Cpt_2055.c: Fifteen parchment fragments with Coptic text on back and front, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 8th centuries in Egypt. The fragments preserve part of a homily citing Revelation 4; from a codex written in two columns. Evidence of damage from a fire.

Cpt_2056.c: Papyrus fragment from an unidentified literary text, written in Sahidic Coptic in Egypt.

Cpt_2059.c: Twenty-three papyrus fragments with Sahidic Coptic texts on front and back, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 6th centuries in Egypt. The fragments preserve portions of Luke (frag 8: 6.9-10, 14-15 and pagination; frag 6: 11.1-2, 6-7; frag 9: 11.49-52, 53-12.3 and 2 Corinthians (frag 2: 4.12-17, 18-5.4; frag 12: 6.17-7.4, 5-8), and pagination; and are from a codex of the Gospel of Luke and 2 Corinthians (see Pap 2028 and Cpt 2024).

Cpt_2060.c: Twenty-one papyrus fragments with Sahidic Coptic texts on front and back, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 6th centuries in Egypt. The fragments preserve portions of Luke (frag 21: 2:38, 43-44 and pagination; frag 10: 3.7-13, 14-4:2 and pagination) and pagination (frags 11 and 22), and are from a codex of the Gospel of Luke and 2 Corinthians (see Pap 2028 and Cpt 2024).

Cpt_2062.c: Nine papyrus fragments with Sahidic Coptic texts on front and back, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 6th centuries in Egypt. The fragments preserve portions of Luke (frag 7: 5.25-27, 30-32; frag 5: 9.18-19, 22; frags 2/4: 11.48-52, 53-12.3) and 2 Corinthians (frag 6: 5.10-11, 15-16; frag 1: 8.10-14, 14-20 and pagination); and are from a codex of the Gospel of Luke and 2 Corinthians (see Pap 2028 and Cpt 2024).

Cpt_2063.t: Papyrus fragments including Luke 1.63, 1.70; 4.8, 13-15; 4.28-29, 34 and 2 Corinthians title, 1.1, 1.6; 4.12-17, 4.18-5.4; 11.22, 26
Cpt_2063.c: Fourteen papyrus fragments with Sahidic Coptic texts on front and back, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 6th centuries in Egypt. The fragments preserve pagination and titling including portions of Luke (frag 9: 1.63, 1.70; frag 10: 4.8, 13-15; frag 13: 4.28-29, 34), pagination (frags 11 and 7) and 2 Corinthians (frag 12: title, 1.1, 1.6; frag 4: 4.12-17, 4.18-5.4; frag 2: 11.22, 26), and are from a codex of the Gospel of Luke and 2 Corinthians (see Pap 2028 and Cpt 2024).

Cpt_2064.t: Papyrus fragments of Luke 2.18-21, 23-25 and 2 Corinthians 4.12-17, 4.18-5.4; 6.17-7.4, 7.5-8
Cpt_2064.c: Four papyrus fragments with Sahidic Coptic text on front and back, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 6th centuries in Egypt. The fragments preserve portions of Luke (frag 2: 2.18-21, 23-25) and 2 Corinthians (frag 4: 4.12-17, 4.18-5.4; frags 1 and 3: 6.17-7.4, 7.5-8), and are from a codex of the Gospel of Luke and 2 Corinthians (see Pap 2028 and Cpt 2024).

Cpt_2065.c: Papyrus fragments preserving the Martyrdom of St Cephalon, an unknown Coptic martyr, executed under the prefect of Egypt, Clodius Culcianus. Text written in Sahidic Coptic in Egypt and dated to the 6th or 7th century AD. Text on both sides (presumably continuous) suggests the fragment originally formed part of a codex. The text features the prefect presiding over the martyr's trial, Cephalon the martyr, and a third figure whose name is broken, perhaps Eusebios. (See also Cpt 2022)

Cpt_2066.t: Papyrus fragments of Luke 18.1-11, 13-15 and 2 Corinthians 3.7-13, 14-4.2
Cpt_2066.c: Two papyrus fragments with Sahidic Coptic texts on front and back, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 6th centuries in Egypt. The fragments preserve portions of Luke (frag 2: 18.1-11, 13-15) and 2 Corinthians (frag 1: 3.7-13, 14-4.2 with pagination), and are from a codex with the Gospel of Luke and 2 Corinthians (see Pap 2028 and Cpt 2024).

Cpt_2067.c: Papyrus roll preserving with Coptic magical texts on front and back, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 6th centuries in Egypt. Christian amulet with some Greek formulae as well as Coptic prayers, invocations to Gabriel and Iao and 2 wing formations based on Ablanathanalba and Achramachamari.

Cpt_2068.c: Papyrus roll preserving with Coptic magical texts on front and back, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 6th centuries in Egypt. Probably a Christian amulet.

Cpt_2070.t: Papyrus fragment possibly from a letter
Cpt_2070.c: Papyrus fragment with Coptic text on both sides, possibly from a letter with the address on the back, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 6th centuries in Egypt.

Cpt_2071.c: About 38 papyrus fragments with Coptic text on front and back, probably literary texts, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 8th centuries in Egypt.

Cpt_2072.c: Thirty-eight mostly blank papyrus fragments made in Egypt, possibly from fragmentary Coptic manuscripts in the collection.

Cpt_2073.t: Papyrus fragments from the Acts of Peter
Cpt_2073.c: Seven papyrus fragments with Sahidic Coptic text on both sides, preserving part of the story of Marcellus from the Acts of Peter, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 6th centuries in Egypt.

Heb_752.c: Samaritan Pentateuch written on parchment by the copyist and liturgical hymn author Abisha ibn Pinhas ibn Joseph, dated 740 AH (1339-1340 AD), see folios 238-253. The text is arranged as a one-letter manuscript (with some instances of two-letter spacing), where justification was achieved by detaching a letter from the first and last words of each line. The manuscript retains notes from previous owners and deeds of sale on f.69: 23 Rajab 1308 AH (4 March 1891 AD), f.129: Jumada II 887 AH (July/August 1482 AD), f.169v: undated, two on f.227: Shawwal 844 AH (February/March 1441 AD) and 1308 AH (1890/1891 AD), and f.276v: 867 AH (1462/1463 AD). Signs of kissing are found on f.140v (Leviticus 9.22-10.1), f.179 (Numbers 6.21-23) and f.209v (Numbers 25.10).

Heb_753_1.c: Fragment of a Samaritan Pentateuch comprising 4 bifolios (16 pages) containing Numbers 3.36–9.15, written on parchment and dated to between the 14th and early 16th centuries. It is a 'two-letter' manuscript, where justification was achieved by detaching the first letter from the first word and the last two letters from the final word of each line.

Heb_753_2.c: Fragment of a Samaritan Pentateuch comprising 3 bifolios (12 pages) containing Exodus 2.21–7.26, written on parchment and dated to between the 14th and early 16th centuries. It is a 'two-letter' manuscript, where justification was achieved by detaching the first letter from the first word and the last two letters from the final word of each line.

Heb_753_3_1.c: Folio from a Samaritan Pentateuch containing Numbers 26.7–27, written on parchment and dated to between the 14th and early 16th centuries. It is a 'two-letter' type manuscript, where justification was maintained by detaching two letters from the final word of each line to square the text.

Heb_753_3_2.c: Folio from a Samaritan Pentateuch containing Numbers 31.13–32.1, written on parchment and dated to between the 14th and early 16th centuries. Separator dots or colons appear at the end of almost every line and some separation of the letters occurs to maintain justification but it is not consistent.

Heb_753_4.t: Genesis 41.39–42.13 and 43.22–44.17 from a Samaritan Pentateuch
Heb_753_4.c: Bifolio from a Samaritan Pentateuch containing Genesis 41.39–42.13 and 43.22–44.17, written on parchment and dated to between the 14th and early 16th centuries. Justification is achieved by detaching the first letter of the first word and the last letter or two of the final word of each line.

Heb_753_5.t: Leviticus 20.1–21.15 and 24.4–25.27 from a Samaritan Pentateuch
Heb_753_5.c: Bifolio from a Samaritan Pentateuch containing Leviticus Leviticus 20.1–21.15 and 24.4–25.27, written on parchment and dated to between the 14th and early 16th centuries. Justification was achieved by detaching the first letter from the first word and the last letter from the final word of each line.

Heb_754.c: Folio from a Samaritan Pentateuch containing Exodus 8.2-9.17, written on parchment, in the 15th or 16th century probably in Palestine, Syria or Israel. Vertical and horizontal guide lines were impressed on the page to assist the scribe. It is a 'two-letter' manuscript, where symmetry is maintained by detaching two letters from the final word of each line to square the text.

Heb_755.t: Deuteronomy 9.7–11.12 and 12.17–14.28 from a Samaritan Pentateuch
Heb_755.c: Three bifolios (12 pages) from a single quire of a Samaritan Pentateuch containing portions of Deuteronomy written in Samaritan majuscule on paper, and dated to the 14th–17th centuries. The central bifolio (4 pages) of the quire is missing. The first letter of the first word and the last letter of the last word on each line is separated for text justification.

Heb_761.c: Hebrew Yemenite Pentateuch, with great Mazhor and small Mazhor, written on paper in Yemeni semi square script and dated to the 14th century. The combination of historic water and insect damage has caused the spine area to 'block' together into sections, leaving much of the manuscript inaccessible for handling, display and digitisation. However, folios 335-353, which were in better condition, have been fully conserved and are accessible (see Heb 761.1).

Heb_761_1.c: Folios 335–353 from a Hebrew Yemenite Pentateuch, with great Mazhor and small Mazhor, written on paper in Yemeni semi square script and dated to the 14th century.

Heb_762.t: Treatise on Astronomy (Sefer Ha-Tekhuna) by Hayyim Vital
Heb_762.c: Manuscript containing a Treatise on Astronomy (Sefer Ha-Tekhuna) by Hayyim Vital (1542–1620), written in Hebrew in a rabbinic script in Damascus in the early 17th century. It contains 17 diagrams in gold, red and blue, with titles in gold. Two previous owners signed the first folio: Raphael Mosche Galico and Hayyim de Rosa, both Jewish kabbalists based in Damascus in the 18th century. Hayyim Vital was a prominent kabbalist and the chief disciple of Isaac Luria in Safed (Israel), whose teachings are primarily known through Vital’s compendium, Etz Hayyim (Tree of Life). This treatise is one of Vital’s own works.

Heb_763.c: Esther scroll (Megilat Ester) written in Hebrew on parchment in an Italian square script with Ashkenazi traits and tagin (crowns), probably made in Italy in the 18th century. The parchment is divided into 'pages' with folds at regular intervals. The beginning of the roll is scalloped and tapers to a point with attached leather strap, but is otherwise undecorated. The Book of Esther recounts the story of the salvation of the Jews in the Persian Empire through the actions of the eponymous heroine. The text is read in synagogues on the spring holiday of Purim (Festival of Lots).

Heb_764.c: Festival prayer book (Mahzor) written on parchment in Hebrew in an Italian square script and dated to the 14th or 15th century, with an illuminated frontispiece and Italianesque red and blue penwork throughout. The lower border of the frontispiece contains an unidentified coat of arms of a lion or rampant on a field of azure.

Heb_765.c: Esther scroll (Megilat Ester) written in Hebrew on parchment in an Italian square script, probably made in Italy in the 18th century. The beginning of the sroll is rounded and the other end is attached to a wooden roller. Each 'page' or column of text is decorated with a border painted with an orange pigment. The Book of Esther recounts the story of the salvation of the Jews in the Persian Empire through the actions of the eponymous heroine. The text is read in synagogues on the spring holiday of Purim (Festival of Lots).

Heb_766.c: Esther scroll (Megilat Ester) written in Hebrew on parchment in an Italian square script with tagin (crowns), probably made in Italy in the 18th or 19th century. The Book of Esther recounts the story of the salvation of the Jews in the Persian Empire through the actions of the eponymous heroine. The text is read in synagogues on the spring holiday of Purim (Festival of Lots).

Heb_767.c: Large portion of a Sefer Torah on vellum containing Genesis to Exodus 39, written in Hebrew in an Ashkenazic square script possibly in Italy, and dated to the 19th century. It retains one wooden roller.

Heb_768.c: Esther scroll (Megilat Ester) written in Hebrew on parchment in an Italian square script with tagin (crowns), probably made in Italy in the 18th century. The 'pages' or columns of text are divided by painted borders. Its silver case is housed separately (Heb 768.1). The Book of Esther recounts the story of the salvation of the Jews in the Persian Empire through the actions of the eponymous heroine. The text is read in synagogues on the spring holiday of Purim (Festival of Lots).

Heb_768_1.t: Silver case for an Esther scroll (Megillah)
Heb_768_1.c: Embossed silver case for an Esther scroll (Megillah) probably made in Italy and dated to the 18th century. It is decorated with scroll work, floral design and an unidentified coat of arms ornamented with the 'hands of Cohen' and surmounted by a crown. The scroll was originally housed within the case, and when read was unfurled through the vertical slot then rerolled using the silver roller still attached to the scroll (see CBL Heb 768).

Heb_769.c: Esther scroll (Megalit Ester) written in Hebrew on parchment in an Italian square script with tagin (crowns), probably made in Italy in the 18th century. The very beginning of the scroll is not preserved. The Book of Esther recounts the story of the salvation of the Jews in the Persian Empire through the actions of the eponymous heroine. The text is read in synagogues on the spring holiday of Purim (Festival of Lots).

Heb_770.c: Esther scroll (Megalit Ester) written in Hebrew on parchment (sheep skin) in an Italian square script with tagin (crowns), probably made in Italy in the 18th or 19th century, attached to a single wooden roller. The Book of Esther recounts the story of the salvation of the Jews in the Persian Empire through the actions of the eponymous heroine. The text is read in synagogues on the spring holiday of Purim (Festival of Lots).

Heb_771_1.c: Small scroll on parchment containing the Shema Yisrael prayer and two verses from Exodus (column 1: Exodus 13.1-10; column 2: Exodus 13.11-14; column 3: Deut 6.4-9 (shema), probably dated to the 19th century. Traditionally, mezuzah scrolls include both Deuteronomy 6 and 11 on a single parchment, while a head-tefillin/phylatery box contains fours biblical texts (Deuteronomy 6 and 11 and two passages from Exodus 13) each written on individual parchments; the arm-phylactery contains all four passages on a single parchment.

Heb_771_2.c: Small scroll on parchment containing the Shema Yisrael prayer (Deuteronomy 11.13-21), probably dated to the 19th century. Traditionally, mezuzah scrolls include both Deuteronomy 6 and 11 on a single parchment, while a head-tefillin/phylatery box contains fours biblical texts (Deuteronomy 6 and 11 and two passages from Exodus 13) each written on individual parchments; the arm-phylactery contains all four passages on a single parchment.

Heb_771_3.c: Mezuza ('doorpost') on parchment containing the Shema Yisrael prayer (Deut 6.4-9 and 11.13-21), probably dated to the 19th century. Traditionally, mezuzah scrolls include both Deuteronomy 6 and 11 on a single parchment.

Heb_772.c: Illuminated Hebrew Bible (Tanakh) on vellum, written in an Italian square script in Italy and dated to the 14th or 15th century, ornamented with Italianesque red and blue penwork throughout and bound in a contemporary leather binding. Bookplate of a previous owner, Baron Horace de Landau (1824-1903), on lower cover paste-down.

Heb_773.c: Almost complete Sefer Torah on parchment containing Genesis 21:10 to the end, written in Hebrew in a Sefardic square script possibly in Italy, and dated to the 17th or 18th century.

Heb_774.c: Portion of a Sefer Torah on parchment containing Deuteronomy 9:13-33:19 written in Hebrew in a Sefardic square script, and dated to the 17th century.

Heb_775_1.c: Fragment of a Sefer Torah containing Genesis 1.1-31.19, written in Hebrew in an Italian square script in Italy in the 18th or 19th century.

Heb_775_2.c: Fragment of a Sefer Torah containing Genesis 10.21-14.10, written in Hebrew in an Italian square script in Italy in the 18th or 19th century.

Heb_776_1.c: Portion of a Sefer Torah on parchment containing Leviticus written in Hebrew in an Italian square script and made in Italy in the second half of the 18th century. The manuscript is preserved in two parts with the second portion containing Numbers 21.9-29.19.

Heb_776_2.c: Portion of a Sefer Torah on parchment containing Numbers 21.9-29.19 written in Hebrew in an Italian square script and made in Italy in the second half of the 18th century. The manuscript is preserved in two parts with the first portion containing Leviticus.

Heb_777.c: Sefer Torah on parchment written in Hebrew in a Sefardic square script in the 18th century.

Heb_778.c: A 19th-century book of remembrances or memorial book (Yizkor book) for the family of Judah ben Menahem. The title on the wooden cover says 'The Book of Life', a typical euphemism for a book commemorating the dead, with a crude carving of the tomb of Rachel. Ten members of the family are included, each with their name and date of death followed by longer Yizkor passages. Dates range from 1838 (Judah ben Menahem) to 1887 (Keyle Marcus). The illustration on f.1 is dated 1889.

Heb_779.t: Just measure (Kav ha-Yashar) and Orchard of pomegranates (Pardes Rimonim)
Heb_779.c: Paper folio with text written in Hebrew in an Oriental script, copied in the 18th or 19th century by a non-professional scribe in North Africa or the Middle East. The recto appears to be the title page for Kav ha-Yashar (Just measure) and a prayer from Pardes Rimonim (Orchard of pomegranates) is written on the verso. The title on the recto, ספר קב הישר (Sefer Kav ha-Yashar), is written beneath בשם רחמן (in the name of the Merciful One). Below this the scribe has written 'I am hereby beginning to write the Sefer Kav ha-Yashar, with the help of the Name (=God)', followed by a blessing on anyone who reads it (spelled incorrectly) and a curse on anyone who steals it. The drawing is probably a series of columns in emulation of contemporary printed-book title pages, with the beginning of the alphabet written in the damaged right-hand panel. Beneath the title for Kav ha-Yashar on the verso is a prayer from the Kabbalistic work Pardes Rimonim (An orchard of pomegranates).

In_02.c: Stars of the Sciences (Nujum al-'ulum). This is an encyclopaedic survey of astrology and astral magic. Composed in Bijapur, apparently by Sultan `Ali `Adil Shah himself, the text interweaves many different cosmological accounts of the heavens and the earth, including Islamic and Hindu traditions. There are almost 400 paintings, charts and diagrams, of constellations, planets, angels, talismans and other cosmic and earthly forces. Codex, 348 folios, ink, colours and gold on paper, black leather binding, Persian text with 365 paintings, composed by Sultan `Ali `Adil Shah (r.1557-1579), Bijapur, India, dated 14 Rabi` I 978H, 1570. The manuscript lacks a full colophon, and is not complete.

In_03.t: The history of Akbar (Akbarnama), by Abu'l-Fazl `Allami
In_03.c: The history of Akbar (Akbarnama), by Abu'l-Fazl `Allami. The Akbarnama was composed by Akbar's court historian, minister and friend, Abu’l-Fazl `Allami. This codex forms volume two and part of volume three of the biography of the Mughal emperor Akbar (r. 1556-1605), covering the years 1556 to 1579. Volume one is now in the British Library (Or. 12988). Codex, ink, colours and gold on paper, 213 folios, Persian text in nasta`liq script, with illuminated headings (fols. 1v, 177v, for start of volumes 2 and 3) and 3 paintings (fols. 177r, 212r, 212v), the History of Akbar (Akbarnama), by Abu’l-Fazl ibn Mubarak `Allami (1551-1602), covering Mughal emperor Akbar's biography for the years 1556-1579, unsigned (no colophon), tooled leather binding signed Muhammad Zaman `Abbasi, Agra, India, undated, c. 1603-1605. Also in this museum are 58 folios (with full colour and nim qalam paintings) detached from this codex, and four further paintings pasted onto folios from Farhang-i Jahangiri, purchased

In_03_1.t: The coronation of Akbar in February 1556, from the History of Akbar (Akbarnama), by Abu'l-Fazl

In_03_1.c: The coronation of Akbar in February 1556, folio from the History of Akbar (Akbarnama) by Abu’l-Fazl. Detached folio, ink, pigments and gold on paper, Persian text with tinted drawing (nim qalam) attributed to Madhu, Agra, India, c. 1603-1605. This is one of fifty-eight folios now detached from its codex (Chester Beatty In 03). A slave from Balkh worked as a falconer for a rich merchant, and became embittered when the merchant's wife ignored his attentions. As revenge, he taught two green parrots to repeat an accusation (in the Balkhi language) about the wife cheating on her husband with someone else (the household porter): the first painting here shows the devious falconer handing the parrots to his master as a gift. The second painting shows the parrots repeating the slander in front of the merchant's guests at a banquet: the merchant doesn't understand the language, but some of the guests translate it - to general consternation. This folio is from a copy of a highly-regarded Persian text, written by Husayn Va`izi Kashifi (d.1504-05), a preacher and scholar at the Timurid court in Herat (modern Afghanistan).

In_04_36.c: The monkey king meets the river tortoise, by Shankar Gujarati, from Lights of Canopus (Anvār-i Suhaylī) by Ḥusayn Vā`iẓ Kāshifī. Writing in a sophisticated court style, Kāshifī composed an updated version of these lively animal fables, which have a long transmission history going back to Persian, Arabic and Sanskrit texts. In this story, Kardana the wise monkey king has been removed from power, and gone quietly into exile. He makes a new life living on a river island, where he passes the time throwing figs from the tree into the water below. A river tortoise comes to eat the fallen figs. The monkey and tortoise begin talking, and over time the two become friends, meeting every day. In_04_40.t: The tortoise swims with the monkey king on his back, by Payāg, from Lights of Canopus (Anvār-i Suhaylī) by Ḥusayn Vā`iẓ Kāshifī
In_04_40.c: The tortoise swims with the monkey king on his back, by Payāg, from Lights of Canopus (Anvār-i Suhaylī) by Ḥusayn Vā`iẓ Kāshifī. Writing in a sophisticated court style, Kāshifī composed an updated version of these lively animal fables, which have a long transmission history going back to Persian, Arabic and Sanskrit texts. In this story, Kardana the wise monkey king has made a new life in exile, living on a river island, where he becomes close friends with a river tortoise. This takes a dark turn when the tortoise’s wife become suspicious of her husband’s regular absence, and doesn’t believe his explanation. She pretends to be fatally ill, telling her worried husband that the only known cure is a monkey’s heart. The tortoise invites Kardana to climb on his back, to swim across the river: once they have left shore, he glumly admits his plan to kill his friend for his heart. In_04_41.t: The monkey king returns safely to his fig tree, by `Āṣī, from Lights of Canopus (Anvār-i Suhaylī) by Ḥusayn Vā`iẓ Kāshifī
In_04_41.c: The monkey king returns safely to his fig tree, by `Āṣī, from Lights of Canopus (Anvār-i Suhaylī) by Ḥusayn Vā`iẓ Kāshifī. Writing in a sophisticated court style, Kāshifī composed an updated version of these lively animal fables, which have a long transmission history going back to Persian, Arabic and Sanskrit texts. In this story, Kardana the wise monkey king has made a new life in exile, living on a river island, where he becomes close friends with a river tortoise. Their friendship ends after the tortoise tries to trick the monkey, but is outwitted in return. The tortoise invites Kardana to climb on his back, to swim across the river: once they have left shore, he glumly admits his plan to kill his friend. He has been fooled into believing that a monkey’s heart is the only cure for his wife’s pretended illness. In_04_74.c: Solomon takes advice from the animals, folio from Lights of Canopus (Anvar-i Suhayli), a reworking of the animal fables Kalila and Dimna (Kalila wa Dimna), composed by Husayn Va`izi Kashifi. Solomon was known for his great wisdom, and for his ability to speak with all creatures. One day, he had the opportunity to drink the water of life, and to live forever. Hesitating, he decided first to take advice from the animals and birds. They all gathered at his court, and discussed the great decision. The heron advised the king not to choose immortality. There was only enough water for one person, the bird said, so if Solomon were to drink it, then he would outlive everyone he loved. In_07A_6.t: Portrait of Shāhnavāz Khān Ṣafavī (d. 1659) by Hāshim (recto), Persian calligraphy by Mīr `Alī (verso), folio from the Minto Album
In_07A_6.c: Portrait of Shāhnavāz Khān Ṣafavī (d. 1659) by Hāshim (recto), Persian calligraphy by Mīr `Alī (verso), folio from the Minto Album. Many of the Mughal emperors ordered full-length profile portraits of senior court figures, arranged together in albums (muraqqa`). Son of Iranian exile Mirza Rustam Safavi, Shahnawaz Khan Safavi had served Shah Jahan as a military officer and government official close to the royal family. Towards the end of his life, Shah Jahan was imprisoned by his rebellious son Awrangzib, who killed the heir apparent Dara Shikoh (his brother) in 1659, and took control. Shahnawaz Khan was killed in battle the same year, fighting Awrangzib in the war of succession. This portrait was in the captive Shah Jahan's possession, presumably in an intact royal album. The emperor wrote a note beside the painting (on the left): "A likeness of the martyred Shahnawaz Khan, the best of Mirza Rustam’s sons". In_07A_10.t: Shah Jahan on a globe with his four sons, by Balchand (recto), Persian calligraphy by Mir `Ali (verso), folio from the Minto Album
In_07A_10.c: Shah Jahan on a globe with his four sons, signed Balchand (recto), Persian calligraphy signed Mir `Ali (verso), folio from the Minto Album. In this allegorical family portrait, Shah Jahan stands on the globe, with his haloed head in profile and two hovering putti in the clouds above holding a crown. The emperor's four young sons stand around him: (from right) Dara Shikoh offering a tray of jewels, Muradbakhsh, Awrangzib (the next Mughal ruler) and Shah Shuja holding a jewelled turban ornament. Behind the boys, a Persian inscription runs from right to left, praising Shah Jahan and comparing his power to that of the sun. The "Minto Album" refers to a set of forty album pages, now in the collections of the Chester Beatty and the Victoria and Albert Museum (London). In_07A_15.t: Persian prose calligraphy by Mīr `Alī (recto), Jahāngīr shooting the head of Malik Ambar, by Abū al-Ḥasan (verso), folio from the Minto Album
In_07A_15.c: Persian prose calligraphy by Mir `Ali (recto), Jahangir shooting the head of Malik Ambar, by Abu'l-Hasan (verso), folio from the Minto Album. Full of imperial wishful thinking and cosmic allegory, this profile portrait of Jahangir depicts the emperor shooting an arrow at the head of his formidable political enemy, Malik Ambar (1548-1626), the East African-born chief minister and army commander for the Nizamshahi sultanate of Ahmadnagar, in the Deccan. In fact, Malik Ambar lived into old age, a respected leader whose monuments in Khirki (re-named Awrangabad by the Mughals) still stand. On his death in 1626 (ten years after this painting), Jahangir's diarist noted that Malik Ambar "had no equal in warfare, in command, in sound judgment, and in administration". This painting is therefore a Mughal allegory about seizing power, and a fantasy of hatred. Owls (unlucky in Islamic culture) flutter around Malik Ambar's head. In_07A_17.t: Persian and Chaghatay Turkish calligraphy by Mir `Ali (recto), youth with swans and rabbits, by `Abd al-Karim (verso), folio from the Minto Album
In_07A_17.c: Persian and Chaghatay Turkish calligraphy by Mir `Ali (recto), youth with swans and rabbits, by `Abd al-Karim (verso), folio from the Minto Album. A young man stands in a complex landscape setting, holding up a book. Two swans and two collared rabbits are by his feet. Behind him in the rocky landscape are domed buildings, a shepherd and flock, and a red-sailed ship approached by a small boat. Inscribed (not signed) as "the work of the Wonder of the Age, master `Abd al-Karim", the painting was probably produced in the Deccani sultanate of Ibrahim `Adil Shah II (r. 1579-1627). Painted in a different tone to Mughal works, Deccani paintings were known and admired in Mughal contexts, and artworks were sent as diplomatic gifts. For example when Ibrahim's daughter married Jahangir's brother Daniyal in 1601, 2,000 volumes were sent from Bijapur to the Mughal court. In_07A_18.t: Youth by a flowering tree, by Farrukh Beg (recto), Persian and Chaghatay Turkish calligraphy by Mir `Ali (verso), folio from the Minto Album
a: Farrukh Beg, attributed to; Mir `Ali Haravi
In_07A_18.c: Youth by a flowering tree, by Farrukh Beg (recto), Persian and Chaghatay Turkish calligraphy by Mir `Ali (verso), folio from the Minto Album. A young man stands by flowering trees, holding a striped sash. Looking toward the right, he may have been painted as a deliberate pendant to a Bijpuri painting of another young man (In 07A.17), attributed to `Abd al-Karim. Mughal emperor Jahangir added the side-note (right), stating that this is "the work of Farrukh Beg, who drew it in his seventieth year", dateable to 1615. A notably flexible artist, Farrukh Beg had come to the Mughal court from Kabul in 1585, and worked on manuscript projects for Jahangir's father Akbar. On the other side of this folio, the sixteenth-century Persian calligraphy of Mir `Ali has been embellished by a Mughal painter with a lively backdrop of colourful birds among trees. The "Minto Album" refers to a set of forty album pages, now in the collections of the Chester Beatty and the Victoria and Albert Museum (London).

In_07A_19.t: Mughal emperors Akbar, Jahangir and Shah Jahan with their ministers, by Bichitr (recto), foliate design in gold (verso), folio from the Minto Album
In_07A_19.c: Mughal emperors Akbar, Jahangir and Shah Jahan with their ministers, by Bichitr (recto), foliate design in gold (verso), folio from the Minto Album. This allegorical group portrait outlines the importance of succession to the emperor Shah Jahan (seated on the right). Three Mughal generations are seated under a canopy: Akbar (r. 1555-1605) in the centre, his son Jahangir (r. 1605-1627) on the left, and Jahangir's son Shah Jahan (r. 1628-58) on the right. Akbar hands a jewelled crown not to his actual successor Jahangir, but to his grandson Shah Jahan: this anachronism underlines the current ruler's dynastic legitimacy. Before the thrones stand the three rulers' respective chief ministers: from left to right I‘timaduddawla (d. 1622, served Jahangir), Mirza `Aziz Koka Khan-i A'zam (d. 1624, served Akbar), and Abu'l-Hasan Asaf Khan (d. 1641, served Shah Jahan). In_07B_21.c: Persian calligraphy (recto), equestrian portrait of Akbar (verso), folio from the Late Shah Jahan Album. This portrait of the Mughal emperor Akbar was commissioned during the reign of his grandson Shah Jahan, long after Akbar's death in 1605. Later portraits of Akbar always repeat the three-quarter face pose of portraits made during his lifetime, even though imperial Mughal portrait style had since shifted to strict profiles. In the original album layout, this equestrian portrait may have been mounted opposite a similar portrait of Shah Jahan (Goenka Collection): the two emperors facing each other across the page-opening. The calligraphy side, in turn, may have faced a very similar folio (Washington, DC, Freer-Sackler S1986.91), signed by the calligrapher Mir `Ali Haravi (d. 1544). This folio comes from an imperial Mughal Indian album, produced for Shah Jahan towards the end of his reign (c. 1650-1658), and referred to as the “Late Shah Jahan Album”. In_07B_22.t: Portrait of a nobleman in purple jama and orange turban (recto), Persian calligraphy by Mir `Ali (verso), from the Late Shah Jahan Album
In_07B_22.c: Portrait of a nobleman in purple jama and orange turban (recto), Persian calligraphy by Mir `Ali (verso), folio from the Late Shah Jahan Album. This folio comes from an imperial Mughal Indian album, produced for Shah Jahan towards the end of his reign (c. 1650-1658), and referred to as the “Late Shah Jahan Album”. Now dismantled, the album’s grand format folios are today dispersed in public and private collections worldwide, with twenty folios in the Chester Beatty. The album layout was planned with matching artworks facing each other: calligraphy opposite calligraphy, paintings opposite paintings. These artworks are rarely contemporary with the album project: they have been assembled, and are presented together as a carefully curated collection. As with other Mughal albums, the borders are a very significant part of the Late Shah Jahan Album’s presentation, with a consistent visual theme continuing throughout the folios. In_11A_10.c: Indian vulture. This careful study of an Indian (or long-billed) vulture is based closely on an earlier Mughal album-painting, by the artist Mansur, dateable c. 1620 (New York: Met 55.121.10.12v). Another version (attributed to the nineteenth century) is also known (Washington, DC: Freer-Sackler F1948.19v). Such repetitions confirm the enduring power of Mansur's work, but also reveal information about the trajectory of the original album-folio, during the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. Folio, ink, colours and gold on paper, mounted on gold-flecked album page, an Indian vulture (also called the long-billed vulture) perched on a rock against blank backdrop, probably copied from a seventeenth-century Mughal painting by Mansur, mounted here with Persian verses from Sa`di's Gulistan above and below the painting, unsigned, India, c. 1700-1750.

In_11A_20.c: Prince at a hunting encampment. This group scene focuses on the couple in the centre: the prince with the wine cup, as the woman holds up a small saucer, suggesting that she has just offered the drink to him. While the others sit calmly, one other woman lies dismayed on the cushions beside them, perhaps in jealous reaction. Folio, colours and gold on paper, mounted on album page, a prince at an enclosed hunting encampment, sitting with a small group of men (on the left) and women (on the right), taking a wine-cup from the woman beside him, attributed to Payag, Agra, India, painting c. 1650-1660, album c. 1750-1800.

In_11A_22.t: Portrait of Shah Jahan on a globe
In_11A_22.c: Portrait of Shah Jahan on a globe. Painting, ink, colours and gold on paper, allegorical portrait of Shah Jahan (r. 1628-1658) holding out an octagonal jewel, with angels (European style putti) holding royal emblems of a sword, crown and parasol (chhatri, inscribed with his imperial genealogy) in the clouds above, and on the globe beneath his feet is a pair of weighing scales (representing justice under Shah Jahan's rule), a lion resting with a sheep (representing harmony), and two groups of religious men with rosaries, each holding up an inscribed scroll praising the emperor as the "friend of dervishes", close copy of a 1629 portrait (dated 1038H, attributed to Hashim, Freer-Sackler F1939.49a), India, undated, possibly c. 1800-1850.

In_11A_24.t: Two rulers feasting at an encampment
In_11A_24.c: Two rulers feasting at an encampment. Folio, colours and gold on paper, full-page painting of two rulers drinking together on one throne, surrounded by an entourage of companions, servants, musicians and huntsmen, inscribed (over the two rulers, on the tent panels) "Khusrau Parviz" and "Qaysar-e Rum", composition copied closely from an (unidentified) earlier c. 1590 manuscript, signed (in gold against the dark encampment wall, to right and left) "naqalahu" (copied it) `Ali Quli, India, undated, c. 1615.

In_11A_31.c: Yogini with a mynah bird, from the Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah Album. In_11A_69.t: Women playing on a rock slide
In_11A_69.c: Women playing on a rock slide, album-page from Lucknow. In_16.c: Ocean of Immortality (Bahr al-Hayat), by Muhammad Ghwath Gwaliori (d. 1562). This book consists of ten chapters explaining the philosophy of hatha yoga, with paintings showing twenty-one different positions (asanas). Written in Persian, the work was composed in Gujarat c. 1550 by Muhammad Ghwath Gwaliori (d. 1562), a prominent Sufi, drawing from an earlier Arabic version (Pool of life, or Hawd al-hayat), of an original Sanskrit text (Amrita Kunda, now lost). This manuscript was produced in early seventeenth-century Mughal India: it is one of three yoga-related texts commissioned for prince Selim (the future Mughal emperor, Jahangir). The paintings are now detached from the codex, on twelve separately-mounted folios (also in the Chester Beatty collection). Codex, ink, colours and gold on paper, 52 folios, Persian text in nasta`liq script, the Ocean of Immortality (Bahr al-Hayat), by Muhammad Ghwath Gwaliori (d. 1562), unsigned, Allahabad, India, c. 1600-1604.

Written in Persian, the work was composed in Gujarat c. 1550 by Muhammad Ghwath Gwaliori (d. 1562), a prominent Sufi, drawing from an earlier Arabic version (Pool of life, or Hawd al-hayat), of an original Sanskrit text (Amrita Kunda, now lost). This manuscript was produced in early seventeenth-century Mughal India: it is one of three yoga-related texts commissioned for prince Selim (the future Mughal emperor, Jahangir). In_17A.t: Folios from the Book of Kings (Shahnama) by Firdausi
In_17A.c: Folios from the Book of Kings (Shahnama) by Firdausi. Now bound together, these six non-sequential folios come from a dispersed manuscript copy of the Book of Kings (Shahnama) by Firdausi, produced in India, probably c. 1600-1610. At different times, Beatty bought three portions from the same dispersed manuscript: In 17 (codex, 298 folios), In 40 (codex, 259 folio), and this set of 6 illustrated folios (In 17A). Further folios are also known in international private and public collections. The folios here are illustrated with the following epic scenes (not in narrative order): Isfandiyar slays the dragon (f. 1v), Rustam trapped in the pit with Rakhsh shoots Shaghhad dead (f. 2v), Isfandiyar's army (f. 3v), Zawara and Faramurz lead Rustam's army into battle (f. 4r), Rustam injured in battle by Isfandiyar (f. 5v), Iskandar with the dying Dara during the battle (f. 6r). In_20_23.t: Corner details of cheetahs and sheep, folio from the Five Treasures (Panj Ganj) by Jāmī
In_20_23.c: Corner details of cheetahs and sheep, folio from the Five Treasures (Panj Ganj) by Jāmī (d. 1492). This page of Persian poetry comes from a book entitled the Five Treasures (Panj Ganj), which is also at Chester Beatty (CBL In 20). The Five Treasures in the title are selected from the Seven Thrones (Haft Awrang), an anthology of seven great works composed by the Persian Sufi poet and statesman `Abd al-Raḥmān Jāmī (d. 1492), who lived in Herat (Afghanistan) under the Timurid dynasty. The book has seen two major phases of production, as well as several shifts in political history. The text was written out by the great master calligrapher Sulṭān `Alī Mashhadī in 1520, the final year of his life. His career had overlapped with that of Jāmī, and the two must have known of each other in Herat, where they both served the Timurid ruler Sulṭān Ḥusayn Bāyqarā (d. 1506). In_21_39.t: The king's parrot offers him the fruit of life, from Tales of a Parrot (Ṭūṭīnāma) by Ẓiya’ al-Dīn Nakhshabī (d. 1350)
In_21_39.c: The king's parrot offers him the fruit of life, from Tales of a Parrot (Ṭūṭīnāma) by Ẓiya’ al-Dīn Nakhshabī (d. 1350). This anthology of stories was adapted c. 1330 from a Persian text (Jewels of Evening Tales, Javāhir al-asmār, by `Imād ibn Muḥammad al-Thughrī, c. 1213), based in turn on a Sanskrit anthology (The Parrot’s Seventy Tales, Shuka-saptati, compiled by Hema Chandra). The story of the ninth night is about the king of Syria, who owned a parrot so wise that the king refused to keep him in a cage. Having served for years as the king's trusted advisor, one day the loyal bird brought his master an extremely rare gift: a fruit that would grow into a tree of eternal life. The mystery fruit was planted and it duly grew into a fruit-bearing tree. The moment of trust came when the king finally held the promised fruit in his hand, and had to decide whether or not to eat it. This anthology of stories was adapted c. 1330 from a Persian text (Jewels of Evening Tales, Javāhir al-asmār, by `Imād ibn Muḥammad al-Thughrī, c. 1213), based in turn on a Sanskrit anthology (The Parrot’s Seventy Tales, Shuka-saptati, compiled by Hema Chandra). The story of the eighteenth night is about an exiled young prince seeking adventure. He makes a trade with a wandering dervish, who takes the prince’s ring in exchange for the dervish’s good luck. Right away the prince meets a magical woman who joins him on his travels. The two then encounter a hungry snake attacking a frog. Interrupting, the prince persuades the snake to stop: both frog and snake transform magically into two men, and the four friends now continue on their adventure. In_21_67.t: Khojasta listens to the parrot’s story for the twenty-first night, from Tales of a Parrot (Ṭūṭīnāma) by Ẓiya’ al-Dīn Nakhshabī (d. 1350)
In_21_67.c: Khojasta listens to the parrot’s story for the twenty-first night, from Tales of a Parrot (Ṭūṭīnāma) by Ẓiya’ al-Dīn Nakhshabī (d. 1350). Tales of a Parrot is a collection of fifty-two stories. Each begins with a conversation between a woman named Khojasta and her pet parrot, sitting together at home while her husband is away for a long work trip. To keep Khojasta from getting bored, the green parrot tells her a long and entertaining story from his cage, every evening, for fifty-two nights. The stories were adapted c. 1330 from a Persian text (Jewels of Evening Tales, Javāhir al-asmār, by `Imād ibn Muḥammad al-Thughrī, c. 1213), based in turn on a Sanskrit anthology (The Parrot’s Seventy Tales, Shuka-saptati, compiled by Hema Chandra). In_21_69.t: The deer and gazelle flatter the lion to save the man’s life, from Tales of a Parrot (Ṭūṭīnāma) by Ẓiya’ al-Dīn Nakhshabī (d. 1350)
In_21_69.c: The deer and gazelle flatter the lion to save the man’s life, from Tales of a Parrot (Ṭūṭīnāma) by Ẓiya’ al-Dīn Nakhshabī (d. 1350). This anthology of stories was adapted c. 1330 from a Persian text (Jewels of Evening Tales, Javāhir al-asmār, by `Imād ibn Muḥammad al-Thughrī, c. 1213), based in turn on a Sanskrit anthology (The Parrot’s Seventy Tales, Shuka-saptati, compiled by Hema Chandra). The story of the twenty-first night is about a wealthy man who suddenly lost all his money and left his home city. Out in the wilderness, he accidentally walked into a lion’s court. Just before the man was eaten, two ministers spoke up: the deer and gazelle flattered their pompous king, explaining that even human beings now come to admire him. Delighted, the lion gave the man some of the treasure kept from people he had previously eaten. Relieved to escape with his life (and new wealth), the man returned to his home. In_21_71.t: The lion chases the greedy man up a tree, from Tales of a Parrot (Ṭūṭīnāma) by Ẓiya’ al-Dīn Nakhshabī (d. 1350)
In_21_71.c: The lion chases the greedy man up a tree, from Tales of a Parrot (Ṭūṭīnāma) by Ẓiya’ al-Dīn Nakhshabī (d. 1350). This anthology of stories was adapted c. 1330 from a Persian text (Jewels of Evening Tales, Javāhir al-asmār, by `Imād ibn Muḥammad al-Thughrī, c. 1213), based in turn on a Sanskrit anthology (The Parrot’s Seventy Tales, Shuka-saptati, compiled by Hema Chandra). The story of the twenty-first night is about a foolish man who narrowly escapes being eaten at a lion's court, thanks to two thoughtful ministers who speak up for him, allowing him to leave safely and with great riches. In_23.c: Abridged Book of Kings (Muntakhab-i Shahnama), by Tawakkul Beg. This is a shorter prose version of Firdausi's epic poem, the Book of Kings (Shahnama). The prose summary also includes verse extracts from the original. The abridgement was written in Kabul in 1643, by a military officer Tawakkul Beg, on the order of the Mughal governor of Kabul. At least twenty years later, this densely-illustrated copy was made in Sikakol, on the Deccan peninsula. Codex, ink, colours and gold on paper, 423 folios, Persian text in nasta`liq script, 61 paintings, abridged prose version of Firdausi's Book of Kings (Shahnama), composed by Mughal court official Tawwakul Beg in Kabul, 1643, colophon (spuriously) dated 20 Jumada I 948H, 12 September 1541, Sikakol, Golconda, India, dateable 1660-1680.

In_26_1.t: Portrait of a young man, from the Mirza Birjis Qadr Album
In_26_1.c: Portrait of a young man, from the Mirza Birjis Qadr Album. Described as an album, this group of 29 drawings offers a series of portraits with closely-drawn faces and often more loosely sketched bodies. They have been linked with the brief and contested rule of Mirza Birjis Qadr as nawab of Lucknow (Mirza Muhammad Ramzan `Ali Bahadur, 1845-1893, r. 1857-8), because the portrait of his mother Hazrat Mahal notes that she is the "regent of Mirza Qadr". The original patron of the series is not known. Drawing, graphite on paper, portrait of a young man seated with hands folded, folio from the Mirza Birjis Qadr Album, unsigned, Lucknow, Uttar Pradesh, India, undated, c. 1850-1858.

In_30.t: Dhakhīra-ye Khwārazmshāhī, by Zayn al-Dīn al-Jurjānī (d. 1136)
a: Bābā Mīrak of Herat, known as Muḥammad Sa`īd
In_30.c: Dhakhīra-ye Khwārazmshāhī, by Zayn al-Dīn al-Jurjānī (d. 1136) Codex, ink, colours and gold on paper, leather bookbinding, 603 folios, Persian text in naskh script, with mid-text keywords in red, blue and gold, and 12 illuminated section headings, Treasure of the Khwarazmshah (Dhakhīra-ye Khwārazmshāhī), by Zayn al-Din Ismā`īl ibn Ḥasan al-Jurjānī (1042-1136), originally composed 1110 (504H), medical encyclopaedia organised in ten sections by subject matter, copied by Bābā Mīrak of Herat, known as Muḥammad Sa`īd, Golconda, Deccan, India, dated 22 Sha`ban 980H, 28 December 1572. Produced within the Golconda court (bi-dār al-salṭana) of Sultan Ibrahim Quli Qutb-Shah (r. 1550-1580), although this ruler is not mentioned by name. The first two folios (illuminated double frontispiece), detached from the volume, are also in this museum collection (CBL In 30.1).

In_30_1.t: Double frontispiece from the Treasure of the Khwarazmshah (Zakhira-yi Khwarazmshahi), by Zayn al-Din al-Jurjani
a: Baba Mirak of Herat, known as Muhammad Sa`id
In_30_1.c: Double frontispiece, from The Treasure of the Khwarazmshah (Zakhira-yi Khwarazmshahi), by Zayn al-Din al-Jurjani. These two folios introduce a medical encyclopaedia, and are now detached from the rest of the manuscript (also in this museum, In 30). The book was produced in Golconda, and has been associated with the court of Sultan Ibrahim Qutb-Shah (r. 1550-1580), although he is not mentioned by name. Filled with angels, red dragons and simurgh birds, the double frontispiece presents an elaborate illuminated frame around the opening text, which is written on a gold ground. Double folio, ink, colours and gold on paper, Persian text in naskh script, two folios detached from codex (In 30), Treasure of the Khwarazmshah (Zakhira-yi Khwarazmshahi), by Zayn al-Din Abu Ibrahim Isma`il al-Jurjani (d. 1135), originally composed 1110-11 (504H), medical encyclopaedia, copied by Baba Mirak of Herat, known as Muhammad Sa`id, Golconda, Deccan, India, dated (colophon f. 605v) 22 Sha`ban 980H, 1572.

In_37.t: Mrigāvatī, or Rāj Kunwar, by Quṭban of Jaunpur
In_37.c: Mrigāvatī, or Rāj Kunwar, by Quṭban of Jaunpur. Codex, ink, colours and gold on paper, with red silk book covers, 113 folios, Persian text (Avadhi dialect) in nasta`liq script, with 33 paintings, Mrigāvatī (the Doe-Woman, alternative title Rāj Kunwar), by Shaykh Quṭban Suhrawardī, composed in Jaunpur in 1503, Premakhyan literary genre blending Sufi mysticism with romance adventure from Indian folklore, text copied by Burhān (signed colophon, fol. 132r), paintings attributed to Bishndas, Haribans, Kesu Das, Salim Quli and five others, for Mughal prince Salim (later emperor Jahangir, r. 1605-1627), Allahabad, India, dated 1012H, 1603-1604. A further 19 folios are now detached and mounted separately, also in this collection.

This scene sets up the tale, as the young man plays the skillful game of polo with his friends, contented with his privileged life. In_37_6.c: Rāj Kunwar follows the deer into the forest pool, from Mrigāvatī (or Rāj Kunwar) by Quṭban of Jaunpur. Out riding in the forest on a hunting trip, the prince has a strange experience that will change his life. He tracks and chases after a doe, which escapes him by diving into a lake. There she transforms into a woman: she is Mrigavati, a beautiful shape-shifter. Astonished, the lovestruck prince follows her into the water, but she has vanished. In_37_16.c: Mrigāvatī and Rāj Kunwar are happily married, from Mrigāvatī (or Rāj Kunwar) by Quṭban of Jaunpur. The prince waits by the lake for months, to the amazement of his friends and family. His understanding father builds a beautiful temple by the lakeside, and his wise nurse advises him how to keep Mrigavati if she should return: hide her magical clothes. Eventually the Doe-Woman reappears to visit the new temple, and Raj Kunwar convinces her to marry him. In_37_20.t: Mrigāvatī flies away, from Mrigāvatī (or Rāj Kunwar) by Quṭban of Jaunpur
In_37_20.c: Mrigāvatī flies away, from Mrigāvatī (or Rāj Kunwar) by Quṭban of Jaunpur. After living happily together, the couple separate when the prince goes to visit his father the king. In his absence, Mrigavati finds where Raj Kunwar has hidden her magical clothes, immediately puts them back on, and sprouts wings. Before she flies away, she explains her feelings to the prince’s wise nurse from the palace roof. Raj Kunwar must seek her out, if he only has the courage. Abandoning his worldly comforts, he dresses humbly as a Hindu holy man, and walks away from his court life in search of her. All around him the natural world is filled with loving pairs of animals and birds. This plot development combines romance adventure with a more spiritual journey for the maturing prince. In_37_28.c: The wandering prince encounters giant serpents, from Mrigāvatī (or Rāj Kunwar) by Quṭban of Jaunpur. The prince journeys onward together with an older sage who teaches him as they travel. At one stage they witness a giant serpent attacking other travellers (folio recto), and the prince's guide advises him to remain calm. A second snake then appears and kills the first (folio verso). In_37_29.t: The prince meets Rupman trapped in the demon’s beautiful garden, from Mrigāvatī (or Rāj Kunwar) by Quṭban of Jaunpur
In_37_29.c: The prince meets Rupman trapped in the demon’s beautiful garden, from Mrigāvatī (or Rāj Kunwar) by Quṭban of Jaunpur. After many adventures on the road, the prince meets Rupman, a beautiful princess trapped in a magnificent garden. She is the prisoner of a seven-headed demon, but Raj Kunwar fights the demon and frees her. The lovestruck couple marry, but the prince cannot forget his first wife Mrigavati, the Doe-Woman. In the end, all three agree to live together. In_41_3.c: Portrait of Awrangzib as a young prince, from an unidentified album. Album page, ink, colour and gold on paper, drawing mounted on card with gold-painted borders, portrait of prince Awrangzib (later Mughal emperor, r. 1657-1707) standing with hands resting on a straight sword, referring to his tenure as governor of Deccan, inscribed (possibly by Shah Jahan) "likeness of Awrangzib bahadur, done by La`l Chand", Delhi, India, undated, c. 1640-44, album folio c. 1700-1800.

In_44_1.t: Young courtier, folio from the Salim Album
In_44_1.c: Young courtier, folio from the Salim Album. This painting shows a well-dressed young man leaning on a staff, and echoing the framing Persian verses: "the sapling stature of youths is the staff of our old age". The Salim Album refers to a group of thirty (known) folios, today dispersed in international collections. These were once part of a small album of paintings and calligraphy, assembled for the Mughal Indian prince Salim (who from 1605 would reign as the emperor Jahangir), probably during the brief years (1600-1604) that he spent in his own court at Allahabad. Eight of these folios are in the Chester Beatty. Although many have been trimmed down, the surviving Salim Album folios share a similar border scheme, of distinctive gold-painted geometric, cloud collar and floral motifs. In_44_2.c: Portrait of Raisal Darbari, folio from the Salim Album. In_44_4.t: Madonna and child, folio from the Salim Album
In_44_4.c: Madonna and child, folio from the Salim Album. This tinted drawing (nim qalam) shows the artist referring to at least two separate Christian compositions, probably from a European print source. On the left is the Virgin Mary and infant Jesus, and below them a woman washes a man's foot, echoing the repentant Mary Magdalene anointing the feet of Jesus. The seated man holds a t-shaped (tau) cross, which suggests another iconographic source. The framing Persian poem refers to romantic love: "I have become dust under your feet: perhaps you will place your foot on my head". In_44_5.c: A Jesuit priest, folio from the Salim Album. The Jesuit order first came to the Mughal court in 1580, and remained a longterm presence in India. This priest holds open his book, while the surrounding Persian poetry refers to the debate over religious imagery: "a God-worshipper calls me an idolater. God bless him: he says what is. In_44_7.t: Qanun player with his cat, by Jagjivan
In_44_7.c: Qanun player with his cat, by Jagjivan. The musician sits with his striped cat on a carpet in a raised platform with elaborate carved pillars, and red curtains. His shoes are on the lower left. Folio, colours and gold on paper, tinted drawing of a qanun player seated with his cat, inscribed "Jagjivan", drawing mounted on gold-painted album page, blank verso, possibly Agra, India, c. 1590-1595.

In_45_1.t: Portrait of emperor Jahangir with a straight sword, from an unidentified album
In_45_1.c: Portrait of emperor Jahangir with a straight sword, from an unidentified album. Painting, ink, colours and gold on paper, mounted on card, trimmed down from an album page, standing portrait of Mughal emperor Jahangir (r. 1605-1627) leaning on straight sword, holding jewelled rosary, wearing strings of pearls, rubies and emeralds, semi-transparent white jama with two contrasting patkas (one tie-dyed) tied at the waist, striped trousers and green shoes, with kard dagger and four archer's rings hanging from his waist, against light blue-green ground, inscribed Balchand (lower right), Agra, India, c. 1620.

In_45_7.c: Woman nursing a child. There are several known Indian versions of this composition, dateable to the seventeenth and eighteenth century, all drawing ultimately from a European print image. Painting, colours and gold on paper, mounted on card, seated woman breastfeeding a child, with cup, fruit and books on a grey stone ledge in foreground, draped purple curtain above, and plain landscape and sky behind, composition based on Flemish print engraving, Lucknow, Uttar Pradesh, India, undated, c. 1775.

In_45_8.c: Red hibiscus, attributed to Mihr Chand. Painting, colours and gold on paper, mounted on card, flowering red hibiscus plant on gold ground, with dark blue border with gold floral scroll, painting attributed to Mihr Chand, Lucknow or Faizabad, Uttar Pradesh, India, c. 1760-1770.

In_47_12.c: Folio from the Gulshan Album, compiled for Mughal emperor Jahangir (1569-1627). This is a single page from a renowned album (or muraqqa`) prepared for the Mughal emperor Jahangir, and completed under his son Shah Jahan. Each page offers a selection of images on one side, and Persian calligraphy on the other, all gathered together to show a diverse art collection. Throughout the album, the Mughal Indian borders follow a consistent presentation, binding the full sequence together: the arranged groups of images sit in borders decorated with gold foliage and brightly-coloured birds, while the calligraphy pages are mounted in borders with a golden landscape full of lightly-painted people and animals. Here, three tinted drawings from Iran are placed together with a Nuremberg engraving and a line of Persian calligraphy quoting the poet Sa`di. The tinted drawing of a seated figure is signed by Reza `Abbasi (d. 1635), of Isfahan. On the verso, illuminated panels of Persian verses quote the poet

In_47_14.c: Musician and acrobat, by Shaykh `Abbāsī. Album folio, ink, colours and gold on cream paper, tinted drawing of two performers, one playing a drum, the other doing a back flip, signed Shaykh `Abbāsī ("bahā gereft cho gardīd Shaykh `Abbāsī, 1064", between the figures), two blank spaces on right and left, within ruled borders on cream paper frame with yellow stencilled foliate design and Persian verses in reserved cartouches, all mounted on gold-flecked cream card album page, blank card verso, Isfahan, Iran, dated 1064H, 1653-1654.

In_48_1.t: Portrait of Mirza Raja Jai Singh with his son Kunwar Ram Singh
In_48_1.c: Portrait of Mirza Raja Jai Singh with his son Kunwar Ram Singh. Tinted drawing, ink, colours and gold on paper, with silk brocade border, profile portrait of Mirza Raja Jai Singh I (r. 1617-1666) seated on a throne handing a jewelled sarpech to his son Kunwar Ram Singh (later Mirza Raja Ram Singh I, r. 1666-1668), inscribed in Persian "likeness of Mirza Raja Jai Singh" (left) and "of Kunwar Ram Singh" (right), Amer Fort, Jaipur, Rajasthan, India, c. 1645-1650.

In_69_6.t: Women on a palace terrace with a panoramic view
In_69_6.c: Women on a palace terrace with a panoramic view. On a palace terrace, a seated woman with her attendants watches a bottle-balancing act accompanied by musicians. Behind them rises a steep vertical panorama of the palace gardens, rivers and a distant battle landscape. Painting, colours and gold on paper, on a palace terrace, Faizabad, Awadh (Oudh) state, India, 1770.

In_73_3.c: Women visiting an ashram. Painting (tinted drawing, or nim qalam), colours and gold on paper, mounted on card, three women and a child stand before an ascetic, seated on a tigerskin outside a domed ashram with another sadhu, while a younger acolyte (chela) looks out from a doorway, inscribed "the work of Kamal Muhammad [and Muhammad?]", possibly Bijapur (Vijayapura), Deccan, India, c. 1675-1700.

In_74_6.c: Begum Samru and her army. This painting shows the ruler of Sardhana, Begum Samru (r. 1778-1836), riding on an elephant, surrounded by her armies of cavalry, infantry and artillery marching on parade. The artillery includes guns mounted on camels (zamburak), and ox-drawn cannon. Painting, colours on paper, procession of Begum Samru (r. 1778-1836), Sardhana, Uttar Pradesh, India, c. 1805-1826.

In_74_7.c: Begum Samru and her household, by Muhammad A`zam. This crowded scene shows the ruler of Sardhana, Begum Samru (1751-1836) and her extensive household, receiving four guests who are seated in a row in the centre. Every figure has been named in a small inscription, including the four visitors (three nawabs and a bakshi or paymaster), who have been linked with the Mughal court of Akbar Shah II in Delhi. The Begum's international household included David Dyce-Samru (sitting on her right), to whom she would bequeath most of her wealth, and John Thomas (beside Dyce-Samru), an Irish-Indian officer in her army, who had been adopted into her court in 1795. Painting, colours on paper, Begum Samru and her extensive household receiving four guests, all figures' names inscribed in ink, artist's name Muhammad A`zam inscribed in lower left corner, possibly Delhi, India, 1820-1825.

InE_1415.c: Hanging scroll cosmographical painting (representation of the universe) from the Hindu faith, painted in colours on cotton in Nepal, dating to the 17th or 18th century. In this painting, the universe is conceptualised as a series of concentric circles spreading out from the sacred Mount Meru. Immediately surrounding Mount Meru is Jambu-dvipa, the earth or 'island of the rose-apple tree'. Jambu-dvipa is surrounded by a salt ocean and spreading out from here are seven further lands, separated by various oceans, until the realm of darkness is reached at the outer edge of the universe. Within Jambu-dvipa are a number of lands, including India. In the central lotus the god Brahma is surrounded by other deities.

InE_1420.t: Song of the Lord (Bhagavadgita) and other Vaishnavite texts
InE_1420.c: Book of the Song of God (Bhagavadgita) and other Vaishnavite texts, maker unknown, 1801, Kashmir. Ink, colours and gold on paper with lacquered paper covers. The Bhagavadgita is a 700-verse poem which takes the form of a dialogue between Prince Arjuna and his charioteer and guide, Krishna.

InE_1444.c: Folios from a Ramayana, made in ink, colours, gold and silver on paper, in the late 18th century, in Marwar. The set of 151 folios depicts scenes from book 1 (Bala Kanda), book 4 (Kishkindha Kanda), book 5 (Sundara Kanda) and book 7 (Uttara Kanda) of a Ramayana which is similar to the Northern recension of the Valmiki Ramayana.

InE_1450.t: Untitled work on the life of Krishna and three shorter works
InE_1450.c: Untitled work on the life of Krishna and three shorter works, maker unknown, late 18th century, probably Punjab. Ink, colours and gold on paper with cloth cover. The book comprises a text on the life of Krishna in rhyming couplets preceded by three shorter works on similar subjects. Two of the shorter texts have colophons signed Moti Ram, at Sialkot, 1749 CE.

InE_1461.c: Manuscript containing extracts from the Mahabharata, made in ink, colours and gold on paper with lacquered covers, in 1798, in India.

InE_1463.t: Perfection of wisdom sutra in 25,000 verses (Panchavimshatisahasrika Prajnaparamita)
InE_1463.c: Palm leaf manuscript of the Perfection of wisdom sutra in 25,000 verses (Panchavimshatisahasrika Prajnaparamita) with wooden covers, produced by unknown makers in the Bengal region and dated 1089. The museum's collections include 59 folios from this Buddhist religious text, together with its painted wooden covers. The covers feature depictions of episodes from the Buddha’s life and Buddhist deities; some folios are also illustrated. The manuscript originally comprised 560 folios. Further folios believed to be from the same manuscript are preserved in the Metropolitan Museum of Art (New York), the Baroda Museum and Picture Gallery (Vadodara, Gujarat), Brooklyn Museum (New York), McGill University Library (Montreal) and various private collections. The date is given on the colophon in the collections of the Baroda Museum.

InE_1478.c: Handscroll amulet of Sacred histories of God (Bhagavata Purana), inscribed by Jayarama in 1718, probably in Kashmir. Ink, colours and gold on paper with a silver case. This small illustrated scroll contains all twelve chapters (skandha) of the Bhagavata Purana, including chapter ten which narrates the life of Krishna.

InE_1479.c: Book of the Song of God (Bhagavadgita), maker unknown, 1798, possibly Kashmir. Ink, colours and gold on paper. The Bhagavadgita is a 700-verse poem which takes the form of a dialogue between Prince Arjuna and his charioteer and guide, Krishna.

InE_1651.t: Book of ritual (Kalpa-sūtra) and Story of the monk Kālaka (Kālakācārya-kathā)
InE_1651.c: Manuscript of the 'Book of ritual' and 'Story of the monk Kālaka' (Kalpa-sūtra and Kālakācārya-kathā), written in Devanagari script with paintings in ink, colours and gold on paper; made in Gujarat, India, dated 1522. The Book of Ritual (Kalpa-sūtra) is among the most fundamental texts of the Jain faith. Often paired with stories of the pious monk Kālaka (Kālakācārya-kathā), it features episodes from the lives of the Jina: enlightened humans who guide others out of the cycle of rebirth. The last of the Jina born in this era was Mahāvīra, who is thought to have lived in the sixth century BC. The miniature paintings show scenes related to his life.

InE_1661.c: Embroidered silk manuscript cover, made in Gujarat, India, possibly in the 19th century. Symbols of Queen Trishala’s fourteen lucky dreams are depicted on the full side of the cover: an elephant, a bull, a lion, the goddess Sri, a garland, the moon, the sun, a banner, a vase of plenty, a lotus pond, an ocean of milk, a celestial chariot, a heap of jewels and a raging smokeless fire.

InE_1668.c: Hanging scroll cosmographical painting (representation of the universe), painted in colours on cotton in India, possibly during the 18th century. In the Jain tradition, the universe is divided into three worlds: the upper heavenly world, the middle mortal world, and the lower world of the damned. This painting is a representation of the world of the mortals. Paintings of the mortal world have remained popular with the devout as it is within this world that liberation from the chain of rebirth is possible.

Is_1401.o: Approved Category 2017/Manuscript/Codex; Object by Function/Documents by function/Religious text/Qur'an
Is_1401.c: Folios from an `Abbasid Qur'an. Codex, ink, colours and gold on parchment, 20 folios, Arabic text in kufic script, with illuminated motifs (knots, stars, lobed medallions) as tenth verse counters throughout, sections from the Qur'an, suras 13:34 to 18:110 (but not continuous), probably Iraq, c. 800-900.
