There is a full page of illumination at the start and conclusion of the text, each in a different design of interlocking circles (at the start) and checkerboard (at the end). The layout is typical for a multi-volume Qur'an of this date, each separate volume would have splendid illumination panels, usually on facing pages at the beginning and at the end of the book. However this manuscript does not contain a complete "thirtieth" (juz') or "sixtieth" (hizb) of the Qur'an's full text, and is therefore a fragment of the original volume. Is_1414.c: Miniature Qur'an. Very small format Qur'ans are easily carried, and have long been used to provide personal protection to their owners in times of need, such as war or sickness. This small codex measures 9.6 x 5.9 cm, with thirteen clearly-written lines per page. Two notes have been added by later owners, recording the birth of sons, in the years 1011 and 1022: was this Qur'an kept close during childbirth? Codex, ink, colour and gold on parchment, 21 folios, Arabic text in kufic script, partial text of juz' 29 of the Qur'an (sura 71:3 to 99:98), with later notes added (to the inner covers) recording the birth of a son in 1011 (4 Jumada 402H), and again in 1022 (16 Shawwal 413H), possibly Iraq, undated, c. 800-900.

Is_1417A.o: Approved Category 2017/Manuscript/Codex; Object by Function/Documents by function/Religious text/Qur'an
Is_1417A.c: Juz' 3 of the Khayqani Qur'an. The Khayqani Qur'an is an important early example of the Arabic script known as "New Style" (also called eastern kufic), which developed gradually in Qur'anic calligraphy away from the more angular kufic script. This multi-volume Qur'an has been dated to c. 900 because of a note added to Juz' 19: on the final page is a statement in Persian, signed by someone called Ahmad ibn Abi'l-Qasim al-Khayqani. He notes that he has checked the text and made corrections, signing and dating his comment to the month of Sha`ban 292H (June 905). There have been doubts about the authenticity of this extra note, but not about the manuscript itself. Codex, ink, colours and gold on parchment, 47 folios, Arabic text in New Style III (aka eastern kufic) script, illuminated verse-markers, Juz' 3 of the Qur'an (2:253 to 3:91), from a thirty-volume set, of which Juz' 19 (CB Is 1417D) has a note signed al-Khayqani and dated 292H (June 905), probably Iran, c. 900

Is_1431.o: Approved Category 2017/Manuscript/Codex; Object by Function/Documents by function/Religious text/Qur'an
Is_1431.c: The Ibn al-Bawwab Qur’an was produced in Baghdad in the year 1000. Its smooth cursive calligraphy is the work of Abu’l Hasan `Ali ibn Hilal (d. 1022), more commonly known as Ibn al-Bawwab (meaning "son of the doorkeeper"). Ibn al-Bawwab is renowned as one of Islam’s greatest master-calligraphers, and this manuscript is held to be the only Qur’an genuinely written in his hand. It is also important for being one of the earliest dated Qur’ans copied on paper (as opposed to parchment) and one of the earliest written in a cursive script. In the year 1000, Baghdad was ruled nominally by the `Abbasid caliphs, who were in turn controlled by the Buyid dynasty. While this Qur'an is not documented as a royal commission, Ibn al-Bawwab had connections to the Buyid rulers: before coming to Baghdad, he had served as chief librarian for a Buyid amir's collection in Shiraz, Iran. Is_1437C.c: Partial copy of Juz' 30 of a Mamluk Qur'an. This Qur'an is written out in tumar script, as opposed to the more fashionable Mamluk scripts thuluth or muhaqqaq. The calligrapher has been identified as Ibn al-Wahid (d. 1311), a renowned practitioner born in Damascus in 1249, who studied under Yaqut al-Musta`simi (d. 1298) in Baghdad and settled in Cairo. Together with the master-illuminator Sandal, Ibn al-Wahid worked on a monumental Qur'an project (today in the British Library) for the Mamluk Sultan Baybars in 1306, and they may also have worked together on this manuscript. Much is recorded of Ibn al-Wahid's biography (and personality), including that he worked in Sultan Baybars' chancery, where the secretary complained of his negligence. However he was greatly admired for his calligraphic skill by the forgiving Baybars. The unusual use here of tumar (normally a chancery script) may further support the manuscript's attribution to Ibn al-Wahid. Codex, ink, colours and gold on paper, 116 f

Is_1457_1.c: Folio from a Mamluk Qur'an. This single folio belongs to a codex (also in this museum: Is 1457I and II). Each side is beautifully illuminated, and each was created as a double page design: the geometric star design on the recto (here) would have faced an identical folio, which is now lost. As often with Qur'ans from Mamluk Cairo, the white kufic inscriptions at the top and bottom are different Qur'anic quotations, referring to the holy book itself: "Indeed We have sent [the Qur'an] down in a Night of Blessings" (Qur'an 44:3, top), and "Indeed We have sent down [the Qur'an] in the Night of Destiny (Laylat al-Qadr)" (Qur'an 97:1, bottom). On the verso, different illumination frames the first sura of the Qur'an. This text should face the second sura of the Qur'an, with matching designs: that opposite page remains in the codex (CB Is 1457I). Is_1476.c: Qur'an from Mamluk Cairo. This manuscript contains Juz' 27 of the Qur'an, and it was originally one of a thirty-volume set of the complete text. The opening folios present an illuminated double page, with matching panels of radial geometric design. The central octagons read "The Twenty-Seventh Juz'", in angular white kufic script. Set against gold ground, four lines of smaller text frame these central panels, with a Qur'anic quotation: "Truly this [Qur'an] is a revelation, From the Lord of the worlds, Which the true Spirit has brought down upon your heart, That you may be one of the warners, In clear Arabic language" (Qur'an 26:192-5). Codex, ink, colours and gold on paper, 48 folios, Arabic text in muhaqqaq script, with sura headings in thuluth, and illuminated double page frontispiece (fols. 1v-2r), Juz' 27 of the Qur'an, illumination and calligraphy attributed to Ahmad ibn Kamal ibn Yahya al-Ansari al-Mutatabbib (unsigned), Cairo, Egypt, c. 1332-1336.

Is_1500.o: Approved Category 2017/Manuscript/Codex; Object by Function/Documents by function/Religious text/Qur'an
Is_1500.c: Qur'an from Timurid Herat This magnificent copy of the Qur'an was produced at the Timurid court in Herat, almost certainly for Prince Baysunghur (d. 1433). The first page-opening is a double-page composition of illumination, with a radiating geometric star pattern. This deliberately echoes designs from the late thirteenth century, although the central lobed medallion is very much up to date for Timurid design. The Timurid calligrapher has also referred deliberately to the late thirteenth century, by signing in the name of the highly-regarded master-calligrapher Yaqut al-Musta`simi, who died in 1298. A very similar Qur'an was signed by the Timurid master-calligrapher Shams al-Baysunghuri, in 1434 (837H), and is today in the Turkish and Islamic Art Museum in Istanbul (TIEM 294). Codex, ink, colours and gold on paper, 273 folios, Arabic text in naskh script, and angular kufic for first two sura headings, with initial double frontispiece of radial strapwork (fols. 1v-2r), complete Qur'an,

Is_1505.c: Juz' 5 of a Mamluk Qur'an. Codex, ink, colours and gold on paper, leather bookbinding with gold-painted lobed medallion design and filigree openwork doublures, 45 folios, Arabic text in rayhan script, with illuminated medallion (shamsa, fol. 1r), opening double page (chahar-lawh, fols. 1v-2r) and concluding panel (fol. 45v), Juz' 5 of the Qur'an (Sura 4:24–147), with short final prayer (fol. 45r), unsigned, Cairo, Egypt, undated, c. 1400-1424, with additional waqf donation note (fol. 1r) stating this volume was endowed on behalf of Mamluk sultan al-Malik al-Ashraf Sayf al-Dīn Barsbāy (r. 1422-1438) to his madrasa on khatt al-ḥarīriyīn on 24 Rabi` II 827H, 26 March 1424.

Is_1527.t: Qur’ān copied by Ḥasan Çelebi, for Sokollu Meḥmed Pāshā
Is_1527.o: Approved Category 2017/Manuscript/Codex; Object by Function/Documents by function/Religious text/Qur'an
Is_1527.c: Qur’ān for Ottoman grand vizier Sokollu Meḥmed Pāshā (d. 1579). Codex, ink, colours and gold on paper, leather bookbinding, 356 folios, Arabic text in rayhan and naskh scripts, with illuminated medallion (shamsa, fol. 1r), double page frontispiece (fols. 1v-2r), framed text (chahar-lawh, fols. 2v-3r, border 3v-4r), sura headings and marginal markers throughout, complete text of the Qur’ān, with concluding Khatm prayer (fol. 355r), dedicated (fols. 355v-356r) to Sokollu Meḥmed Pāshā (1505-1579, at this time grand vizier to Ottoman sultan Selim II), signed (fol. 356v) by Ḥasan ibn Aḥmad al-Qaraḥiṣārī (Ḥasan Çelebi, d. 1594), Istanbul, Turkey, dated Ramadan 977H, February 1570.

Is_1544.o: Approved Category 2017/Manuscript/Codex; Object by Function/Documents by function/Religious text/Qur'an
Is_1544.c: Qur'an from Safavid Iran. Codex, ink, colours and gold on paper, 310 folios, Arabic text in naskh script, with illuminated medallions (shamsa, fols. 1v-2r), double frontispiece (turanj design, fols. 2v-3r), sura headings and marginal markers throughout, and two double finispieces (fols. 307v-309r), complete Qur'ān, with final prayer (khatm, fols. 307v-308r) and divination index (fālnāma, fols. 308v-309r), signed by Niẓām al-Dīn Maḥmūd (fol. 307r), possibly Shiraz, Iran, dated 975H, 1567-1568.

Is_1547.o: Approved Category 2017/Manuscript/Codex; Object by Function/Documents by function/Religious text/Qur'an
Is_1547.c: Qurān. Codex, ink, colours and gold on paper, leather bookbinding with gold, 322 folios, Arabic text in thuluth and naskh scripts in alternating sizes, with illuminated double pages (fols. 1v-2r, 12v-13r, 23v-24r, 34v-35r, 45v-46r, 56v-57r, 67v-68r, 162v-163r, 321v-322r, signalling the first seven of thirty juz’ sections, the start of Sura 19 Maryam, and the final two suras al-Falaq and al-Nās) and marginal markers throughout, complete text of the Qur’ān, unsigned, probably India, undated, c. 1550-1600.

Is_1551.o: Approved Category 2017/Manuscript/Codex; Object by Function/Documents by function/Religious text/Qur'an
Is_1551.c: Qur'an from North Africa. Codex, ink, colours and gold on paper, 127 folios, Arabic text in maghribi script, with illuminated frontispiece (fol. 1r), sura-headings and marginal text-markers, partial text of the Qur’an (Sura 1 to 93:1 only), unsigned, North Africa, undated, c. 1600-1700.

Is_1558.o: Approved Category 2017/Manuscript/Codex; Object by Function/Documents by function/Religious text/Qur'an
Is_1558.c: Qur'an, bound codex, 445 folios, ink, gold and pigments on paper, Arabic calligraphy and illumination, signed by Ruzbihan Muhammad al-Tab`i al-Shirazi (f.445r), Shiraz, Iran, c. 1535-1565. Produced in the city of Shiraz, this splendid Qur’an is an extraordinary example of the arts of the book in sixteenth-century Iran. The sacred text was written out by renowned master-calligrapher Ruzbihan. He used three different scripts to copy out the main text and further calligraphic styles for the chapter headings. Throughout the manuscript, the Qur'anic text is accompanied by a rich programme of sophisticated and colourful illumination, dominated by burnished gold and deep lapis blue.

Is_1589.o: Approved Category 2017/Manuscript/Codex; Object by Function/Documents by function/Religious text/Qur'an
Is_1589.c: Qur'an with interlinear Persian. Codex, ink, colours and gold on black tinted paper, with (later) light blue borders, 33 folios, lacquer bookbinding with tortoiseshell pattern, Arabic text in gold naskh script and Persian text in white shikasta script, Qur’an, incomplete text (Sura 2:69-268 and 3:11-78, missing 2:1-69, 2:78-85, 2:268-286, 3:1-11), with (fols. 1-26 only) interlinear Persian translation/gloss, some folios out of sequence or cropped along bottom edge, unsigned, probably Iran, undated, 1700-1800, light blue wove paper borders and binding added 1800-1900.

Is_1614_1.o: Approved Category 2017/Manuscript/Codex/Folio / Bi-Folio (Codex); Object by Function/Documents by function/Religious text/Qur'an
Is_1614_1.c: Opening folio from a Qur'an, illuminated by Muhammad ibn Aybak in Baghdad. This full-page illumination marks the beginning of a superb Qur'an volume produced in Baghdad. It is from a thirty-volume set, now dispersed in international collections or lost. Four of the known volumes contain the signature of the renowned illuminator Muhammad ibn Aybak ibn `Abdullah, who also recorded the date and that he was working "in the City of Peace, Baghdad". From these inscriptions, Ibn Aybak's work schedule becomes clear: he completed volume two in April 1303, ten in February 1305, and thirteen in October 1305, producing an illuminated volume approximately every three months. Folio from a Qur'an, colours and gold on paper, illuminated frontispiece panel with geometric design of central radiating star with quarter-stars repeated in the four corners, and hasp ornament on right margin, right half of a double-page composition, illumination by Muhammad ibn Aybak, opening folio from volume 25 of a 30-volu

Is_1614_2.o: Approved Category 2017/Manuscript/Codex/Folio / Bi-Folio (Codex); Object by Function/Documents by function/Religious text/Qur'an
Is_1614_2.c: Opening folio from a Qur'an, illuminated by Muhammad ibn Aybak in Baghdad. This full-page illumination marks the beginning of a superb Qur'an volume produced in Baghdad. It is from a thirty-volume set, now dispersed in international collections or lost. Four of the known volumes contain the signature of the renowned illuminator Muhammad ibn Aybak ibn `Abdullah, who also recorded the date and that he was working "in the City of Peace, Baghdad". From these inscriptions, Ibn Aybak's work schedule becomes clear: he completed volume two in April 1303, ten in February 1305, thirteen in October 1305, and volume twenty-six in 1306, producing an illuminated volume approximately every three months. Although his work does not figure in this particular folio, this Qur'an's calligrapher was also an important figure: Ibn al-Suhrawardi, trained by the great master Yaqut al-Musta`simi. Folio from a Qur'an, colours and gold on paper, illuminated panel with geometric design of octagon repeats, and hasp

Is_1615I.o: Approved Category 2017/Manuscript/Codex; Object by Function/Documents by function/Religious text/Qur'an
Is_1615I.c: Folios from a Hijazi Qur'an. Now placed in a modern binding, these Qur'an folios date from the first century of Islam, in either the Arabian peninsula or Syria. The Arabic is written in an unusual version of the script known as hijazi - meaning from Hijaz province, where the cities of Mecca and Medina are located. Codex, ink and colours on parchment, 32 folios, Arabic text in hijazi script, with illumination of horizontal chevron bands between chapters (suras), portion of the Qur'an (suras 28:6 to 48:24), unsigned, possibly Medina (modern Saudi Arabia) or Damascus (Syria), undated, c. 675-725.

Is_1615II.o: Approved Category 2017/Manuscript/Codex; Object by Function/Documents by function/Religious text/Qur'an
Is_1615II.c: Folios from a Hijazi Qur'an Now placed in a modern binding, these four Qur'an folios may date from the first century of Islam, in either the Arabian peninsula or Syria. The Arabic is written in an unusual version of the script known as hijazi - meaning from Hijaz province, where the cities of Mecca and Medina are located. Codex, ink and colours on parchment, 4 folios, Arabic text in hijazi script, with illumination of horizontal chevron bands between chapters (suras, on fol. 4v only), portion of the Qur'an (suras 85:3 to 110:1), unsigned, possibly Medina (modern Saudi Arabia) or Damascus (Syria), undated, c. 675-725.

Is_1622.o: Approved Category 2017/Manuscript/Handscroll; Object by Function/Documents by function/Religious text/Qur'an
Is_1622.c: Qur'an scroll, with holy names in reserve. Written in minute ghubar script, this undated copy of the Qur'an shows a strong Shi`a conviction in its design, with the names of the Fourteen Immaculates reserved in large format throughout. This begins with the Prophet Muhammad and his daughter Fatima, followed by her husband `Ali ibn Abi Talib, and their male descendants. Similar scrolls reserve other Shi`a messages against the text of the Qur'an, such as the prayer to Imam `Ali ("Nad-e `Aliyan"). Scroll, ink, colours and gold on paper, leather flap cover, Arabic text in ghubar script, with illuminated heading (sarlawh) at the start, Qur'an with text reserved to form the sacred names of the Prophet Muhammad and his descendants (Fatima, `Ali, Hasan, Husayn, and all the other Shi`a Imams), Iran, undated, c. 1750-1850.

Is_1623.o: Scroll (object name); Object by Function/Documents by function/Religious text/Qur'an
Is_1623.c: Qur'an scroll from Safavid Iran. Measuring over 6.7m in length, this paper scroll contains the entire text of the Qur'ān, written in a tiny script known as "ghubar" (dust). Also included - reserved against the tiny ghubar text - is a series of important prayers and invocations, addressed to the Prophet and his descendants through his daughter Fāṭima and her husband `Alī ibn Abī Ṭālib. Together, they head a family line of altogether Twelve Imāms, who are of deep spiritual significance in Shi`a Islamic tradition. For this Qur'ān scroll, the special praise for the Twelve Imams fits with the cultural environment of Safavid Iran, which from 1501 was a Twelver Shi`a state. Scroll, ink, gold and colours on paper, Arabic text in ghubar script, with illuminated heading, the full text of the Qur'ān, with additional pious texts reserved against main text (the bismillāh, invocations to the Prophet, his daughter Fāṭima and the twelve Imāms (the Fourteen Innocents, or Chahārdah Ma`ṣūm), the prayer N

a: Muhammad ibn Mansur `Ali al-Hanafi al-Husayni al-Kakhtawi
Is_1624.o: Scroll (object name); Object by Function/Documents by function/Religious text/Qur'an
Is_1624.c: Qur'an scroll from Mamluk Cairo. This remarkable Qur'an scroll is over 11m in length. It contains the complete text of the Qur'an, laid out in a sequence of shaped panels and also down the long borders on the sides, with gold-painted margins and leafy illumination throughout. There are also further sections, adding with the powerful primary blessing (baraka) associated with the Qur'an itself: a set of talismanic squares (awfaq) each linked with a different planet, followed by short prayers to the Prophet, the four Rashidun caliphs and Imams Hasan, Husayn and Ja`far al-Sadiq, all to protect the patron. This combination of Islamic faith with astrological concepts is a good example of "licit magic", a widespread social system of invoking protective unseen forces, used in conjunction with more mainstream religion. Scroll, ink, colours and gold on paper, Arabic text in naskh script of varying sizes (ghubar, large naskh, and occasionally larger text reserved against the ghubar), text set in

Is_1625.o: Scroll (object name); Object by Function/Documents by function/Religious text/Qur'an
Is_1625.c: Qur'an scroll. Measuring over 11m in length and only 10cm in height, this scroll conveys the entire text of the Qur'an through a striking sequence of different calligraphic layouts, in which a large pious inscription dramatically overlays the packed and tiny text below. The outer borders meanwhile convey a long band of clearly written Qur'anic text (sura 112), written in gold. Scroll, ink, colours and gold on paper, backed on green silk, Arabic text in varying black, red, gold and white scripts (cursive and angular), periodically overlaying or reserving large thuluth, kufic or square kufic scripts against very small naskh or ghubar scripts, with illuminated sura-headings throughout, Qur'an (originally the complete text, suras 1, 2, 48 now missing), border naskh inscription repeating al-Ikhlas (sura 112), with panel grid of magic squares (awfaq), possibly Iran, undated, c. 1400-1450.

Is_1626.o: Scroll (object name); Object by Function/Documents by function/Religious text/Qur'an
Is_1626.c: Qur'an scroll. Measuring over 7m in length, this narrow paper scroll contains the full text of the Qur'an, neatly written in tiny script. At the leather flap, the initial part of the scroll holds a series of Arabic inscription panels in banna'i script (also called square kufic), written here in black on white squared paper, but more commonly found in tiled architecture. Further banna'i inscriptions also line the border of the main text. Scroll, ink, colours and gold on paper, green cloth backing support, gold-painted leather flap with woven cotton band, Arabic text in naskh and banna'i (square kufic) scripts, with illuminated heading (sarlawh) and inscribed medallions, squares and stepped cartouches at the start, complete Qur'an, with additional prayers, possibly Shiraz, Iran, c. 1500-1600

Is_1627.t: Two Folios from a Mamluk Qur'an
Is_1627.o: Approved Category 2017/Manuscript/Codex/Folio / Bi-Folio (Codex); Object by Function/Documents by function/Religious text/Qur'an
Is_1627.c: Two Folios from a Mamluk Qur'an. These two folios were detached from a monumental Qur'an manuscript, probably in Paris in the late nineteenth century. Four of the six sura-headings (103, 104, 106, 109) do not belong to this page-opening: they have been cut out from other parts of the text, and pasted here over existing lines of text (suras 90-92). This can only have been to inflate the market value of these two folios, in a western context. The diversity of the illumination confirms what was once a splendidly produced Qur'an, with different artists working in distinct styles. Other folios from this same manuscript: CBL Is 1628, Boston Museum of Fine Arts 09.335, and Manchester John Rylands Ar.42 (the codex). Two folios, ink, colours and gold on paper, Arabic text in muhaqqaq, thuluth and kufic scripts, with six illuminated sura-headings and marginal motifs, final lines of sura 90 (al-`Asr) to sura 92 (al-Layl) of the Qur'an, and headings for suras 103, 91, 104, 106, 92, 109 respectivel

Is_1628.t: Closing folios from a Mamluk Qur'an
Is_1628.o: Approved Category 2017/Manuscript/Codex/Folio / Bi-Folio (Codex); Object by Function/Documents by function/Religious text/Qur'an
Is_1628.c: Closing folios from a Mamluk Qur'an. These two folios were the final page-opening of a monumental Qur'an made in Mamluk Cairo, possibly for Sultan al-Ashraf Sha`ban (r. 1363-76). A complex design of overlapping circles and white strapwork forms the framework for the final two sura titles (above), while the lower frame holds a separate quote ("And perfect are the words of your Lord..." Qur'an 6:115). In 1877, the French scholar Prisse d'Avennes published a colour drawing of a detail of this page-opening (fol. 2r, upper left) in his work on Arab art and design: he had seen the manuscript on display at the international exhibition in Paris, 1867. Other folios from this manuscript: CBL Is 1627, Boston Museum of Fine Arts 09.335, and Manchester John Rylands Ar.42 (the codex). Is_As13.c: Amulet, carved with Qur'an sura 114 (al-Nas). Amulet, carnelian, carved with Arabic text in nasta`liq script, sura 114 (al-Nas) of the Qur'an, three lines of text with five-petalled rosettes, set within lobed cartouche, probably Iran, undated, c. 1700-1900.

Is_As30.c: Amulet pendant, plaque with lobed medallion shape and flat top, probably nephrite jade, with carved and gold decoration and Arabic script and numbers, central design of square panel with “Sultan Shah” written in gold, lines of protective magic numbers and Arabic text in the corners, offset inside pointed medallion with foliate design in gold, and carved foliate and floral design around edges and on the back, unsigned, possibly India or Iran, undated, c. 1600-1800.

Is_As31.c: Amulet pendant, heart-shaped plaque with scalloped edges and flat top, white nephrite jade with inset ruby and traces of gold, carved with Arabic text in nasta`liq script (“If God wills it, there is no strength or power except from God almighty, may He forgive”), unsigned, India, dated 1029H, 1619-1620

Is_As44.t: Amulet quoting the Throne Verse from the Qur’an
Is_As44.c: Amulet, carnelian with incised text, Arabic text (around the borders) quoting the Throne Verse (Qur’an 2:255), and (in the centre) naming God, Muhammad and `Ali, Iran, 1676 (1087H)

Is_As51.t: Carnelian amulet carved with protective verses from the Qur'an
Is_As51.c: Amulet, carnelian, oval plaque with carved design, Arabic text in naskh script, four horizontal lines quoting the Qur’an (al-Nas, Sura 114:1-6), possibly India or Iran, undated, c. 1700-1900.

Is_As61.t: Amulet, with design of roses bearing holy names
Is_As61.c: Amulet, quartz with incised inscriptions design centred on a rosebush growing from a pot, labelled with holy names including the Fourteen Immaculates (the Prophet, his daughter Fatima and the Twelve Imams), and Qur'an verses (the Throne Verse 2:255, and al-Nas 112:1-4), Iran or India, 1656 (1067H).

Is_Pp1.t: Papyrus list of names and payments, written in Coptic
Is_Pp1.c: Papyrus list of names and payments, written in Coptic. This document is organised in two columns, consisting of personal names on the left followed by amounts on the right, using Greek letters as numerals. This relates to fiscal administration, recording land measures, tax payments or some other contribution imposed on the individuals listed in the first column. Some names and amounts are marked with an oblique stroke, as a tick or check mark. Some names are preceded by "ar" possibly an abbreviation of the content measurement unit "artabe" or the surface measurement unit "aroura", both of which fit the context of agricultural taxes. On the recto side, some names can be read, for example on column one: Mōne (line 1), George (line 2), Apollo (lines 3, 5), line 6 Ioannes de deacon (daikon, line 6), and on column two: George (line 8); Phib (line 9). Folio fragment, ink on medium brown papyrus, mounted on paper and framed under glass, original cutting lines preserved on the top, left and ri

Is_Pp2.t: Papyrus letter and agricultural lease dated Dhū al-Ḥijja 290H (October-November 903)
Is_Pp2.c: Papyrus letter and agricultural lease for the tax year 290H (903). This papyrus folio was used twice, first as a letter (on the verso side, written in the eighth century) and then for an agricultural legal contract in the year 903 (290H, on the recto). With papyrus breakage at the top and bottom of the folio (on the verso), some text is lost from both start and finish of the letter, but the surviving text begins with blessings wished on the addressee, and asks for a favour. Much of the detail is unclear: the sender requests politely that the addressee might undertake some task for their benefit, and mentions a third person who has passed on some information. On the recto of the papyrus folio the text is complete, and contains an agricultural lease (Ar. qabāla) dated to the month Dhu al-Hijja of the year 290H (October-November 903). The contract is issued by the tenant (mutaqabbil) Mīnā son of Qultah for grazing land (marj wa-marāʿ) on estates belonging to the amir in the town of Ṭuṭūn

Is_Pp3.t: Papyrus memo: tax evaders under arrest
Is_Pp3.c: Papyrus memo about tax evaders under arrest. This memo was issued from the administrative offices of the Arab authorities in Egypt, and deals with the topic of agricultural workers and land-owners who have left their place of fiscal residence and moved to another administrative district. Such "fugitives" (in Arabic s. jālī; pl jāliya) are mentioned in surviving papyrus documentation throughout Egypt’s history, but in the Islamic period they are especially prominent in the record from the end of the seventh and throughout the eighth century. The fugitives were treated variously depending on the circumstances: sometimes they had to pay taxes in their new place of residence, sometimes they had to pay taxes (as well) in their original place of residence while living and working elsewhere, and sometimes they were forced to return to their original place of residence to work the agricultural land and pay taxes there. Is_Pp4.t: Papyrus folios from a Ḥadīth manuscript dated 267H (880-881)
Is_Pp4.c: Papyrus folios from a Ḥadīth manuscript dated 267H (880-881). Two folio fragments, ink on dark brown papyrus, with (on left fragment) traces of the string which bound the original volume, mounted on paper and framed under glass, Arabic text in a practiced cursive hand with a thin pen, part of a surviving set of 3 bifolios and 1 single folio (CBL Is Pp4, 5 and 6), all fragments from the same original codex, Ḥadīth Traditions attributed to the Prophet Muḥammad on the benefits of prayer (du`ā’), compiled by Khayr, (right fragment: single folio) one half of the bifolio that originally formed the book’s cover, with title (verso) stating the author as Khayr, noting that Khayr obtained his text via his teacher Khālid ibn Yazīd in the year 267H (880-881), with three historical anecdotes perpendicular to the writing direction, added later, (left fragment: bifolio) middle part of the bifolio only, Egypt, dated 267H, 880-881.

Is_Pp5.t: Papyrus bifolio from a Ḥadīth manuscript dated 267H (880-881)
Is_Pp5.c: Papyrus bifolio from a Ḥadīth manuscript dated 267H (880-881). Bifolio fragment, ink on dark brown papyrus, mounted on paper and framed under glass, Arabic text in a practiced cursive hand with a thin pen, part of a surviving set of 3 bifolios and 1 single folio (CBL Is Pp4, 5 and 6), all fragments from the same original codex, Ḥadīth Traditions attributed to the Prophet Muḥammad on the benefits of prayer (du`ā’), compiled by Khayr, under supervision from his teacher Khālid ibn Yazīd, Egypt, dated (written in CBL Is Pp4) 267H, 880-881.

Is_Pp6.t: Papyrus bifolio from a Ḥadīth manuscript dated 267H (880-881)
Is_Pp6.c: Papyrus bifolio from a Ḥadīth manuscript dated 267H (880-881). Bifolio fragment, ink on dark brown papyrus, mounted on paper and framed under glass, Arabic text in a practiced cursive hand with a thin pen, part of a surviving set of 3 bifolios and 1 single folio (CBL Is Pp4, 5 and 6), all fragments from the same original codex, Ḥadīth Traditions attributed to the Prophet Muḥammad on the benefits of prayer (du`ā’), compiled by Khayr, under supervision from his teacher Khālid ibn Yazīd, Egypt, dated (written in CBL Is Pp4) 267H, 880-881.

Is_Pp7.t: Papyrus pseudo-script, imitating a written letter
Is_Pp7.c: Papyrus pseudo-script, imitating a written letter. Folio fragment, ink on medium brown papyrus, mounted on paper and framed under glass, original cutting lines preserved on all sides, Arabic text written parallel to the fibres, basmala (line 1), followed by 17 lines of illegible writing in Arabic letter forms and X marks, possibly in magical or coded writing, unsigned, Egypt, undated, c. 800-900.

Is_Pp8.t: Papyrus letter to `Abdullāh ibn As`ad in Fayyūm
Is_Pp8.c: Papyrus letter to `Abdullāh ibn As`ad: an unidentified request. `Abdullāh ibn As`ad is well-known as the administrator of a district south-west of al-Fayyūm, near the town of Narmūda (Gr. Narmouthis) in Egypt, in c. 730-750. This papyrus letter was therefore probably posted to him in al-Fayyūm, but where the letter was sent from remains an open question. The sender, `Amr b. `Abdullāh, is not otherwise known in the historical record. Extensive blessings and greetings take up most of the surviving part of this fragile papyrus letter, which strongly suggests its intended function as a polite letter of request. In the final line just before the papyrus breaks off, `Amr writes that he would like `Abdullāh to do something once he receives his letter: with the rest of the letter missing, it is impossible to know what exactly that amounted to. Folio fragment, ink on fine light brown papyrus, mounted on paper and framed under glass, original cutting lines preserved at top, right and left sides

Is_Pp9.c: Papyrus accounts of the cloth merchant. Folio fragment, ink on medium brown papyrus, mounted on paper and framed under glass, original cutting lines preserved on the right and lower edges (recto) with some text loss at top and left, Arabic text, written in medium thick pen perpendicular to the fibres (on recto) and parallel to the fibres (on verso), accounting sheet for a cloth merchant business, recording separate accounts (min al-ḥisāba), each with columns for (1:) lists of personal names, including identifiable Christian Egyptian (Coptic) and ethnic or professional nisba surnames, (2:) textile goods reckoned in robes, cloth and bales, and (3:) prices in dinars, qīrāṭs and fractions of ‘current’ coins (jawāz), or purses, unsigned, Egypt, undated, c. 800-900.

Is_Pp10.c: Papyrus letter: an unidentified request. Folio fragment, ink on fine light brown papyrus, mounted on paper and framed under glass, original cutting lines preserved at top and right edges, Arabic text, written with a medium thick pen perpendicular to the fibres (on recto) and parallel to the fibres (on verso), (recto:) upper right corner of a letter to an un-named addressee, very politely expressed with extensive opening greetings, probably a request or petition, (verso:) written in the same hand, and probably a fragment of the letter's external address, unsigned, Egypt, undated, c. 800-900.

Is_Pp11.t: Papyrus letter and agricultural lease: sowing wheat
Is_Pp11.c: Papyrus letter and agricultural lease . Folio fragment, ink on dark brown papyrus, mounted on paper and framed under glass, broken off on all sides with text loss of text at top, left and right edges, Arabic text, written in a practiced cursive hand perpendicular to the fibres (on recto), and in a large hand with a thicker pen parallel to the fibres (on verso), two un-related documents, (recto:) agricultural lease (qabāla), witnessed document leasing one faddān of land for the cultivation of wheat, issued to Muḥammad son of `Abdullāh, (verso:) probably a letter, unsigned, Egypt, dated (on recto) between 271-279H or 291-299H, c. 884-911.

Is_Pp12.t: Papyrus letter and agricultural register: the wheat harvest
Is_Pp12.c: Papyrus letter and agricultural register: the wheat harvest. Folio fragment, ink on light brown papyrus, mounted on paper and framed under glass, cut at the top and bottom for re-use, later broken on right side (recto), Arabic text, written with thin pen parallel to the fibres (on recto), and with fine pen perpendicular to the fibres (on verso), two un-related documents, (recto:) commercial letter confirming wheat deliveries and shipments, (verso:) agricultural register of crops sown, land used, wheat and trefoil harvest yield and resulting tax calculations owed by two land-holders, unsigned, Egypt, undated, c. 700-900.

Is_Pp13.t: Papyrus letters: goods delivery and the wheat crop
Is_Pp13.c: Papyrus letters about goods delivery and the wheat crop. Two folio fragments, ink on medium to light brown papyrus, mounted on paper and framed under glass, Arabic text, written with a thick pen perpendicular to the fibres, fragments of two letters, (Letter 1:) papyrus broken off at the top and right, with substantial loss of text, letter confirming the sender has dispatched "two bundles" of goods to the addressee, using Greek letters throughout as numbers, (Letter 2:) papyrus broken off at the top, bottom and right, letter refers to wheat, both documents unsigned, Egypt, undated, 800-900.

Is_Pp14.t: Papyrus tax receipt and payment register
Is_Pp14.c: Papyrus tax receipt and payment register. Folio fragment, ink on fine, light brown papyrus, mounted on paper and framed under glass, broken off on left edge (recto) with substantial text loss, Arabic text, written with a fine pen parallel to the fibres (on recto) and perpendicular to the fibres (on verso), (recto:) tax receipt for Muḥammad son of `Abdullāh, (verso:) six columns of figures, using Greek letters as numerals, for a register of payments or impositions presumably also linked to taxation, text on verso written first, after which the folio was re-used to write the recto text, unsigned, Egypt, dated (on recto) 241-249H, 855-863.

Is_Pp15.c: Papyrus letters: work and taxation. Folio fragment, ink on dark brown papyrus, mounted on paper and framed under glass, original cutting line preserved on the left edge but broken off at the top (recto), Arabic text, written with a medium thick pen parallel to the fibres on recto, and a monumental script with a thick pen on verso, two separate letters about administrative work, (recto:) letter directing the addressee to perform a task, with reference to a paymaster (qusṭāl), (verso:) letter referring to taxation (al-kharāj), written in well-spaced chancery format, first used on the verso side then cut for re-use on the recto, unsigned, Egypt, undated, c. 800-1000.

Is_Pp16.c: Papyrus letters with agricultural discussions. Folio fragment, ink on light brown papyrus, mounted on paper and framed under glass, Arabic text, written with a thick pen parallel to the fibres on recto, and in large well-spaced hand on the verso, two separate letters about agricultural work, (recto:) letter referring to plots of land for ploughing (ḥarth) or leaving fallow (fa-qad ʿaṭṭalat/ʿaṭṭaltu), and to other unnamed correspondents and messengers, (verso:) letter beginning and ending with polite blessings wished upon the (unnamed) addressee, first used on the verso side then cut for re-use on the recto, unsigned, Egypt, undated, c. 800-900.

Is_Pp17.t: Papyrus letters in fragments: something happened
Is_Pp17.c: Papyrus letters in fragments: something happened. Fifteen folio fragments, ink on dark brown papyrus, mounted on paper and framed under glass, Arabic text, written with a thin pen perpendicular to the fibres on recto, and parallel to the fibres on verso, all fragments from the same single folio, two separate letters, (recto:) letter referring to something that happened “today” (fī hādhā al-yawm), and hoping that something else will happen God-willing (in shāʾa allāh), (verso:) letter referring to individuals (al-Ḥusayn, Muḥammad, Abū `Alī), unsigned, Egypt, undated, c. 800-900.

Is_Pp18.t: Papyrus letter about finding a new tenant and selling a pearl in Fusṭāṭ, and a statement of accounts
Is_Pp18.c: Papyrus letter about finding a new tenant and selling a pearl in Fusṭāṭ, and a statement of accounts. Folio fragment, ink on light to medium brown papyrus, mounted on paper and framed under glass, Arabic text, written perpendicular to the fibres, two separate documents, (on recto:) letter from a property-owner in Fayyūm asking a friend in Fusṭāṭ to get his estate agent Zayd ibn Muzāḥim to find a new tenant for a recently-vacated room with the rent set between 6 and 8 dinars a year, and then as a postscript, he asks the friend to follow up an expected payment of 16 dinars for a pearl that was recently sold by `Alā’ the jeweller, (on verso, added later:) list of accounts, in two columns, recording personal names and the money owed or received (in dirhams), unsigned, al-Fayyūm, Egypt, undated, c. 800-900

Is_Pp19.c: Papyrus ledger of accounts. Folio fragment, ink on light brown papyrus, mounted on paper and framed under glass, original cutting lines preserved at top, left and right edges, broken at top and lower right, Arabic text written in two different hands, perpendicular to the fibres (recto) and parallel (on verso), folio from a fiscal ledger with account details presented in columns, with payments from different groups (including shepherds) due or completed in dinars, using Greek letters as numerals, unsigned, Egypt, undated, c. 700-900.

Is_Pp20.t: Six papyrus fragments of letters, lists and other documents
Is_Pp20.c: Six papyrus fragments of letters, lists and other documents. Six folio fragments, ink on papyrus, mounted on paper and framed under glass, Arabic and (for 53 only:) Coptic text, numbered 48 to 53 (stickers on glass frame), fragments from different documents, (48:) written on light papyrus with fine pen perpendicular to the fibres (on recto), (recto:) list of names of men and women, followed by (verso:) columns of numbers in Greek letters, undated, 750-900, (49:) written on medium brown papyrus with thin pen parallel to the fibres (on recto), text repeats the bismillah, with possible pseudoscript, undated, 800-900, (50:) written on light brown papyrus with fine pen perpendicular to the fibres (on recto), fragment of a letter referring to money owed, undated, 700-900, (51:) written with medium thick pen perpendicular to the fibres (on recto), (recto:) fragment of a letter complaining about receiving threats, (verso:) receipt for payment of one dinar, with blessings wished on the addresse

Is_Pp21.c: Block-printed amulet on paper. Amulet scroll, ink and colour on paper backed and edged with recycled fragments of papyrus, mounted on paper and under glass, Arabic block-printed text in angular script, with headings and illuminated panel, pious invocations seeking refuge in God, quoting Qur'an Sura 3:18, blank verso, unsigned, Egypt, undated, c. 900-1400

Is_Pp22.t: Parchment folio from the Prophet's biography
Is_Pp22.c: Folio from the Prophet's biography. Is_Pp30.c: Poetry amulet on paper: Qaṣīda, by Riḍwān ibn Da'ūd. Folio, ink on paper, folded for portable use as an amulet, Arabic text in naskh script, (recto:) title heading, the poem (qaṣīda) by Riḍwān ibn Da'ūd ibn Abū [...], (verso:) poetry verses in rhyming couplets, unsigned, Egypt, undated, 1000-1400.

Is_Pp31.t: Love poetry by Ibn Sūdūn (d. 1464), and magic recipes
Is_Pp31.c: Love poetry and magic recipes from Cairo. Bifolio, ink on paper, from a codex (binding holes in central fold), Arabic text in naskh script, in two different hands, (smaller text:) recipes (ṣifa) for magic potions, noting ingredients (lisān al-thawr =borage, al-`aqrab al-aṣfar =yellow scorpion) in amounts of dirhams, with preparation instructions, (larger text:) verses by the Cairo poet Ibn Sūdūn (d. 1464), unsigned, Egypt, undated, c. 1500-1510

Is_Sc6.c: The astrolabe is an adjustable instrument that maps the stars, and has many other functions. The device can be set to the user’s location on earth, and to the correct time. On the front, the curling pointers on the openwork plate (al-`ankabut in Arabic, or spider) are each labelled with a star’s name. Invented in late classical times, the astrolabe was perfected in the early Islamic period. Astrolabe, brass, with incised text, mapping lines and decoration, instrument with six latitude plates, openwork rete (`ankabut), sight-rule (alidade), wedge (faras) and pin, engraved mapping lines and labels (throughout), dedicated to Safavid shah Sulṭān Ḥusayn (r. 1694-1722), produced and engraved (ṣana`ahu wa nammaqahu) by `Abd al-A’imma ibn `Abd al-Ḥusayn (signature and date on back), Isfahan, Iran, dated 1120H, 1708-1709.

Is_Tx2.t: Velvet panel for a balcony rail
Is_Tx2.c: Velvet panel for a balcony rail. This silk panel is designed to hang over a balcony rail, showing the same image on either side: a row of flowering plants, drafted with careful naturalism. While this reflects court taste in seventeenth-century India, the textile structure reveals that it was produced in contemporary Safavid Iran, almost certainly for export to neighbouring India. According to an inventory note on the back, by February 1648, the panel was in the royal textile store (farrashkhana) in Amer fort in Jaipur, then ruled by Maharaja Jai Singh I (r. 1621-1667). Panel, silk velvet, designed to hang over a balcony rail, two matching designs of leafy flowering plants and curling clouds against cream ground, bordered with floral scollwork of tulips and narcissi, on the reverse are five dated inventory statements written in Hindi in Devanagari script (ranging between 1648 and 1666), recording the textile's size and valuation, added at the royal textile store (farrashkhana) at Amer F

Is_X6.c: Book-stand (rahl). This book-stand folds out into a standing x-shape, to hold an open book. The functional design goes back many centuries, and is also produced in woodwork and other media. This one is very similar to another example (now in the V&A) produced by Mahomed Amin: his award-winning work was displayed at a 1903 exhibition in Delhi, celebrating the accession of Edward VII (r. 1901-1910) as Emperor of India. Folding book-stand (rahl), carved stone (bowenite, a variant of serpentine), with gold-overlaid steel frame, stonework probably Bhera, metalwork probably Sialkot, Pakistan, c. 1900.

Is_X17.c: Pair of doors with ivory inlay. These two doors contain a central design of carved ivory and wooden elements, which have been salvaged from an older pair (probably from a minbar, or pulpit), and re-mounted in modern frames. This type of composite reconstruction was an important woodworking industry in nineteeth-century Cairo, and represented a combination of fragment salvage and historicist imitation. The industry continued into the twentieth century. Few of the original decorative segments remain here, and the joiner has carved new "replacement" panels to fill up the geometric pattern. When closed together, the pair of doors create a single twelve-sided polygon in their central design. Two door (matching pair), wood frame with carved wood (unidentified) and ivory inlays, metal lock and hinges, each with main vertical panel of three half dodecagons (offset) with central radiating stars, smaller ivory-outlined panels at top and bottom, probably Cairo, Egypt, some of the carved ivory fol

Is_X33.c: Amulet case. Case, watered steel with gold inlay, hollow faceted cylinder with rounded ends and three loop attachments, designed to contain a paper scroll written with Islamic prayers, to protect the owner, Iran, c. 1750-1850.

J_0021.t: Netsuke in shape of the twelve zodiac animals
J_0021.c: Netsuke in the shape of animals from the twelve zodiac, made of ivory, carved by Masamitsu in Japan, c. 1870-1890. The animals’ eyes are inlaid with dark buffalo horn. Masamitsu is an artist known for netsuke carved in the shape of groups of tiny puppies or other animals. He was originally a samurai in the service of Tatebayashi Akimoto who governed Jōshū, in present–day Gunma prefecture (province) in eastern Japan. In 1868, the emperor’s rule was restored and the samurai warrior class was abolished which led to the large-scale unemployment of samurai. In order to seek a new career, Masamitsu studied ivory and tusk carving in Tokyo. Exhibited in 'Zodiac Netsuke: Animals of the Japanese Zodiac in Miniature', 6 December 2024 - 23 March 2025.

J_0027.c: Netsuke in the shape of a puppy, made by Waraku in Osaka, Japan around 1850. Stained ivory with eyes inlaid in buffalo horn. In the mid-18th century, fluffy, chubby puppies painted by Kyoto artist Maruyama Ōkyo (1733–1795) became very popular. Netsuke artists were also influenced by this artistic trend. In Japan, the dog became associated with an easy childbirth. Therefore, pregnant women often visit a shrine on the day of the dog which comes once every twelve days. Exhibited in 'Zodiac Netsuke: Animals of the Japanese Zodiac in Miniature', 6 December 2024 - 23 March 2025.

J_0058.c: Stained ivory netsuke in the shape of a goat, made in Japan, c.1890. Eyes inlaid with buffalo horn. By the eighth century, Japanese nobles were familiar with sheep through their exposure to Buddhist texts from China. Since then, sheep have inspired the imagination in Japanese arts and literature. As they were not native to Japan, sheep were often depicted like goats. Exhibited in 'Zodiac Netsuke: Animals of the Japanese Zodiac in Miniature', 6 December 2024 - 23 March 2025.

J_0059.t: Netsuke in shape of rooster on drum with inscription
J_0059.c: Netsuke in the shape of a chicken on a drum, made of boxwood, mother-of-pearl, buffalo horn, lacquer and copper-gold alloy (shakudō), made in Japan around 1850. A chicken sits comfortably on a drum which is not being played. In an ancient Chinese legend, King Yu encouraged the public to sound the drum at the gate of his palace if he was not governing well. Familiar with this legend in Japan, the image of a chicken on a drum symbolised good governance. Exhibited in 'Zodiac Netsuke: Animals of the Japanese Zodiac in Miniature', 6 December 2024 - 23 March 2025.

J_0063.t: Netsuke in shape of horse emerging from gourd
J_0063.c: Netsuke in the shape of a horse emerging from a gourd, made of elephant ivory, carved in Japan around 1780. The Japanese expression ‘a young horse has come out of a gourd’ means something unexpected has happened. The saying likely came from a Chinese story of the immortal, Zhang Guolao, who wandered on a donkey. When Zhang stopped to rest, he would fold the creature up like a piece of paper and store it in a box. When he was ready to resume his wandering, he would pour water over the folded paper to turn it back into a donkey. Exhibited in 'Zodiac Netsuke: Animals of the Japanese Zodiac in Miniature', 6 December 2024 - 23 March 2025.

J_0066.c: Netsuke in the shape of a monkey, made of ivory, carved in the style of Mitsuhide in Japan around 1820. A seated monkey gazes downward as if absorbed in thought. With human-like characteristics, Japanese artists often portrayed monkeys expressing human feelings. Monkeys are messengers for the many mountain gods in Japan. Exhibited in 'Zodiac Netsuke: Animals of the Japanese Zodiac in Miniature', 6 December 2024 - 23 March 2025.

J_0075.c: Netsuke in the shape of a boar, made of boxwood and buffalo horn, carved in Japan around 1870. In Japan, the boar replaced the pig as the last zodiac animal. These wild mountain animals have been associated with the many mountain gods in Japanese folklore. The boar represents strength and fertility. People wish for good health and an easy childbirth by eating a rice cake on the day of the boar in the tenth month, the month of the boar. Exhibited in 'Zodiac Netsuke: Animals of the Japanese Zodiac in Miniature', 6 December 2024 - 23 March 2025.

J_0076.c: Netsuke in the shape of a hare, made of wood, carved in Japan around 1890. In Japan, the hare has been worshiped as a mountain god associated with fertility. In Japan and China, the hare has also been associated with the moon. In China, a hare uses a mortar and pestle to produce an elixir of immortality on the moon; in Japan, the hare prepares a rice cake on the moon. Exhibited in 'Zodiac Netsuke: Animals of the Japanese Zodiac in Miniature', 6 December 2024 - 23 March 2025.

J_0080.t: Netsuke in shape of rat on New Year rice cakes (kagami mochi)
J_0080.c: Netsuke in the shape of a rat on New Year cakes (kagami mochi), made of stained boxwood, carved by Masakatsu in Japan around 1850-70. To welcome the New Year God, Japanese households display two layers of rice cakes (kagami mochi) on a wooden stand called a sampō. The rat is the first of the twelve zodiac animals, but it is also considered a messenger of Daikoku, the god of wealth. When the rat appears on the New Year’s Day, it is considered lucky. The artist Masakatsu was famous for carving boxwood netsuke. Exhibited in 'Zodiac Netsuke: Animals of the Japanese Zodiac in Miniature', 6 December 2024 - 23 March 2025.

J_0084.c: Netsuke in the shape of a tiger, made of boxwood and buffalo horn, carved by Masanao in Japan around 1880. Although not native to Japan, the tiger was a popular animal in Japanese culture as it was believed to prevent illness. To imagine these fierce animals, Japanese artists relied on depictions in Chinese and Korean paintings, or from imported tiger skins. As a result, Japanese images of tigers often resembled cats. Exhibited in 'Zodiac Netsuke: Animals of the Japanese Zodiac in Miniature', 6 December 2024 - 23 March 2025.

J_0108.t: Netsuke in shape of snake attacking toad on waraji sandal
J_0108.c: Netsuke in the shape of a snake attacking a toad on a waraji sandal, made of boxwood and buffalo horn, carved by Shōko in Japan around 1890. A moment is captured as a snake is about to eat his prey. Able to shed its skin and sometimes lethally poisonous, the snake has been associated with eternal life and power. It has been worshiped as either an earth or water god. Exhibited in 'Zodiac Netsuke: Animals of the Japanese Zodiac in Miniature', 6 December 2024 - 23 March 2025.

J_0270.t: Netsuke in shape of ox and herd boy reading
J_0270.c: Netsuke in the shape of an ox and a heard boy reading, made of ivory, carved by Gyokkōsai in Japan around 1880. The image of a herd boy reading on a resting ox represents the ideal of a peaceful life. In Zen Buddhism, the pair appear as an allegory on the different stages of enlightenment: the ox represents the true, enlightened self which the herder is seeking. Exhibited in 'Zodiac Netsuke: Animals of the Japanese Zodiac in Miniature', 6 December 2024 - 23 March 2025.

J_0319.t: Manjū netsuke with dragon in clouds
J_0319.c: Netsuke in the shape of a dragon in clouds, made of yew wood and silver by Eguro Suketada (Shōko) in Japan around 1880. A dragon with beaming eyes of silver is shown emerging from clouds. The dragon is the only mythical and supernatural animal among the twelve animals of the zodiac. The creature is associated with the sky and water – that is why it is often depicted with clouds or among waves. This type of round netsuke is called a manjū, which means ‘steamed bun’. Exhibited in 'Zodiac Netsuke: Animals of the Japanese Zodiac in Miniature', 6 December 2024 - 23 March 2025.

J_1004_1.t: Volume 1 from Biography of Prince Shōtoku (Shōtoku Taishi den)
J_1004_1.c: Manuscript book, Volume 1 from 'Biography of Prince Shōtoku' (Shōtoku Taishi den), the text illustrated with paintings in ink, colours and gold on paper; made in Japan, 17th century. Part of a 5 volume set relating pious deeds, miracles and omens from the life of Prince Shōtoku (574-622), held to be an important figure in the development of Buddhism in Japan.

A part of a 3 volume set relating the origins of the principal deities of Kumano’s three main shrines (Kumano Sansho Gongen). The last volume is missing from the set.

J_1008.t: Album of the thirty-six immortal poets (Sanjūrokkasen jō)
J_1008.c: Album of the thirty-six immortal poets (Sanjūrokkasen jō) made in Japan, mid-17th century. 36 poems are written on decorated square paper in ink. Accompanying portraits of 36 poets are painted by Sumiyoshi Gukei in ink, colours and gold on silk, The thirty-six immortal poets were selected by Fujiwara no Kintō (966-1041) in his anthology Selections of thirty-six poets. Sumiyoshi Gukei (1631-1705) carefully painted the poets, paying attention to fine details. A later index, written in English, is attached inside the cover, and English-language captions are pasted below the poems. Textile covers with metal corner mounts.

J_1016.t: Album of the six great poets (Rokkasen jō)
J_1016.c: Album of the six great poets (Rokkasen jō), painted by Reizei Tamechika in ink and colours on soft-coloured paper; made in Japan in the 19th century. Reizei Tamechika (1823-1864), who revived classical Japanese painting called yamato-e, painted six great poets from the Thirty-six Immortal Poets selected by Fujiwara no Kintō (966-1041). He inscribed his name on the first, third, and sixth image and stamped his seal on each painting.

J_1017_1.t: Volume 1 from Yoshitsune's invasion of hell (Yoshitsune jigoku yaburi)
J_1017_1.c: Manuscript book, Volume 1 from 'Yoshitsune's invasion of hell' (Yoshitsune jigoku yaburi) the text illustrated with paintings in ink, colours and gold on paper, bound with silk covers painted with butterflies; made in Japan, mid-17th century. This pair of volumes relate one of the many stories told of the warrior of Minamoto no Yoshitsune (1159-1189). In this story, the dead Yoshitsune is assigned to the realm of hell inhabited by the ashura demons and reserved for those destined to continue fighting. Hoping to escape the hardships of this realm, Yoshitsune assembles a band of famous warriors and sets out to invade hell's lower reaches. This particular story is notable for its inclusion of a Buddhist ascetic who bears witness to the unfolding events and is responsible for their retelling. This observer (typically shown carrying a fan) can be seen in each illustration.

J_1021_1.t: Volume 1 from Tale of Sumiyoshi (Sumiyoshi monogatari)
J_1021_1.c: Manuscript book, Volume 1 from 'Tale of Sumiyoshi' (Sumiyoshi monogatari) the text illustrated with paintings in ink, colours and gold on paper, bound with silk covers painted with young pines; created by Koizumi, a picture book shop in Kyoto, Japan, in 17th century. Large horizontal format. The Tale of Sumiyoshi is the story of a princess who escapes from her stepmother's bullying to the Sumiyoshi Shrine for protection. Bodhisattva Kannon of Hasedera Temple mystically guides a courtier who falls in love with the princess to the Sumiyoshi Shrine and reunites the couple. They live happily ever after.

a: Unknown; Ogata Kenzan, formerly attributed to
J_1047.c: Manuscript book, 'Hanaya', painted in ink and colours on paper by an unknown artist, Japan, 1573-1744. The story of Hanaya was published in print in 1634. This volume, however, is a manuscript version of the work with hand-painted illustrations. It contains the first part of the story and was likely originally part of a set of two volumes. The date of this work is a matter of debate, with dates either side of the published edition of Hanaya cited. Some scholars date this volume to the Momoyama period (1573-c. 1603), others date it to the early or even mid-Edo period (c. 1603-1868). The attribution to Ogata Kenzan as artist inscribed on the cover is considered spurious.

J_1049_1.c: Folios from a death register (kakocho), written in gold on blue-dyed paper with inset paintings on silk, created in Japan in the 17th or 18th century. These concertina folios are part of a death register or kakocho (CBL J 1049.1-49) of the Jōdo Shinshū Buddhist tradition. The register is divided into thirty days, each presided over by a Buddha or bodhisattva (awakened being). The names of the dead were recorded by date so prayers could be offered on their anniversary. An attached note suggests an association to a daughter of Iwakura Dainagon. Dainagon is a court title, and may in this case refer to Iwakura Tomomi (1825-1883). The majority of the names written into the manuscript have since been erased, leaving only traces of gold. These folios include multiple dedications to Amida Buddha, ‘Namu Amida Butsu’ (the Nembutsu).

J_1050_1.t: Volume 1 from Tales of Ise (Ise monogatari)
J_1050_1.c: Manuscript book, Volume 1 from 'Tales of Ise' (Ise monogatari), the text illustrated with paintings in ink, colours and gold on paper; made in Japan in the late sixteenth century. Part of a 3 volume set of this tenth-century literary masterwork, which combines verse and prose to narrate the romantic and poetic exploits of its protagonist, understood to represent the courtier Ariwara no Narihira (825–880).

J_1112.t: Illustrated scroll of the 12 months (Jūnikagetsu zukan)
J_1112.c: Illustrated scroll of the 12 months (Jūnikagetsu zukan), painted in ink and light colours on paper in Japan in the late-17th century. Poems on birds and flowers of the twelve composed by Fujiwara no Teika (1162-1241) are written on paper dyed in different colours with gold leaf and gold paint. Birds and flowers in Teika's poem are subtly depicted in the accompanying paintings of seasonal events, paired with each month's poem.

J_1113.t: Tales of Uji Shūi (Uji Shūi monogatari emaki)
J_1113.c: Handscroll painting of the 'Tales of Uji Shūi' (Uji Shūi monogatari emaki), painted in ink, colours and gold on paper in Japan probably during the Kanbun era (1661-1673). A compilation of older stories, the Tales of Uji Shūi are thought to have been completed in the first half of the thirteenth century. This Edo-period (c. 1603-1868) painted handscroll includes text and accompanying illustrations for five of these short stories: 'A miracle by the priest Seikan' (tale number 20), 'A curious incident at Minase Palace in the night' (tale 159), 'A hunter from the east prevents a scarifice' (tale 119), 'A pirate who became a monk' (tale 123) and 'Bodhidharma observes the path of priests in India' (tale 137).

J_1117_1.t: Scroll 1 from Tale of Musashibō Benkei (Musashibō e engi jō)
J_1117_1.c: Scroll 1 from 'Tale of Musashibō Benkei' (Musashibō e Engi jō) painted in ink and colours on paper in Japan in the second half of the 16th century. One of a set of three illustrated handscrolls that tell the story of Benkei, a semi-legendary warrior monk and loyal retainer of the warlord Minamoto no Yoshitsune (1159-1189). In the first scroll, an unusual child is discovered living in the wild. Shaving his head, he becomes a monk and takes the name Benkei, but he also grows to be a mighty warrior.

J_1117_2.t: Scroll 2 from Tale of Musashibō Benkei (Musashibō e engi chū)
J_1117_2.c: Scroll 2 from 'Tale of Musashibō Benkei' (Musashibō e Engi jō) painted in ink and colours on paper in Japan in the second half of the 16th century. One of a set of three illustrated handscrolls that tell the story of Benkei, a semi-legendary warrior monk and loyal retainer of the warlord Minamoto no Yoshitsune (1159-1189). In the second scroll, after travelling widely, Benkei encounters the young Minamoto no Yoshitsune. Despite his great strength, Benkei is defeated by the agile youth and pledges his allegiance to him.

J_1117_3.t: Scroll 3 from Tale of Musashibō Benkei (Musashibō e engi ge)
J_1117_3.c: Scroll 3 from 'Tale of Musashibō Benkei' (Musashibō e Engi jō) painted in ink and colours on paper in Japan in the second half of the 16th century. One of a set of three illustrated handscrolls that tell the story of Benkei, a semi-legendary warrior monk and loyal retainer of the warlord Minamoto no Yoshitsune (1159-1189). In the third scroll, Benkei's teacher Kankei is abducted by enemy forces. Taking leave of Yoshitsune, Benkei rescues Kankei before returning to Yoshitsune's side.

J_1118_1.t: Scroll 1 from Illustrated scrolls of recreations of the twelve months (Jūnigatsu asobi emaki)
J_1118_1.c: Scroll 1 from Illustrated scrolls of recreations of the twelve months (Jūnigatsu asobi emaki), painted in ink and colours on paper in Japan in the mid-seventeenth century. Traditional monthly festivals and activities celebrated in and around Kyoto are depicted in this pair of scrolls.

J_1118_2.t: Scroll 2 from Illustrated scrolls of recreations of the twelve months (Jūnigatsu asobi emaki)
J_1118_2.c: Scroll 2 from Illustrated scrolls of recreations of the twelve months (Jūnigatsu asobi emaki), painted in ink and colours on paper in Japan in the mid-seventeenth century. Traditional monthly festivals and activities celebrated in and around Kyoto are depicted in this pair of scrolls.

J_1120.t: Scenes of city and country (Tohi zukan)
J_1120.c: Handscroll painting, 'Scenes of city and country (Tohi zukan) by Sumiyoshi Gukei, painted in ink and colours on silk, Japan, 1691-1705. Serving as official painter to the ruling Tokugawa shogunate in Edo (modern Tokyo), Sumiyoshi Gukei (1631-1705) painted three handscrolls of life in ‘the old capital’: Kyoto. As the scroll moves through the bustling city and out to its environs, the seasons also shift. Although this scroll has suffered extensive discolouration, the close attention to detail that characterises works of the Sumiyoshi school can still be enjoyed. The other two examples are preserved at Tokyo National Museum and Kōfukuin temple, Nara.

J_1121.t: Illustrated scroll of the debate over sake and rice (Shuhanron emaki)
J_1121.c: 'Illustrated scroll of the debate over sake and rice' (Shuhanron emaki) painted in ink and colours on paper by an unknown artist in Japan in the mid-seventeenth century. Presented as a single handscroll, with sheets of calligraphy interspersed with painted scenes, the scroll shows three men embroiled in a debate. The first, Mikinoshō Kasuya no Nagamochi extols the virtues of drinking sake; the teetotaler Iimuro no Rishi Kōhan contends that it is best to avoid alcohol and eat only rice; the third man, Naka no Saemon no Tayū Nakahara no Nakanari, enjoys both sake and rice, and (as his name suggests) advocates for the middle path. The painted scenes present each of these alternatives: a heady drinking party, a gluttonous feast, and a balanced banquet. In the accompanying text, the story is fleshed out as each protagonist expounds upon the virtues of their chosen course. Playful though it might appear, the debate between the three men is in fact an allegory comparing different schools of B

J_1122_1.t: Scroll 1 of Entertainments of the 12 months (Jūnigatsu asobi)
J_1122_1.c: Scroll 1 of Entertainments of the 12 months (Jūnigatsu asobi), handscroll painting in ink, colours and gold on paper, painted by an unknown artist, Japan, second half of 17th century. Scenes of activities of the first six months of the year in the capital, Kyoto.

J_1122_2.t: Scroll 2 of Entertainments of the 12 months (Jūnigatsu asobi)
J_1122_2.c: Scroll 2 of Entertainments of the 12 months (Jūnigatsu asobi), handscroll painting in ink, colours and gold on paper, painted by an unknown artist, Japan, second half of 17th century. Scenes of activities of the last six months of the year in the capital, Kyoto.

J_1123.c: Handscroll painting, Leisurely activities by the waterside, painted in ink and colours on silk by Miyagawa Chōshun in the early 18th century, Japan. Signature: Nihon-e Miyagawa Chōshun zu. Pictures of the floating world—ukiyo-e—were created as paintings as well as in print. In a pair of waterside pavilions, men of wealth and taste relax in the company of male and female beauties. Painted in rich pigments on silk, this painting was probably created for an affluent patron. As this scroll shows spring and summer foliage, it may once have been paired with a scroll with an autumn / winter setting.

J_1124.c: Scroll of 'Tale of Princess Ejima' (Ejima monogatari) the text accompanied by illustrations painted in ink, colours and gold on paper; made in Japan in the mid-17th century. This single scroll was probably once one of a pair. It tells the story of Princess Ejima and her mother, the renowned warrior Lady Hangaku. In the story, both Princess Ejima and Hangaku fight valiantly against the warrior Shinkai Kōshirō, who had killed Hangaku's husband.

J_1125_1.t: Scroll 1 from Tale of the bamboo cutter (Taketori monogatari)
J_1125_1.c: Scroll 1 from the 'Tale of the bamboo cutter' (Taketori monogatari), the text accompanied by illustrations by an unknown artist thought to belong to the circle of Kanō Takanobu, painted in ink, colours, gold and silver on paper; made in Japan in the early 17th century. One of a pair of handscrolls telling the tale of the 'Shining Princess', Princess Kaguya. In Scroll 1, the bamboo cutter discovers a child of supernatural beauty in a bamboo stalk and brings her to his home. There, he and his wife raise her as their daughter, naming her the Shining Princess of the Supple Bamboo. The Chester Beatty scrolls are believed to be the earliest surviving illustrated version of this historic and popular tale. They were conserved with the support of the Sumitomo Foundation at Restorient Studio, Leiden, between 2010 and 2012.

J_1125_2.t: Scroll 2 from Tale of the bamboo cutter (Taketori monogatari)
J_1125_2.c: Scroll 2 from the 'Tale of the bamboo cutter' (Taketori monogatari), the text accompanied by illustrations by an unknown artist thought to belong to the circle of Kanō Takanobu, painted in ink, colours, gold and silver on paper; made in Japan in the early 17th century. One of a pair of handscrolls telling the tale of the 'Shining Princess', Princess Kaguya. In Scroll 2, Princess Kaguya's remaining suitors fail to acheive the tasks she has set them, and the emperor himself falls in love with her. The Princess, however, longs only to return to her original home, the Palace of the Moon, which she does bidding her adoptive parents a sorrowful goodbye. The Chester Beatty scrolls are believed to be the earliest surviving illustrated version of this historic and popular tale. They were conserved with the support of the Sumitomo Foundation at Restorient Studio, Leiden, between 2010 and 2012.

J_1126_1.t: Scroll 1 of Genji text and pictures (Genji kotobae)
a: Anonymous; Prince Gyōjo of Myōhōin (堯恕法親王); Takatsukasa Kanehiro (鷹司兼煕); Prince Yukihito of Arisugawa (有栖川宮幸仁親王); Imadegawa Kinnori (今出川公規); Sono Motoyoshi (園基福); Karasumaru Mitsuo (烏丸光雄); Imadegawa Koresue (今出川伊季)
J_1126_1.c: Scroll 1 of Genji text and pictures (Genji kotobae), painted in ink, colours and gold on paper; made in Japan c. 1688. This set of four handscrolls depicts selected scenes from all fifty-four chapters of the Tale of Genji. Twenty-seven calligraphers of the highest rank each inscribed two chapters on this set of scrolls. This scroll depicts scenes from Chapters 1-14 of the Tale of Genji accompanied by a passage corresponding text written by Prince Gyōjo of Myōhōin (1640-1695), Takatsukasa Kanehiro (1659-1725), Prince Yukihito of Arisugawa (1656-99), Imadegawa Kinnori (1638-1697), Sono Motoyoshi (1622-1699), Karasumaru Mitsuo (1647-1690), and Imadegawa Koresue (1660-1709). The scrolls were conserved through the courtesy of the Japan's Imperial Household with the support of Mr and Mrs Hirose in 1985.

J_1127_1.t: Scroll from Tale of Muramatsu (Muramatsu monogatari emaki)
J_1127_1.c: Handscroll from the 'Tale of Muramatsu' (Muramatsu monogatari emaki) painted in the style of Iwasa Matabei, in ink, colours, gold and silver on paper in Japan in the first half of the 17th century. This is one of three illustrated handscrolls in the Chester Beatty collection that tell the story of Muramatsu, head of a powerful clan. Originally, these scrolls would have belonged to a larger set, and as such, the narrative is incomplete. In this scroll, the Musashi and Sagami clans hold a banquet to welcome the new provincial governors, Kaneuji and his son Kaneie, and Muramatsu builds a luxurious mansion for the governors.

J_1127_2.t: Scroll from Tale of Muramatsu (Muramatsu monogatari emaki)
J_1127_2.c: Handscroll from the 'Tale of Muramatsu' (Muramatsu monogatari emaki) painted in the style of Iwasa Matabei, in ink, colours, gold and silver on paper in Japan in the first half of the 17th century. This is one of three illustrated handscrolls in the Chester Beatty collection that tell the story of Muramatsu, head of a powerful clan. Originally, these scrolls would have belonged to a larger set, and as such, the narrative is incomplete. In this scroll, Kaneie (now married to Muramatsu's daughter) is parted from his wife to join his father Kaneuji in exile on the island of Okinoshima.

J_1127_3.t: Scroll from Tale of Muramatsu (Muramatsu monogatari emaki)
J_1127_3.c: Handscroll from the 'Tale of Muramatsu' (Muramatsu monogatari emaki) painted in the style of Iwasa Matabei, in ink, colours, gold and silver on paper in Japan in the first half of the 17th century. This is one of three illustrated handscrolls in the Chester Beatty collection that tell the story of Muramatsu, head of a powerful clan. Originally, these scrolls would have belonged to a larger set, and as such, the narrative is incomplete. In this scroll, Princess Muramatsu, separated from her husband Kaneie who is exiled from the capital, is living in the household of Takei. Infatuated with the princess, Takei writes her a love letter, but it is intercepted by his wife. Princess Muramatsu's hair is cut short and she is forced to work in the stables and rice fields.

J_1128_1.t: Minister Yuriwaka (Yuriwaka daijin) from the Picture scrolls of ballad dramas (Mai no hon emaki)
J_1128_1.c: Handscroll from the 'Picture scrolls of ballad dramas' (Mai no hon emaki) painted in ink, colours and gold on paper in Japan in the mid-17th century. This is one of six illustrated handscrolls in the Chester Beatty collection that tell stories from Japan's Kōwaka mai ballad dramas. Combining alternating sections of text and illustrations, these scrolls would have belonged to a larger set. This scroll features the story of the Minister Yuriwaka (Yuriwaka daijin). Appointed governor of Kyushu, Yuriwaka leads the army against an invading Mongol fleet, but is then stranded on a desolate island.

J_1128_2.t: Takadachi from the Picture scrolls of ballad dramas (Mai no hon emaki)
J_1128_2.c: Handscroll from the 'Picture scrolls of ballad dramas' (Mai no hon emaki) painted in ink, colours and gold on paper in Japan in the mid-17th century. This is one of six illustrated handscrolls in the Chester Beatty collection that tell stories from Japan's Kōwaka mai ballad dramas. Combining alternating sections of text and illustrations, these scrolls would have belonged to a larger set. This scroll features the story of 'Takadachi', a glorified account of the final battle of hero Minamoto no Yoshitsune (1159-1189).

J_1128_3.t: Tokiwa at Fushimi (Fushimi Tokiwa) and Tokiwa's disputation (Tokiwa mondō) from the Picture scrolls of ballad dramas (Mai no hon emaki)
J_1128_3.c: Handscroll from the 'Picture scrolls of ballad dramas' (Mai no hon emaki) painted in ink, colours and gold on paper in Japan in the mid-17th century. This is one of six illustrated handscrolls in the Chester Beatty collection that tell stories from Japan's Kōwaka mai ballad dramas. Combining alternating sections of text and illustrations, these scrolls would have belonged to a larger set. This scroll features two stories regarding Tokiwa, famed beauty and mother of the hero Minamoto no Yoshitsune (1159-1189). 'Tokiwa at Fushimi' (Fushimi Tokiwa) tells of her flight from Kyoto seeking safety for her children, while in 'Tokiwa's disputation' (Tokiwa mondō) she stands up to a temple superintendent who chastises her for entering the temple's chapel to recite a sutra.

J_1128_4.t: Scroll of the flute (Fue no maki), Chronicle of the future (Miraiki) and Laud of the sword (Tsurugi sandan) from the Picture scrolls of ballad dramas (Mai no hon emaki)
J_1128_4.c: Handscroll from the 'Picture scrolls of ballad dramas' (Mai no hon emaki) painted in ink, colours and gold on paper in Japan in the mid-17th century. This is one of six illustrated handscrolls in the Chester Beatty collection that tell stories from Japan's Kōwaka mai ballad dramas. Combining alternating sections of text and illustrations, these scrolls would have belonged to a larger set. This scroll features two stories from the childhood of hero Minamoto no Yoshitsune (1159-1189) entitled 'Scroll of the flute' (Fue no maki) and 'Chronicle of the future' (Miraiki), followed by a story from the vendetta of the Soga brothers: 'Laud of the sword' (Tsurugi sandan).

J_1128_5.t: Kagekiyo from the Picture scrolls of ballad dramas (Mai no hon emaki)
J_1128_5.c: Handscroll from the 'Picture scrolls of ballad dramas' (Mai no hon emaki) painted in ink, colours and gold on paper in Japan in the mid-17th century. This is one of six illustrated handscrolls in the Chester Beatty collection that tell stories from Japan's Kōwaka mai ballad dramas. Combining alternating sections of text and illustrations, these scrolls would have belonged to a larger set. This scroll features the story 'Kagekiyo': a fictional account of Taira no Kagekiyo's efforts to assasinate Minamoto no Yoritomo around the time of the Genpei War.

J_1128_6.t: Great woven cap (Taishokan) from the Picture scrolls of ballad dramas (Mai no hon emaki)
J_1128_6.c: Handscroll from the 'Picture scrolls of ballad dramas' (Mai no hon emaki) painted in ink, colours and gold on paper in Japan in the mid-17th century. This is one of six illustrated handscrolls in the Chester Beatty collection that tell stories from Japan's Kōwaka mai ballad dramas. Combining alternating sections of text and illustrations, these scrolls would have belonged to a larger set. This scroll tells the legend of the 'Great woven cap' (Taishokan). The great woven cap is worn by Japan's highest official, and in this story refers to Kamatari, Minister of State. When Kamatari's daughter sends him treasures for the temple he is establishing, the Dragon King attempts to seize them for his underwater palace.

J_1130_1.t: Scroll 1 of Account of the deeds of Zōga Shōnin from Tōnomine, Yamato province (Washū Tōnomine Zōga Shōnin gyōgōki emaki)
J_1130_1.c: Scroll 1 of Account of the deeds of Zōga Shōnin from Tōnomine, Yamato province (Washū Tōnomine Zōga Shōnin gyōgōki emaki) painted by Hōjuken Hōgan in ink and colours on paper, Japan, 1711. This pair of handscrolls record the biography of the monk Zōga (917-1003). At a young age, Zōga travelled to Mount Hiei to become a Buddhist monk. While some around him pursued status, Zōga is said to have retreated to Tōnomine to follow a more austere path. Zōga is celebrated for his devotion to the sacred texts of the Lotus Sutra and for restoring the prosperity of the temples at Tōnomine. The Zōga Shōnin handscrolls in the museum’s collection are one of only two sets known. The other is preserved at Tanzan Shrine in Tōnomine, where Zōga did much of his life’s work. The museum's scrolls were fully conserved at Restorient Studio, Leiden, between 2019 and 2022 with the support of the Sumitomo Foundation.

J_1131.t: Dutch mansions in Dejima, Nagasaki (Nagasaki Dejima Rankan no zu)
J_1131.c: Handscroll painting of the Dutch mansions in Dejima, Nagasaki (Nagasaki Dejima Rankan no zu), painted in ink and colours on silk in Japan during the 18th century. During the 1630s, Japan’s ruling shogunate began to tighten restrictions on foreign trade and interaction, and in 1641, the Dutch were ordered to relocate to Dejima, a small artificial island in the bay of Nagasaki. This painting shows the everyday activities of the Dutch traders on Dejima. Prohibited from crossing the bridge to the mainland without permission, the Dutchmen are shown smoking and playing billiards while their Indonesian servants tend to the gardens. From comparison with similar works, it is likely that this was originally part of a larger handscroll painting showing more of the compound. Preserved as two fragments, the painting was conserved and remounted as a handscroll in 2015 with the support of the Friends of the Chester Beatty.

J_1132.c: Scroll of 'Tale of Asaina' (Asaina monogatari) the text accompanied by five illustrations painted in ink, colours and gold on paper; made in Japan between the 16th and mid-17th centuries. The scroll tells the story of strongman Asaina and his escapades in hell. Having defeated the strongest opponents he could find in the mortal realm, Asaina sought a new foe. After drinking heavily, he chased a group of demons into hell. The final painting in the scroll (which shows Asaina being treated to a banquet by the impressed king of hell, Emma) is thought to predate the other illustrations and has been attributed to artist Tosa Mitsunobu (1434-1525). The artist for the remaining paintings remains unknown.

J_1134_1.t: Scroll 1 of Gold mines at Sado (Sado Kanayama zu)
J_1134_1.c: Scroll 1 of Gold mines at Sado (Sado Kanayama zu), handscroll painting in ink and colours on paper, painted by an unknown artist, Japan, mid-18th to mid-19th century. This group of three scrolls offers a predominantly visual exploration of mining and related processes undertaken at Sado.

J_1134_3.c: Scroll 3 of Gold mines at Sado (Sado Kanayama zu), handscroll painting in ink and colours on paper, painted by an unknown artist, Japan, mid-18th to mid-19th century.
