J_1137.c: Handscroll painting of Tea harvesting at Uji painted by Kanō Tansetsu Morisada (1654-1713) in ink and colours on paper, Japan, early 18th century. The scroll opens with the scenery of the bridge over the Uji river before depicting the harvest and processing of the tea for which Uji is renowned.

J_1141.t: Kamo festival in words and pictures (Kamomatsuri ekotoba)
J_1141.c: Handscroll painting of the Kamo festival in words and pictures (Kamomatsuri ekotoba), painted by an unknown artist, Japan, mid-19th century. The ownership inscription at the end of the scroll is dated 1861, and signed for Kano Keien.

J_1145_1.t: Scroll 1 from Tale of Ōeyama (Ōeyama emaki)
J_1145_1.c: Scroll 1 from 'Tale of Ōeyama' (Ōeyama emaki) the text accompanied by illustrations painted in ink, colours and gold on paper; made in Japan in the mid-17th century. One of a set of three handscrolls telling the popular tale of the brave warrior Raikō's defeat of the ogre Shuten Dōji. In Scroll 1, Lord Kunikata discovers that his daughter is missing, likely kidnapped by Shuten Dōji and summons the hero Raikō, dressed in rich red brocade, to defeat the monster. This set of scrolls was conserved with the support of the Sumitomo Foundation at Restorient Studio, Leiden, between 2012 and 2015.

J_1145_2.t: Scroll 2 from Tale of Ōeyama (Ōeyama emaki)
J_1145_2.c: Scroll 2 from 'Tale of Ōeyama' (Ōeyama emaki) the text accompanied by illustrations painted in ink, colours and gold on paper; made in Japan in the mid-17th century. One of a set of three handscrolls telling the popular tale of the brave warrior Raikō's defeat of the ogre Shuten Dōji. In Scroll 2, Raikō and his men find Shuten Dōji's castle on Mt. Ōe and are invited inside. Joining a drinking party, they offer drugged sake to Shuten Dōji, who resumes his demonic form as he sleeps. This set of scrolls was conserved with the support of the Sumitomo Foundation at Restorient Studio, Leiden, between 2012 and 2015.

J_1145_3.t: Scroll 3 from Tale of Ōeyama (Ōeyama emaki)
J_1145_3.c: Scroll 3 from 'Tale of Ōeyama' (Ōeyama emaki) the text accompanied by illustrations painted in ink, colours and gold on paper; made in Japan in the mid-17th century. One of a set of three handscrolls telling the popular tale of the brave warrior Raikō's defeat of the ogre Shuten Dōji. In Scroll 3, Raikō and his men overcome the monstrous Shuten Dōji and his followers, rescuing the women they had held captive. This set of scrolls was conserved with the support of the Sumitomo Foundation at Restorient Studio, Leiden, between 2012 and 2015.

J_1146.t: Picture scroll of the Nikkō mountains and the road to Nikkō (Nikkōsan narabini dōchū zukan)

J_1148.t: Volume 15 of Illustrated scroll of Tale of Heiji (Heiji monogatari emaki)
J_1148.c: Volume 15 of Illustrated scroll of Tale of Heiji (Heiji monogatari emaki) painted in ink and colours on paper in Japan in the mid-17th century. This scroll was a part of a larger set of scrolls narrating the event of the Heiji rebellion (1159–1160).

J_1150.c: Handscroll painting of the Ansei Edo Earthquake, painted in ink and colours on paper by an unknown artist (possibly of the Kobikicho Kano school) in Japan, between 1856 and 1857. The scroll depicts the Ansei Edo Earthquake, which struck the city of Edo (modern Tokyo) in 1855, the second year of the Ansei era. As well as showing the devastation wrought upon the city, the scroll also depicts Edo’s reconstruction, culminating in a view of the shogun’s palace (Edo Castle) against the backdrop of Mt Fuji. The painting is almost identical to one in the Shimazu Family Collection, University of Tokyo. Recent scholarship connects the two scrolls to the wedding between Atsuhime (Tenshōin) and Tokugawa Ieyasu. Atsuhime was adoptive daughter of Shimazu Nariakira, and was also adopted by the higher-ranking Konoe Tadahiro around the time of her marriage. It is suggested that the scrolls, which include cranes flying over Edo Castle, were created to commemorate the wedding of Atsuhime to Tokugawa Iesa

J_1158_1.t: Scroll 1 from Song of Lasting Sorrow (Chōgonka gakan)
J_1158_1.c: Handscroll painting, Scroll 1 from 'Song of Lasting Sorrow' (Chōgonka gakan), painted by Kanō Sansetsu (1590-1651) in ink, colours and gold on silk, in Japan in the late 1640s. The Song of Lasting Sorrow was composed by Chinese poet Bai Juyi in the ninth century. It tells of the love affair between the Emperor Xuanzong (r. 712–756) and the beautiful Yang Guifei (719–756). From their all-consuming romance, to the rebellion blamed upon Xuanzong’s infatuation, and Yang Guifei’s subsequent execution, Bai Juyi’s tragic poem captured hearts across China and beyond, here finding expression through the brush of Japanese master artist, Kanō Sansetsu. Formerly in the collection of Louis Gonse, this pair of handscrolls was acquired by Sir Alfred Chester Beatty in 1954. The scrolls were conserved courtesy of the Art Research Foundation at Handa Kyūseidō conservation studio, Tokyo, between May 1994 and April 1995.

J_1164_1.t: Scroll 1 from Tale of Tawara Tōda (Tawara Tōda monogatari)
J_1164_1.c: Scroll 1 from 'Tale of Tawara Tōda' (Tawara Tōda monogatari) the text accompanied by six illustrations painted in ink, colours and gold on paper; made in Japan in the mid-17th century. One of a set of three handscrolls telling the popular tale of the Japanese warrior Tawara Tōda Hidesato (also known as Fujiwara no Hidesato). Recorded for his role in the suppression of the rebel Taira no Masakado in the year 940, over time Hidesato's exploits took on a more fantastic edge. In Scroll 1, Hidesato is shown coming to the aid of the underwater Dragon Kingdom by defeating the giant centipede of Mt. Mikami. This set of scrolls was conserved with the support of the Sumitomo Foundation at Restorient Studio, Leiden, between 2015 and 2018.

J_1164_2.t: Scroll 2 from Tale of Tawara Tōda (Tawara Tōda monogatari)
J_1164_2.c: Scroll 2 from 'Tale of Tawara Tōda' (Tawara Tōda monogatari) the text accompanied by seven illustrations painted in ink, colours and gold on paper; made in Japan in the mid-17th century. One of a set of three handscrolls telling the popular tale of the Japanese warrior Tawara Tōda Hidesato (also known as Fujiwara no Hidesato). In Scroll 2, Hidesato pays a visit to Taira no Masakado and warns the emperor of his intentions. This set of scrolls was conserved with the support of the Sumitomo Foundation at Restorient Studio, Leiden, between 2015 and 2018.

J_1164_3.t: Scroll 3 from Tale of Tawara Tōda (Tawara Tōda monogatari)
J_1164_3.c: Scroll 3 from 'Tale of Tawara Tōda' (Tawara Tōda monogatari) the text accompanied by six illustrations painted in ink, colours and gold on paper; made in Japan in the mid-17th century. One of a set of three handscrolls telling the popular tale of the Japanese warrior Tawara Tōda Hidesato (also known as Fujiwara no Hidesato). In Scroll 3, Hidesato finds the means to defeat Taira no Masakado, overcoming his magical armour and his team of supernatural body doubles. This set of scrolls was conserved with the support of the Sumitomo Foundation at Restorient Studio, Leiden, between 2015 and 2018.

J_1170.t: Night parade of one hundred demons (Hyakki yagyō zu)
J_1170.c: Handscroll painting of 'Night Parade of One Hundred Demons' (Hyakki yagyō zu) painted in ink an light colours on paper by an unknown artist in Japan during the first half of the nineteenth century. Perfectly attuned to the handscroll format, the ‘Night Parade of One Hundred Demons’ provided a playful subject for scroll paintings from the fifteenth century. Unusually, some of the monsters in this scroll are named including 'Nozoki-men' or 'Peeping face' and 'Gotoku-neko' or 'Trivet cat'. Accompanied by shape-shifting raccoon dogs and an animate umbrella, they march through the night until the burning rays of the dawn sun drive them back into the shadows.

J_1174.t: Illustrated scroll of the Tales of Ise (Ise monogatari emaki)
J_1174.c: IIlustrated scroll of the Tales of Ise (Ise monogatari emaki) painted in ink and colours on paper by Hon'ami Kōetsu (1558-1637) in Japan in the early-17th century.

J_1178.c: Tale of Bunshō (Bunshō sōshi) painted in ink, colours and gold on paper by an unknown artist in Japan between 1651-1675.

J_1184.t: Picture scroll of seasonal scenery (Jūnikagetsu kachō zukan)
J_1184.c: Japanese scroll 'Picture scroll of seasonal scenery', painted in ink and colours on silk by Sumiyoshi Hiromori (1705-1777) in the mid-18th century. Painting and poetry enjoy a very close relationship in Japan. This painted handscroll of seasonal imagery is inspired by the birds and plants introduced by poet Fujiwara no Teika (1162–1241) to describe the changing seasons. The scroll is read from right to left, with the seasons changing from autumn to winter. It was probably once paired with a scroll of spring and summer scenery.

J_1186_1.t: Scroll from Tale of Bunshō (Bunshō sōshi)
J_1186_1.c: Handscroll from the 'Tale of Bunshō' (Bunshō sōshi), painted in ink and colours, gold and silver on paper in Japan during the mid-17th century. The story of Bunshō combines rags-to-riches with romance. This popular tale of a lowly servant of Kashima Shrine turned entrepreneurial saltmaker was first enjoyed in the late Muromachi period (1336–1573), but took on a new relevance in Japan’s Edo period (c. 1603–1868). Part of the reason for this upturn in interest was Kashima’s proximity to the shogun’s city, Edo. Originally comprising three scrolls, only the middle and final scrolls of the set survive. This scroll tells the middle section of the story. Overcome by love when hearing of the beauty of Bunshō's daughters, a handsome captain of court rank disguises himself as a merchant and travels from Kyoto to visit Bunshō's mansion.

J_1186_2.c: Handscroll from the 'Tale of Bunshō' (Bunshō sōshi), painted in ink and colours, gold and silver on paper in Japan during the mid-17th century. The story of Bunshō combines rags-to-riches with romance. This popular tale of a lowly servant of Kashima Shrine turned entrepreneurial saltmaker was first enjoyed in the late Muromachi period (1336–1573), but took on a new relevance in Japan’s Edo period (c. 1603–1868). Part of the reason for this upturn in interest was Kashima’s proximity to the shogun’s city, Edo. Originally comprising three scrolls, only the middle and final scrolls of the set survive. This scroll tells the last section of the story. Capturing the heart of one of Bunshō's daughters, the handsome captain returns with her to Kyoto.

J_1188_1.t: Scroll 1 of Tale of the bamboo cutter (Taketori monogatari)
J_1188_1.c: Scroll 1 of Tale of the bamboo cutter (Taketori monogatari), illustrated narrative handscroll in ink, colours and gold on paper, painted by an unknown artist, Japan, 17th or early 18th century.

J_1201.t: Fragment of Volume 7 of the Garland Sutra (Kegonkyō or Avataṃsaka sūtra)
J_1201.c: Handscroll, Fragment of 'Volume 7 of the Garland Sutra' (Kegonkyō or Avataṃsaka sūtra), written in silver on blue-dyed paper by an unknown scribe, Japan, 729-749 CE, with later cover, frontispiece and mountings. It is possible that the fragment may be part of a sixty-volume set of the Garland Sutra (Kegonkyō in Japanese) found in the ash after Nigatsu-dō hall of Tōdaiji temple burned down in 1667. The sutra is sometimes called the 'Burned sutra of Nigatsu-dō' because of its fire damage. Although the upper and lower borders of this scroll fragment have been trimmed, slight burn marks can still be seen.

J_1202.t: Scroll 579 of Sutra of the perfection of wisdom in 600 chapters (Daihannyakyō)
J_1202.c: Scroll 579 of 'Sutra of the perfection of wisdom in 600 chapters' (Daihannyakyō), written in ink on light yellow paper, Japan, late 8th century. One of a set of 600 scrolls containing the Buddhist sacred text, Sutra of the perfection of wisdom (Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra in Sanskrit).The sutra is one of the largest Buddhist sacred texts and was translated from Sanskrit into Chinese by the Chinese Buddhist monk, Xuanzang (602-664) in the 7th century. In Japan, sutras translated by Xuanzang into Chinese were used for rituals at temples. The back of the scroll is stamped 'Yakushiji Kondō', which suggests that this scroll was formerly the property of Yakushiji temple, Nara prefecture, Japan.

J_1204.t: Verses from the Benchūhenron sutra (Benchūhenron honju)
J_1204.c: Handscroll entitled 'Verses from the Benchūhenron sutra' (Benchūhenron honju) written and painted in gold and silver on paper dyed with indigo, made in Japan between 1117 and 1126. With its alternating columns of gold and silver script, this scroll is considered to be one of a group of scrolls known as the Chūsonji-kyō: a compilation of Buddhist religious texts and regulations commissioned by the warlord Fujiwara no Kiyohira (1056–1128) for dedication to the temple of Chūsonji in northern Japan. The frontispiece painting shows Shakyamuni preaching on Vulture Peak.

J_1206.t: Scroll 26 of Monastic rules in five parts (Gobunritsu)
J_1206.c: Handscroll, 'Scroll 26 of Monastic rules in five parts' (Gobunritsu), written in gold and silver pigment on indigo-dyed paper with painted frontispiece, Japan, inscribed between around 1149 and 1185, Heian period (794-1185). Around 1149, retired emperor Toba ordered a new transcription of Buddhist sacred texts. The red seal suggests that this scroll was part of this set, given to Jingoji temple by Toba’s son in 1185.

J_1208.t: Text of the Universal Gateway of the Bodhisattva Kannon (Kanzeon bosatsu fumonbon), Chapter 25 of the Lotus Sutra (Myōhō renge kyō)
J_1208.c: Handscroll containing text of the 'Universal Gateway of the Bodhisattva Kannon' (Kanzeon bosatsu fumonbon), Chapter 25 of the Lotus Sutra (Myōhō renge kyō) in gold pigment on blue-dyed paper as copied by Matsudaira Terutaka in 1778, Japan. Matsudaira Terutaka (1725-1781) was the lord of the Takasaki domain in Kozuke province in the mid-Edo period (c. 1603-1868). According to the colophon of this scroll, he transcribed this text in year 7 of the An'ei era (1778) when he would have been 54 years of age. Many sacred Buddhist texts were brought to Japan in their Chinese translation and continued to be used in this form.

J_1209.c: Handscroll painting of Senju Kannon (Avalokitêśvara), painted in ink and colours on silk by an unknown artist, Japan, late 16th century. The bodhisattva Avalokitêśvara is worshipped in Japan as Kannon. Avalokitêśvara appears in many forms and different genders across the Buddhist world. In East Asia, Avalokitêśvara is often portrayed as female. Senju Kannon means Kannon of One Thousand Arms. This form of Kannon relates to Kannon's compassionate response to those in need. Senju Kannon is endowed with 1000 eyes to witness suffering and 1000 arms to alleviate it. In sculpture and painting, the execution of 1000 arms is challenging. Frequently, as here, 42 arms are used to represent the full 1000.

J_1212.c: Hanging scroll painting of a Bodhisattva painted in ink and colours on silk by an unknown artist, Japan, 18th or 19th century.

J_1213.c: Hanging scroll painting of Amida (Amitābha), painted in ink, colours and gold on silk by an unknown artist, Japan, 18th or 19th century. This striking golden portrait depicts Amida Nyorai (Amitābha Tathagata), the Buddha of Limitless Light. Treasured for his benevolence, Amida welcomes any who call upon him to the Western Paradise over which he presides. Amida is the central deity of Japan’s popular Pure Land (Jōdo shū) sects.

J_1214.c: Hanging scroll painting of Jizō Bosatsu painted in colours on silk in Japan in the 15th century. Often represented with a wish-granting jewel in one hand and a monk's staff in the other, Jizō is among the most popular bodhisattvas in Japanese Buddhism. The Sanskrit term bodhisattva (bosatsu in Japanese) means ‘awakened being’. In Mahayana Buddhism, bodhisattvas are beings that have achieved supreme knowledge, but choose to remain in the world to help others on that path. Jizō is particularly venerated as a guardian of children and those suffering in hell.

J_1215.t: Seven patriarchs of the Jōdo shinshū sect
J_1215.c: Hanging scroll painting of the Seven patriarchs of the Jōdo Shinshū sect, painted by an unknown artist in ink and colours on silk, Japan, early to mid-19th century. The 'Seven Patriarchs' (Shichi kōsō) were chosen by Shinran, founder of the Jōdo Shinshū sect. The seven include Buddhist figures from India (Nagarjuna and Vasubandhu), China (Tanluan, Daochuo and Shandao) and Japan (Genshin and Honen) whose teachings Shinran felt were essential to the deliverance of the nembutsu practice of chanting of the name of Amida Buddha. Hanging scroll paintings depicting the Seven Patriarchs are displayed in Jōdo Shinshū temples near the temple's principal image.

J_1216_1.t: Diamond World from Mandala of the Two Worlds (Kongōkai Taizōkai mandara)
J_1216_1.c: Hanging scroll painting of the Diamond World from ‘Mandala of the Two Worlds’ (Kongōkai Taizōkai mandara), painted by an unknown artist in colours on silk, Japan, 15th century. In Japanese Esoteric Buddhism, paintings of the Diamond World and Womb World are paired as the Mandala of the Two Worlds. While the Diamond World mandala is known as the mandala of wisdom, the Womb World mandala is known as the mandala of principle. Often hung on facing walls in the temple hall, together they offer the means to reveal ultimate truth.

J_1216_2.c: Hanging scroll painting of the Womb World from ‘Mandala of the Two Worlds’ (Kongōkai Taizōkai mandara), painted by an unknown artist in colours on silk, Japan, 15th century. J_1614_1.t: Volume 1 of 100 views of Mount Fuji (Fugaku hyakkei)

J_1614_1.o: Approved Category 2017/Printed Material/Printed Book/Woodblock printed book
J_1614_1.c: Woodblock printed book, Volume 1 of '100 views of Mount Fuji' (Fugaku hyakkei) by Katsushika Hokusai, printed in ink on paper with blocks carved by Egawa Tomekichi, and published in Edo (modern Tokyo), Japan, by Nishimura Yūzō and Nishimura Yohachi in 1834. Katsushika Hokusai (1760–1849) was already 75 years old by Japanese reckoning when he completed work on the first volume of this illustrated book, which highlights the beauty and spirituality of Japan’s venerated mountain through masterful compositions.

J_1615.c: Woodblock printed book, 'Picture book of glories of Japan and China' (Ehon Wakan no homare) by Katsushika Hokusai, published by Kawachiya Bunsuke in Edo (Tokyo), 1850. Hokusai designed this picture book of renowned warriors from the legends of China and Japan when he was aged 76; it was published posthumously.

J_1621_1.t: Volume 1 of Fat tails of lucky mice (Fukunezumi shirio no futozao jō)
a: Utagawa Toyohiro; Yamadaya Sanshirō; Ōmiya Yohei
J_1621_1.o: Approved Category 2017/Printed Material/Printed Book/Woodblock printed book
J_1621_1.c: Colour woodblock printed book, Volume 1 of 'Fat tails of lucky mice' (Fukunezumi shirio no futozao jō) written by Sakuragawa Jihinari with illustrations by Utagawa Toyohiro, published by Yamadaya Sanshirō and Ōmiya Yohei in Edo (Tokyo), 1804. The leading roles in this entertaining novel are taken by elegantly-whiskered white mice. Even among mice the course of true love rarely runs smoothly, and this story describes the obstacles faced by its protagonists. Richly printed in colour, it is a luxurious work. Five months after publication, magistrates ordered that it be printed in black ink only.

J_1622_1.t: Volume 2 of Album of pictures by Kōrin (Kōrin gafu)
a: Nakamura Hōchū; Ogata Kōrin, style of
J_1622_1.c: Volume 2 of 'Album of pictures by Kōrin' (Kōrin gafu) featuring pictures designed by Nakamura Hōchū in the style of Ogata Kōrin, block-printed and hand-applied colour on paper, published in Japan in 1802. The illustrations in these two albums were designed by Nakamura Hōchū (died 1819), an artist credited with playing an important role in the revival of Rinpa painting and decorative arts in the early nineteenth century. This bold and decorative aesthetic style is named for the celebrated Kyoto painter Ogata Kōrin (1658-1716), emulated here. Although the Chester Beatty albums lack the printed preface, postscript and colophon, they share many features in common with works belonging to the original 1802 edition. The use of hand-applied colour is is particularly interesting in this regard.

J_1623.t: Picture book of loyal heroes of the Water Margin (Chūgi Suikoden ehon)
a: Katsushika Hokusai; Hanabusaya Heikichi, attributed to
J_1623.o: Approved Category 2017/Printed Material/Printed Book/Woodblock printed book
J_1623.c: Woodblock printed book, 'Picture book of loyal heroes of the Water Margin' (Chūgi Suikoden ehon) by Katsushika Hokusai, understood to have been published by Hanabusaya Heikichi in Edo (Tokyo), 1829. This picture book depicts heroes from the Chinese novel ‘The Water Margin’ (Shuihu zhuan) as depicted by Hokusai. First enjoyed in Japan in the early seventeenth century, a new edition of this fourteenth century heroic epic was published between 1805 and 1839. Written in vernacular Japanese and featuring illustrations by Hokusai, it spanned 91 volumes. Also designed by Hokusai, this picture book would have further captured contemporary interest in the story.

J_1625.t: Pictures of women in the scenery of 53 stations (Gojūsan tsugi keshiki iri onna ga)
a: Utagawa Kunisada; Sanoya Kihei; Moriya Jihei
J_1625.o: Approved Category 2017/Printed Material/Printed Book/Woodblock printed book
J_1625.c: Colour woodblock print album, 'Pictures of women in the scenery of 53 stations' (Gojūsan tsugi keshiki iri onna ga) by Utagawa Kunisada, published by Sanoya Kihei and Moriya Jihei in Edo(modern Tokyo), Japan, between 1833 and 1836. This series of prints by Utagawa Kunisada presents beauties against the landscape of the Tōkaidō highway. Designs from Utagawa Hiroshige’s contemporary Tōkaidō series (the Hōeidō Tōkaidō) provide the backdrop for 43 of Kunisada’s 56 prints. In each, Kunisada changes the format of the composition from landscape to portrait and adds a beautiful woman. The full series has been mounted in a concertina album with printed title slip.

J_1651.t: Hokusai’s Precepts for women (Hokusai onna imagawa)
J_1651.o: Approved Category 2017/Printed Material/Printed Book/Woodblock printed book
J_1651.c: Woodblock printed book 'Hokusai’s Precepts for women' (Hokusai onna imagawa), with illustrations by Katsushika Hokusai (1760–1849), published in the mid-19th century in ink and colours on paper in Edo (Tokyo), Japan. In 1687, Japanese female author Sawada Kichi composed Onna Imagawa, a famous text on the conduct of women. This reproduction embellished Sawada’s text with illustrations of women from literature and theatre, and contemporary genre scenes designed by artist Katsushika Hokusai.

J_1657_1.t: Part 1, Volume 1 of Picture book of the exploits of Toyotomi Hideyoshi (Ehon Toyotomi kunkōki shohen ichi)
a: Utagawa Kuniyoshi; Egawa Sentarō; Izumiya Ichibei
J_1657_1.o: Approved Category 2017/Printed Material/Printed Book/Woodblock printed book
J_1657_1.c: Woodblock printed book Part 1, Volume 1 of 'Picture book of the exploits of Toyotomi Hideyoshi' (Ehon Toyotomi kunkōki shohen ichi) written by Ryūsuitei Tanekiyo with illustrations by Utagawa Kuniyoshi, blocks carved by Egawa Sentarō and published by Izumiya Ichibei; printed in ink and light colour on paper, published Edo (Tokyo), 1857. The Chester Beatty has the first 5 parts (totalling 50 volumes, published between 1857 and 1860) of this illustrated biography of the warlord Toyotomi Hideyoshi (1536/37-1598). Commentary in the back of certain volumes indicates that the series was intended to run to 120 volumes, but a maximum 90 volumes are known to have been produced with Part 9 published 1874.

J_1657_12.o: Approved Category 2017/Printed Material/Printed Book/Woodblock printed book
J_1657_12.c: Woodblock printed book Part 2, Volume 2 of 'Picture book of the exploits of Toyotomi Hideyoshi' (Ehon Toyotomi kunkōki nihen ni) written by Ryūsuitei Tanekiyo with illustrations by Utagawa Kuniyoshi, blocks carved by Egawa Sentarō and published by Izumiya Ichibei; printed in ink on paper, published Edo (Tokyo), 1858. The Chester Beatty has the first 5 parts (totalling 50 volumes, published between 1857 and 1860) of this illustrated biography of the warlord Toyotomi Hideyoshi (1536/37-1598). Commentary in the back of certain volumes indicates that the series was intended to run to 120 volumes, but a maximum 90 volumes are known to have been produced with Part 9 published 1874.

J_1662.o: Approved Category 2017/Printed Material/Printed Book/Woodblock printed book
J_1662.c: Woodblock printed book, 'Monthly activities' (Tsukinami no asobi) illustrated by Hishikawa Moronobu, published by Urokogataya Sanzaemon in Edo (modern Tokyo), Japan, 1691. This book depicts popular events and customs of the twelve months. An inscription at the back of the book records that the same work was originally published in 1680 by publisher Kashiwaya Yoichi. This volume, however, was printed from a new set of blocks re-cut in 1691 by publisher Urokogataya Sanzaemon. Certain works by Hishikawa Moronobu appear to have been republished in this way. It is thought that the great fire of 1682 may have destroyed the blocks and business of publisher Kashiwaya Yoichi. The handwritten title slip reads 'Appointed goods of the 12 months' (Jūnigatsu shina sadame).

J_1673_1.t: Volume 1 of Both banks of the Sumida river at a glance (Sumidagawa ryōgan ichiran)

J_1675_1.c: Colour woodblock printed book, Volume 1 of 'Picture book of selected insects' (Ehon mushi erami) by Kitagawa Utamaro, published by Tsutaya Jūzaburō in Edo (modern Tokyo), Japan, in 1788. In this two-volume work, short, witty verses (known as kyōka) penned by Edo's leading poets are paired with elegant insects and other small creatures captured by the artist Utamaro. Exquisitely carved and printed, small touches of glittering mica complete the luxurious feel. Chester Beatty acquired this book in 1956.

J_1680.t: Eight views of Tōei's foothills (Tōeiroku hakkei)
J_1680.c: Folding album of colour woodblock prints entitled 'Eight views of Tōei's foothills' (Tōeiroku hakkei) unsigned and printed in ink and colours on paper in Japan around 1777. This set of eight chūban format colour woodblock prints depicts scenes from the area of Tōeizan in the city of Edo, now Tokyo's Ueno district. The series follows the Chinese model of temporal descriptions of landscape known as the Eight views of the Xiao and Xiang rivers, but matched to contemporary Edo. The stacked-triangle mark of publisher Urokogataya Magobei is just visible in the ground of ‘Night rain on the alley shop’, but the artist's name is not recorded. Most recently, it is thought that they are the work of artist Kitao Shigemasa. The poems above have been attributed to Ōta Nanpo and Kimuro Bōun. J_1683_1.t: Volume 1 of Tales of Ise (Ise monogatari)
a: Unknown; Hon'ami Kōetsu, manner of; Nakanoin Michikatsu
J_1683_1.c: Printed book, Volume 1 of 'Tales of Ise' (Ise monogatari) with text edited by Nakanoin Michikatsu, printed under the direction of Suminokura Soan in Kyoto, Japan, in 1608. Saga-bon edition, printed on coloured paper. The Saga-bon edition of the 'Tales of Ise' is the earliest non-religious Japanese book to be printed with illustrations complementing a text. While the text was printed using wooden moveable type ('katsuji' in Japanese), the illustrations, which are by unknown artist, were printed from woodblocks.

J_1693.c: Takuhon printed scroll, 'On a riverboat journey' by Itō Jakuchū with poems by Daiten Kenjō, Japan, around 1767. In the spring of 1767, artist Itō Jakuchū and Zen monk Daiten Kenjō took a riverboat from Kyoto to Osaka to see friends from their literary circle. As they floated downstream past temples, shrines and villages, the two sought to capture the changing landscape around them in a spirit of lighthearted competition. Each adopting their chosen medium—picture and verse—this scroll is the combined result of their efforts. The printing technique used to reproduce their work, takuhon, is more commonly associated with rubbings of script from stone stele.

J_1697_1.t: Pagoda from Darani of one million pagodas (Hyakumantō darani)
J_1697_1.c: Wooden pagoda from the 'Darani of one million pagodas' (Hyakumantō darani), made in Japan between 764 and 770. These one million miniature wooden pagodas (a religious building in the form of a tall tower) and the printed Buddhist invocations (darani) they contained, were created at the order of Empress Shōtoku (718-770) for dedication to ten major temples around the capital at Nara. Each printed prayer was rolled and placed inside a pagoda. These prayers remain the earliest known printed texts from Japan.

J_1697_2.t: Prayer from Darani of one million pagodas (Hyakumantō darani)
J_1697_2.c: Printed prayer (darani) from the 'Darani of one million pagodas' (Hyakumantō darani), printed in ink on paper in Japan between 764 and 770. These one million printed Buddhist invocations (darani) and the miniature wooden pagodas crafted to house them were created at the order of Empress Shōtoku (718-770) for dedication to ten major temples around the capital at Nara. Each printed prayer was rolled and placed inside a pagoda. These prayers remain the earliest known printed texts from Japan.

J_1699_4.t: Scroll 4 of the Lotus Sutra (Myōhō renge kyō)
J_1699_4.c: Scroll 4 of the Lotus Sutra (Myōhō renge kyō, also Hokkekyō), printed in ink on paper decorated with gold and silver pigments and cut leaf, Japan early 17th century. One of a set of eight scrolls containing the text of the Buddhist sacred text, the Lotus Sutra (Saddharma-pundarika sutra in Sanskrit). Many of Buddhism's sacred texts were used in Japan in their Chinese translations, as here. The text is printed from woodblocks onto richly decorated paper of the highest quality. Further refinement can be seen in the cover and mounts. The cover of the scroll is hand-painted with lotus arabesques on the outside and a scene of Buddha at Vulture Peak on the inside. The roller ends are quartz crystals set in metal mounts.

J_2163.t: Women of Ōhara with bundles of firewood
J_2163.o: Approved Category 2017/Printed Material/Print/Relief Print/Woodblock print; Object by Function/Documents by function/Surimono
J_2163.c: Colour woodblock print, Women of Ōhara with bundles of firewood by Katsushika Hokusai, printed in Japan, 1805. Yatsugiriban format, surimono print with poems signed Hanyūan Wabizumi, Shūchōdō Monoyana and Yomo Utagaki Magao (leader of the Yomo group). Calendar information is incorporated in the design through the line-up of women and oxen. These respectively represent the sequence of short and long months in 1805. The woman with no bundle of firewood stands for an adjusting intercalary month, added periodically to keep the lunar calendar on track with the solar year and seasons.

J_2241.t: Number 3: In the shade of a tree (San kinoshitakage)
J_2241.o: Approved Category 2017/Printed Material/Print/Relief Print/Woodblock print; Object by Function/Documents by function/Surimono
J_2241.c: Colour woodblock print, ‘Number 3: In the shade of a tree’ (San kinoshitakage) from the series ‘Famous horses’ (Meiba zoroe) by Yanagawa Shigenobu II, Japan, 1834. Shikishiban format, surimono print with poems signed Goshintei Mizaru, Bokubokutei Kineo of Kaga province and Shinryūtei Harukaze. This print would have been made for a poetry group to exchange at New Year of 1834, year of the Horse. The titles of each print in the series make subtle reference to these animals by ending in -ge or ‘fur’, an ending typically used to indicate the colours of horses. The gourd-shaped title cartouche refers to the legend of the Daoist immortal Chokkarō, who carried his hourse in a gourd.

A dramatic retelling of historical events around the fall of the Han dynasty, the Chinese novel Romance of the Three Kingdoms (Sanguo yanyi) became popular in Japan during the Edo period (c. 1603-1868). This distinctive glaive (known in Chinese as a guandao) has a blade emerging from the mouth of a dragon. In the story, it was cited as the favoured weapon of the general Guan Yu.
