Per_277_15.t: Manuchihr pursuing Tūr, his father's murderer, from the Book of Kings (Shāhnāma) by Firdausī
Per_277_15.c: Manūchihr pursuing Tūr, his father's murderer, from the Book of Kings (Shāhnāma) by Firdausī. To complete Firdausi’s tale of king Farīdūn, the injustice of Iraj’s murder is finally resolved a generation later. Iraj’s grown son Manūchihr rides after one of the murderers, his uncle Tūr, and will shortly avenge his innocent father’s death. Folio, ink, colours and gold on paper, Persian text in nasta`liq script, with painting (on recto) and gold-painted borders, from the Book of Kings (Shāhnāma) by Firdausī (d. 1020), folio produced Qazvin or Isfahan, Iran, c. 1590-1600, this painting (or possibly entire folio) added as part of an intervention led by Muḥammad Zamān, Isfahan, Iran, 1675-1676. Per_277_16.t: Salm and Tūr organise the murder of their brother Īraj, by Muḥammad Zamān, from the Book of Kings (Shāhnāma)
a: Muhammad Zaman ibn Haji Yusuf; Unknown
Per_277_16.c: Salm and Tūr organise the murder of their brother Īraj, by Muḥammad Zamān, from the Book of Kings (Shāhnāma). Angry over the succession plan, the two embittered sons of Farīdūn have organised the murder of their innocent brother Īraj. They send his head to their horrified father, seated here on the left. Farīdūn is dressed in contemporary Safavid fashion, and he may be understood also as Muḥammad Zamān's royal patron, Shah Sulaymān. The scene takes place in front of a European architectural composition in startling illusionistic perspective. The source image was a print by the Dutch artistprintmaker Hendrik Hondius (died 1650), adapted in turn from Hans Vredeman de Vries (died 1607). A specialist painter in the European mode (farangi-saz, in Persian), Isfahan court painter Muḥammad Zamān was appointed to add modern paintings to this older manuscript from the royal library, in 1675-6. Per_277_17.t: Ṭahmūras defeats the demon army, attributed to Reẓā `Abbāsī (d. 1635), from the Book of Kings (Shāhnāma)
Per_277_17.c: Ṭahmūras defeats the demon army, attributed to Reẓā `Abbāsī (d. 1635), from the Book of Kings (Shāhnāma). Across a rocky mountain, king Ṭahmūras and his army defeat the rebellious dīvs (or demons). On horseback, Ṭahmūras delivers a blow with his mace to the Black Dīv, while his forces scatter the others. The demons offer to surrender, and promise in return for peace that they will teach the art of reading and writing to mankind. Tahmuras learns almost thirty scripts. Per_277_22.t: Rustam's horse Rakhsh fights a lion while Rustam sleeps, from the Book of Kings (Shahnama) by Firdausi
Per_277_22.c: Rustam's horse Rakhsh fights a lion while Rustam sleeps, from the Book of Kings (Shahnama) by Firdausi. Pausing during a long journey, the hero Rustam sleeps while his brave horse Rakhsh fights and kills a lion. On waking up, Rustam scolds the horse for risking his own life as well as their mission to Mazandaran, to save the king of Iran from the White Div. Folio, ink, colours and gold on paper, pasted to card, Persian text in nasta`liq script, with painting (unfinished) and gold-painted borders (on recto), and blank verso, from the Book of Kings (Shahnama) by Abu al-Qasim Firdausi (d. 1022), folio possibly produced Qazvin, Iran, c. 1590-1600, this painting worked as part of an intervention led by Muhammad Zaman, Isfahan, Iran, 1675-1676. Per_278.t: History of the world-adorning Shāh Ismā`īl (Tārīkh-e jahānārā-ye Shāh Ismā`īl)
Per_278.c: History of the world-adorning Shāh Ismā`īl (Tārīkh-e jahānārā-ye Shāh Ismā`īl). The dramatic military successes of Ismā`īl I (r. 1501-1524) were remembered for generations, in works of formal history as well as in popular story-telling tradition. One of a number of similar anonymous histories, this manuscript was made in 1683 in Isfahan, under the second-last of the Safavid shahs, Sulaymān (reigned 1666–1694). Codex, ink, colours and gold on paper, 245 folios, Persian text in nasta`liq script, with title heading (sarlawh, fol. 1v), 18 paintings (fols. 20r, 47v, 77r, 89v, 119v, 136v, 149r, 152v, 160r, 162v, 167v, 176v, 191r, 193r, 195r, 197v, 199v, 215r), History of the world-adorning Shāh Ismā`īl (Tārīkh-e jahānārā-ye Shāh Ismā`īl bahādur khān), anonymous, account of the Safavid dynasty from Ismā`īl I (r. 1501-1524) to `Abbās II (r. 1642-1666) copied by Muḥtashim Iṣfahānī (colophon fol. 245v), Isfahan, Iran, dated Monday 16 Safar1094H, 14 February 1683.

Per_279.t: History of the Safavid shahs up to 1667, by Murtaẓā Qulī
Per_279.c: History of the Safavid shahs up to 1667, by Murtaẓā Qulī. Codex, ink, colours and gold on gold-sprinkled paper, lacquer book covers, 138 folios, Persian text in nasta`liq script, with illuminated title page (sarlawh, fol. 1v) and gold foliate borders (fols. 1v-2r), and 22 paintings, (1: fols. 1v-86) untitled history of the Safavid shahs up to the initial accession of Safī II in 1666 (1077H), composed 1667-1668 (1087H) by Murtaẓā Qulī, Ardabil shrine guardian, (2: fols. 87-138r) poetry, (3: fols. 1r, 138v) verses signed `Alī Reẓā al-Kātib, paintings signed Muẓaffar `Alī (fols. 6v, 44r, 63v) and Reẓā-ye Muṣavvir (fol. 11r, 17v, 27v, 32v), Isfahan, Iran, undated, c. 1670.

Per_292_2.t: Angels above the Ka`ba in Mecca, folio from a dispersed anthology
Per_292_2.c: Angels above the Ka`ba in Mecca, folio from a dispersed anthology. This night-scene shows rows of angels among golden clouds, two of whom carry a covered tray, billowing scented smoke to represent blessings (barakat). Far below them is the Ka`ba sanctuary in Mecca, with pilgrims around it. The angels all face toward the right, because this painting is from a double-page composition: on the opposite page (Chester Beatty Per 292.1), the Prophet Muhammad rides his magical steed Buraq through the skies, accompanied by more angels, on his Night Journey (Mir`raj) or Ascension (Isra'). This image was often used for the opening pages of poetry anthologies, together with verses praising the Prophet. Folio, ink, colours and gold on paper, Persian poetry in nasta`liq script with full-page painting (recto), left side of a double-page composition, folio trimmed and remounted on album page, Shiraz, Iran, c. 1410.

Per_292_3.t: Rustam kills the dragon, from the Book of Kings (Shahnama) by Firdausi
Per_292_3.c: Rustam kills the dragon, from the Book of Kings (Shahnama) by Firdausi. The hero Rustam undertakes seven heroic trials (haft khan), while travelling to Mazandaran to rescue his king, Kay Kavus. Here, for his third feat, he charges his brave horse Rakhsh into a fire-breathing dragon, and kills it. Folio, colours and gold on paper, single framed painting, probably cut down from a manuscript folio for re-mounting in an album (muraqqa`), Iran, c. 1450.

Per_293_1.t: Sa`d fights the demon army, from the Book of the East (Khāvarānnāma) by Ibn Ḥusām (d. 1470)
Per_293_1.c: Sa`d fights the demon army, from the Book of the East (Khāvarānnāma) by Ibn Ḥusām (d. 1470). In a rocky landscape, the hero Sa`d-e Vaqqāṣ charges his horse towards one demon (or dīv), striking it with his mace, while his valiant horse tramples another two. Meanwhile four more demons hurl down rocks from all sides. In the silver sea, beneath a scaly sea-monster in the lower left corner, the painter Farhād has signed his name and written the date 881H (1476-77). Per_294.c: Timurid Anthology of Six Persian Poets. This manuscript was made in Timurid Shiraz, in the 1430s. Although now in damaged and incomplete condition, this was a magnificent court production, shown by the complex illuminated medallions, the paintings and the paper itself. Five of the pages were made not in Iran but in Ming China: these heavily-sized olive green folios are block-printed with meandering gold designs. There are other known examples of the same heavy Chinese paper used in Timurid manuscripts, and Iranian papermakers soon imitated the fashion for gold-decorated coloured pages. The Timurid courts exchanged several embassies with Ming China at this period, including one 1419-22 mission with the artist Ghiyath al-Din Naqqash in the delegation. Per_297_6.c: Ascension of the Prophet (Mi`raj), from the Garden (Bustān) of Sa`di. The Ascension and Night Journey of the Prophet Muhammad is noted in the Qur'an, and many later writers have described and praised this mystical narrative, including the poet Sa`di. Surrounded by golden flames (to show holiness), the Prophet rides through the night sky, upon his magical steed Buraq, with a retinue of angels. His guide is the angel Jibril (Gabriel, on the upper left), who leads the Prophet on his journey to the furthest mosque (al-Masjid al-Aqsa'), to the circles of hell and heaven, and then back. Per_297_22.c: The king's graffiti, from the Garden (Bustān), by Sa`di. The poet Sa`di tells this brief tale about Jamshīd, the mythical wise king from ancient Iran: the verses are written around the frame of this painting. While riding in the wilderness, the king stopped beside a flowing mountain stream. Inspired by its everlasting beauty, he wrote some lines of poetry onto the nearby rockface: “At this spring, just as I do today, many other kings have lived and breathed before my time, and they have passed on since then. We all seized the world by force, but not one of us could take it with us to the grave”. In this painting, the king's servants stand waiting, one of them holding his pencase and inkpot. In black ink on the rock, the king has already written the first words of his message “at this spring…” The king’s graffiti leaves a reflective message for future readers, who may also stop at this beautiful place and think about the temporary nature of power. Per_298_7.t: Portrait of Safavid Shah Sulaymān (d. 1694), by Shaykh `Abbāsī
Per_298_7.c: Portrait of Safavid Shah Sulaymān (d. 1694), by Shaykh `Abbāsī. Immaculately dressed in stripes, the king sits upright, one hand resting on his jewelled dagger and the other holding up a pink rose. On this right, a small note reads “Shah Sulayman”. The first two years of his reign did not go well. The shah was crowned in late 1666, as Safi II. There then followed so many unlucky events (drought, illness, border raids and a major earthquake) that his officials decided to start again. The palace organised a second coronation, on the more auspicious date of 20 March (Persian New Year, or Norouz) in 1668. The shah’s name also changed, to Sulayman. Per_312.t: Merits of Isfahan (Maḥāsin-e Iṣfahān), by Ḥusayn ibn Muḥammad al-Āvīl
Per_312.c: Fine aspects of Isfahan (Mahāsin-e Iṣfahān), Persian translation of al-Māfarrukhī's Arabic original. An important centre of culture, learning and political history, the city of Isfahan held a proud literary tradition of works listing Isfahan’s urban legends, beautiful monuments, famous visitors and local inhabitants. This book also includes descriptions of the city’s parks, and of the pleasures of spring in Isfahan. The author lived in Isfahan in the late eleventh century, and the translator lived there in the fourteenth century. Per_344.t: Quintessence of Purity (Ṣafvat al-ṣafā’), by Ibn Bazzāz Ardabīlī (d. 1371)
Per_344.c: Quintessence of Purity (Ṣafvat al-ṣafā’), by Ibn Bazzāz Ardabīlī (d. 1371). The Safavid shahs were direct descendants of the saintly Shaykh Ṣafī al-Dīn (died 1334), whose holy tomb at Ardabil for centuries attracted pilgrims, Sufi followers, and shrine patronage. This manuscript is Shaykh Ṣafī's biography, and describes his pious life, sayings and miracles, as well as his family history. Under Shah Ṭahmāsp (r. 1524-1576), a re-worked official version underlined the Ardabil saint’s ancestry, linking his family tree directly back to the Seventh Imam, Mūsā al-Kāẓim (died 799). By extension, this information also transformed the sacred identity of the Safavid shahs themselves, confirming their holy status as sayyids, descended from the Prophet Muḥammad. Codex, ink on paper, 380 folios, Persian text in black nasta`liq script, with red rubrics, Quintessence of Purity (Ṣafvat al-ṣafā’), composed c. 1358 by Tavakkulī ibn Ismā`īl ibn Bazzāz Ardabīlī (d. 1371), biography of Shaykh Ṣafī al-Dīn Is

Per_377.c: Compilation of Shi`i narratives. Codex, ink, colours and gold on paper, painted and glossed cotton binding backed with leather, 8 folios, Persian text in nasta`liq shikasteh script, with illumination (sarlawh, fol. 1r) and gold-ruled dark blue borders, Compilation of accounts and quotations about Shī`ī figures, copied by Muḥammad Rafī` al-Ḥasanī, possibly Isfahan, Iran, dated (fol. 8v) 6 Sha`ban 1076H, 11 February 1666.

Per_378.t: Kashkul, by Shaykh Bahā’ al-Dīn Muḥammad `Āmilī (d. 1621)
Per_378.c: Kashkul, by Shaykh Bahā’ al-Dīn Muḥammad `Āmilī (d. 1621). One of the great intellectuals of Shah `Abbās’s court in Isfahan, Shaykh Bahā’ī was the shah’s leading religious authority. He was a scientist and a poet, and a well-travelled scholar of Islamic law. Entitled Kashkul (the beggar’s bowl), Bahā’ī’s famous anthology gathers entertaining works of poetry, stories, quotations and mathematical proofs. Codex, ink, colours and gold on paper, 144 folios, Persian text in nasta`liq script, with illuminated heading (sarlawh, fols. 1v, 53v, 90v) and leafy gold-painted margins (fols. 1v-2r), Kashkul, literary anthology by Shaykh Bahā’ al-Dīn Muḥammad `Āmilī, known as Shaykh Bahā’ī (Baalbek 1547-1621 or 22 Isfahan), copied by Muḥammad Masīḥ, probably Isfahan, Iran, dated Dhu’l-Hijjah 1076H, June 1666.

Per_385.t: Garden of Purity (Rawḍat al-ṣafā), volume 8, by Mīr Khwānd (d. 1498)
Per_385.c: Garden of Purity (Rawḍat al-ṣafā), volume 8, by Mīr Khwānd (d. 1498). Codex, ink, colours and gold on paper, gold-painted leather bookbinding, 198 folios, Persian text in nasta`liq script, with occasional Arabic text in thuluth script, with illuminated title heading (sarlawh, fol. 1v), floral borders (fols. 1v-2r), Garden of purity on the lives of prophets, kings and caliphs (Rawḍat al-ṣafā fī sīrat al-anbiyā’ wa al-mulūk wa al-khulafā’), by Muḥammad Khawāndshāh ibn Maḥmūd, or Mīr Khwānd (d. 1498), volume 8 of his universal history, copied by Muḥammad Ja`far, “at the blessed port” (dar bandare mubārak) Sūrat, Gujarat, India, dated Thursday 7 Jumada I 1149H, 13 September 1736.

Per_395_1.t: Iskandar (Alexander) builds a wall against Gog and Magog, from the Book of Divination (Fālnāma) for Shah Ṭahmāsp, (d. 1576)
Per_395_1.c: Iskandar (Alexander) builds a wall against Gog and Magog, folio from the Book of Divination (Fālnāma). Iskandar sits in conversation with the prophets Khidr and Ilyas (Elijah), while a team of demons (divs) and men toil together to build Iskandar's bronze wall against the monstrous inhabitants of Gog and Magog. This single folio is from a large-scale manuscript of the Book of Divination (Fālnāma), produced for the Safavid Shah Ṭahmāsp, and now dispersed in international collections. There are two folios in the Chester Beatty (CBL Per 395.1 and 395.2). The Fālnāma is not intended to be read from cover to cover, but consulted for divination (as bibliomancy): the seeker opens a page at random, and that chosen page-opening provides the intended augury, in answer to the seeker's question. The text (beginning: "O augury user...") is on the left and a large painting (often depicting sacred figures and prophets) is on the right. For this page-opening, with a scene depicting Alexander the Great

Per_395_2.t: The Prophet and Imām `Alī at the gates of Qamūṣ fortress in Khaybar, from the Book of Divination (Fālnāma) for Shah Ṭahmāsp, (d. 1576)
Per_395_2.c: The Prophet and Imām `Alī at the gates of Qamūṣ fortress in Khaybar, folio from the Book of Divination (Fālnāma). This folio is from a large-scale manuscript of the Book of Divination (Fālnāma), produced for the Safavid Shah Ṭahmāsp (r. 1524-1576), and now dispersed in international collections. There are two folios in the Chester Beatty (CBL Per 395.1 and 395.2). The Fālnāma is not intended to be read from cover to cover, but consulted for divination (as bibliomancy): the seeker opens a page at random, and that chosen page-opening provides the intended augury, in answer to their question. The text (beginning: "O augury user...") is on the left and a large painting (often depicting sacred figures and prophets) is on the right. For this page-opening, depicting the Prophet Muḥammad and his son-in-law Imām `Alī at the battle of Khaybar (in 628), the future is very positive. Per_398.t: World of knowledge (Jahān-e dānesh), by Sharaf al-Dīn al-Mas`ūdī
Per_398.c: World of knowledge (Jahān-e dānesh), by Sharaf al-Dīn al-Mas`ūdī. Codex, ink and colour on paper, 136 folios, Persian text in naskh script, with labelled diagrams (throughout) and world map (fol. 79r), World of knowledge (Jahān-e dānesh), by Sharaf al-Dīn Muḥammad ibn Mas`ūd ibn Muḥammad al-Mas`ūdī al-Marwazī, Persian translation of the author’s Arabic work Compendium of Cosmography (al-Kifāya fī `ilm hay’at al-`ālam, composed Samarqand, 1150), unsigned, Iran or Uzbekistan, dated Thursday 12 Ramadan 608H, 24 February 1212.

Sum_1110.t: Protective magic against an enemy's weapons (pagar panutupi)
Sum_1110.c: Book containing magic spells to be used against an enemy’s weapons (pagar panutupi), maker unknown, 19th or early 20th century, northern Sumatra. Ink on bark with wooden covers. The term ‘Batak’ covers a number of linguistic groups. This tree-bark book was made by the Simalungun of northern Sumatra. The small size of the object suggests it was made to be worn as an amulet.

Sum_1134.t: Instructions on the use of tables of signs in the sky (pangarambui) and other divination texts
Sum_1134.c: Book containing instructions on the use of diagrams of signs in the sky (pangarambui) and other divination texts, maker unknown, 19th or early 20th century, northern Sumatra. Ink on bark with one wooden cover and plaited rattan band. The tree-bark books made by the Batak peoples of northern Sumatra are called pustaha or pustaka. The small size of this bark book suggests it was made to be worn as an amulet.

Sum_1146.c: Amulet containing a series of laments of a wandering lover (bilang-bilang), maker unknown, early 20th century, northern Sumatra. Ink on bamboo. The term ‘Batak’ covers a number of linguistic groups. This amulet was made by the Karo-Batak of northern Sumatra. After the lover’s laments, the author describes the coming of Dutch colonial government to the region.

Sum_1150.t: Amulet used against enemy bullets (sarang timah)
Sum_1150.c: Amulet used to protect against an enemy’s bullets during battle (sarang timah), maker unknown, 19th or early 20th century, northern Sumatra. Ink on animal bone. The term ‘Batak’ covers a number of linguistic groups. This amulet was made by the Karo-Batak of northern Sumatra. One side is inscribed with a magical text; the reverse features magical drawings including dragons and a diagram representing the cosmic order (bindu matoga).

Sum_1171.t: Romantic tale of Si Dajang Rindu
Sum_1171.c: Bark book from the Lampung districts in south Sumatra, containing the romantic tale of Si Dajang Rindu, dating to the 19th or early 20th century.

Syc_703.c: Harklean Gospels written in Syriac on parchment in Estrangela script by the scribe Isho’bar Romanos, completed in 1177 at the Church of the Holy Mother (Deipara Maria) situated near Tella d’Arsinos (modern Turkey). It was commissioned by the scribe’s uncle, Rabban Ahron, a priest and monk in Tella. The leather cover is ornamented with interlace borders, interlace cross on the front and an interlaced box on the back, possibly intended to represent the empty tomb. The Gospel book includes the Eusebian letter, canon tables, liturgical lessons, kephalaia (chapters), titles, colophons, and notes from the scribe. The canon tables, which occupy the first ten folios, are contained within architectural frames and decorated with a variety of birds, trees and flowers. This is followed by a stepped cross with interlace ornament and border, echoing the front cover. Square and circular interlaced medallions are found in the lower margin throughout. The manuscript has several dedications, autographs

Syc_705.c: Parchment codex containing an evangeliary or the Nestorian lectionary written in the 12th or 13th century in Syria. It is written in the Estrangela script of Syriac with the title in Arabic on the back. It is bound with blind-tooled and stamped leather covers. Nearly every chapter is decorated with a coloured 'ribbon-over-a-rod' decoration in red, green and yellow.

Syc_709.t: Ephrem's Commentary on the Diatessaron / Letters: Severus of Antioch and Julian of Halicarnassus (folios 1-10)
Syc_709.c: Parchment manuscript containing two distinct texts written in Syriac. The first ten folios reproduce an exchange of letters between Severus of Antioch and Julian of Halicarnassus relating to the corruptibility or incorruptibility of the body of Christ. It was written in a mixture of estrangela, nestorian and serta scripts in the 8th or 9th century in Egypt. The remaining sixty-five folios, also produced in Egypt, contain a substantial portion of Ephrem's Diatessaron Commentary written in estangela script and dated to the late 5th or early 6th century. The two texts were acquired in 1957 and bound together in 1960. This portion of the Commentary comprises chapters 1.2-1.27, 9.14-18.3, and 21.4-22.5, prayers and a short section on the evangelists. Chapters 2.4-9.10 (with some lacunae) are preserved as CBL Syc 709.1. A single folio in Barcelona preserves 1.31-2.4. Taken together, approximately 80% of the original codex survives (107 of the estimated 134 original folios). The Diatessaron w

Syc_709_1.c: Parchment manuscript containing a substantial portion of Ephrem's Diatessaron Commentary written in Syriac in estangela script in Egypt and dated to the late 5th or early 6th century. It was acquired in two parts, five folios in 1984 and a further 36 in 1986. This portion of the Commentary comprises chapters 2.4-9.10 (with lacunae at 2.15-20, 3.6-15, 4.2-6 and 7.25-27), the end of Matthew's infancy narrative to Jesus's meeting with Martha and Mary. Chapters 1.2-1.27, 9.14-18.3, and 21.4-22.5, prayers and a short section on the evangelists are preserved as CBL Syc 709. A single folio in Barcelona preserves 1.31-2.4. Taken together, approximately 80% of the original codex survives (107 of the estimated 134 original folios). The Diatessaron was a gospel harmony written by Tatian (120–173 AD), a second-century Christian theologian. T_401.c: Dīvān of Amīr Hidāyatullāh. T_402.c: Historical calendar (Taqwim-i tarikhi), with astrological advice and a world map. T_406.t: Book of Solomon (Suleymannama) by Sharaf al-Din Musa, Firdausi of Bursa
T_406.c: Book of Solomon (Suleymannama) by Sharaf al-Din Musa, Firdausi of Bursa. Codex, ink, colours and gold on paper, 332 folios, Arabic and Persian text in naskh script, illuminated headings, spaces left blank throughout for illustrations never included, dedicated to Ottoman Sultan Bayazid II (r. 1481-1512), Istanbul, Turkey, c. 1480-1510. The first two folios of this manuscript feature a double-page frontispiece painting of Solomon and Bilqis (Queen of Sheba) enthroned: these have been detached from the codex and are also in the Chester Beatty: T 406.1 and T 406.2.

T_406_1.t: Solomon Enthroned, from the Book of Solomon (Suleymannama) by Firdausi of Bursa
T_406_1.c: Solomon Enthroned, from the Book of Solomon (Suleymannama) by Sharaf al-Din Musa, Firdausi of Bursa. Folio, gold and colours on paper, full-page painting depicting Solomon enthroned above horizontal rows of his subjects, including turbanned scholars, crowned rulers, soldiers, demons (divs) and birds, right half of a double-frontipiece composition, from a manuscript dedicated to Ottoman Sultan Bayazid II (r. 1481-1512), Istanbul, Turkey, c. 1480-1510.

T_406_2.t: Bilqis Queen of Sheba Enthroned, from the Book of Solomon (Suleymannama) by Firdausi of Bursa
T_406_2.c: Bilqis Queen of Sheba Enthroned, from the Book of Solomon (Suleymannama) by Sharaf al-Din Musa, Firdausi of Bursa. Folio, gold and colours on paper, full-page painting depicting Bilqis (the Queen of Sheba) enthroned above horizontal rows of her subjects, including crowned women, angels, demons (divs) and monsters, left half of a double-frontipiece composition, from a manuscript dedicated to Ottoman Sultan Bayazid II, Istanbul, Turkey, c. 1480-1510

T_408.t: Forty Sayings of the Prophet (Chehel Hadith-i Rasul) by Mir `Ali Shir Nava'i
T_408.c: Forty Sayings of the Prophet (Chehel Hadith-i Rasul) by Mir `Ali Shir Nava'i. This beautiful book was copied out in Samarqand by the celebrated calligrapher, Mir `Ali Haravi (meaning from Herat). As well as the exquisite small format calligraphy employed here, Mir `Ali also produced larger scale single-folio "display pieces" (collected in Mughal albums, such as the "Minto Album" folios, CB In 07A), and designs for monumental inscriptions in architectural tilework (for example, at the shrine of Imam Reza in Mashhad). When the political landscape changed with the fall of the Timurid dynasty, Mir `Ali was reportedly conscripted to the court of `Abd al-`Aziz Khan in Bukhara, where he eventually ended his days. Codex, ink, colours and gold on paper, 10 folios, Arabic text, Chaghatay Turkish translation and verse commentary in nasta`liq script, illuminated sarlawh (fol. 1v), gold-flecked borders throughout, Forty Sayings of the Prophet Muhammad (Chehel Hadith-i Rasul) composed after the poet

T_410.t: Evidences of Prophecy (Shavahid al-Nubuvva) by Thana'i
T_410.c: Evidences of Prophecy (Shavahid al-Nubuvva) by Thana'i An account of the miraculous signs reported for the Prophet, the Caliphs, the Twelve Imams and the Prophet's Companions, gathered together by the author in honour of the Ottoman Sultan Suleyman the Magnificent (r. 1520-1566). Codex, gilt leather binding, ink and gold on paper, 129 folios, Turkish prose, Arabic and Turkish verses and Persian headings in nasta`liq calligraphy, dedicated to Sultan Suleyman, Konya, Turkey, dated Rab`i I 961H, February 1554.

T_413.t: History of Sultan Süleyman, by Sayyid Luqman
T_413.c: Concluding History of the Ottoman Sultan Süleyman by Sayyid Luqmān. The Ottoman court historian (şahnameci) Sayyid Luqmān (or Seyyid Lokman) composed this versified account of Süleyman the Magnificent's last seven years of life, describing events in the capital Istanbul, the sultan's military campaigns in the Balkans, Austria, Hungary, on Malta, and on Chios, and concluding with the sultan's death and funeral in 1566. Luqmān was continuing the Ottoman dynastic chronicles established by his two immediate predecessors: Eflatun and before him the renowned court historian `Ārif. `Ārif composed the multi-volume Book of kings of the House of Osman (Shāhnāma-yi Āl-i Osmān): Luqmān’s work (CB T 413) carefully follows this work’s form in language and general layout. `Ārif also worked on two other important accounts of the Ottoman sultan: Mujmal al-Tumar (imperial scroll, 1584) and Hünername (begun 1577), which were completed by his two court successors. T_413_5.c: Sultan Süleyman in a walled garden, from the History of Sultan Süleyman by Sayyid Luqman. This is the first painting in the book, which begins in the year 1559 with an account of the sultan's suppression of his rebellious son Bayazid. Süleyman sits by a water fountain in a walled garden, surrounded by his attendants. The prow of his waiting boat is visible on the lower right. T_413_12.c: Fortifications along the Ottoman frontier with Safavid Iran, from the History of Sultan Süleyman by Sayyid Luqman. This section discusses different measures for defending the frontiers of the Ottoman empire. To the east, the Ottoman border with Safavid Iran was carefully marked with the construction of fortresses. Here, a sheep is sacrificed to bless the construction of one fort, while further defensive architecture may be seen in the distance. T_413_14.t: Iranian envoy bringing diplomatic gifts, from the History of Sultan Süleyman by Sayyid Luqman
T_413_14.c: Iranian envoy bringing diplomatic gifts, from the History of Sultan Süleyman by Sayyid Luqman. Diplomatic relations between the Ottoman empire and Safavid Iran were carefully negotiated with treaty agreements, but periodically also led to military conflict. Here an envoy wearing the Safavid taj turban bows to Sultan Süleyman, flanked very closely by two Ottoman officials. Rows of Ottoman janissaries bring hunting birds, possibly part of a diplomatic gift. Three other Safavid officials stand on the lower left, also under close supervision. This scene shows the Ottoman army, cannons, and fleet at the capture of Santiermu (Fort St Elmo) in June 1565, in advance of the unsuccessful siege of Malta against the Knights Hospitaller. T_413_33.t: Giacomo Cristo, last podesta of Chios, arrested in 1566, from the History of Sultan Süleyman by Sayyid Luqman
T_413_33.c: Giacomo Cristo, last podesta of Chios, arrested in 1566, from the History of Sultan Süleyman by Sayyid Luqman. The podesta was the hereditary governor of the island of Chios, appointed by the Doge of Genoa on behalf of the Genoan republic. Under Ottoman control, the island was ceded and gradually integrated into the imperial administration. At first the podesta continued to rule Chios by paying an annual tribute to Istanbul. In 1566, this tribute was doubled, and the podesta refused to pay. Chios thereafter became an Ottoman sancak territory. The Ottoman court historian (sahnameci) Sayyid Luqman composed this versified account of Süleyman the Magnificent's last seven years of life, describing events in the capital Istanbul, the sultan's military campaigns in the Balkans, Austria, Hungary, on Malta, and on Chios, and concluding with the sultan's death and funeral in 1566. T_413_38.t: Süleyman's Pilgrimage to Eyüp, from the History of Sultan Süleyman by Sayyid Luqman
T_413_38.c: Süleyman's Pilgrimage to Eyüp Shrine, from the History of Sultan Süleyman by Sayyid Luqman. The Ottoman court historian Luqman composed this versified account of Süleyman the Magnificent's last seven years, describing events in the capital Istanbul, as well as the sultan's many military campaigns abroad. In this scene, the elderly Süleyman enters the Eyüp shrine just outside Istanbul, to pray at the sacred tomb complex of Abu Ayyub al-Ansari, one of the Prophet's Companions. The sultan's entourage of three pages stand behind him, while his janissary soldiers wait outside the shrine walls. T_413_55.t: John Sigismund Zapolya kneels before Sultan Süleyman in 1566, from the History of Sultan Süleyman by Sayyid Luqman
T_413_55.c: John Sigismund Zapolya kneels before Sultan Süleyman, from the History of Sultan Süleyman by Sayyid Luqman This double-page scene shows the king of Hungary (later prince of Transylvania) John Sigismund Zapolya (d. 1571) paying homage to the Ottoman sultan, who had defended his rule against challenge from the Hapsburgs. T_414.t: The Cream of Histories (Zubdat al-tawarikh) by Sayyid Luqman-i 'Ashuri
T_414.c: The Cream of Histories (Zubdat al-tawarikh) by Luqman-i 'Ashuri. Codex, leather binding, 242 paper folios, Turkish text with 31 paintings and two maps, Istanbul, Turkey, c. 1585-1590. A further twelve folios are detached, and also in the collection. Composed by Ottoman court historian Sayyid Luqman-i `Ashuri, this is an extensive survey of Islamic history, compiled from many earlier sources. According to the preface, Luqman commissioned the painter Sun'i to illustrate his text, and presented the finished work to Habeshi Mehmed Agha (d.1590), head of the Topkapi palace eunuchs. The text begins by reviewing the cosmos, describing heaven, hell and the regions of the earth, before presenting a survey of Islam's prophets from Adam to the Prophet Muhammad, and then of subsequent dynasties of rulers up to the Ottomans themselves, concluding with Murad III (d.1595).

T_419_3.t: Miqdad ibn Aswad in battle, from The Life of the Prophet (Siyer-i nebi), by Mustafa Darir

T_420.c: al-Kawākib al-durriyya fī madḥ khayr al-bariyya, by al-Būṣīrī (d. 1294). T_423.t: Genealogical tables (silsilanāma) and Cream of Histories (Zübdet-üt Tevarih), from Ottoman Baghdad
T_423.c: Genealogical tables (silsilanāma) and Cream of Histories (Zübdet-üt Tevarih), from Ottoman Baghdad. Produced in Baghdad in 1598, this book provides a visual synopsis of universal history, and presents the Ottoman sultanate as its culmination. The first section is organised in diagrammatic tables to show the genealogy of the Prophet Muhammad, listing his family, household, companions and successors, up to the Umayyad caliph `Umar ibn `Abd al-Aziz (d. 720). The second part is laid out as a genealogical tree with portrait medallions: ten of these folios are now mounted separately (CBL T 423.18 to 423.24, 423.26 to 423.28). This tree follows the sequence of Islam's prophets (starting with Adam, up to the Prophet Muhammad), as well as kings and rulers, from ancient pre-Islamic Iran, then selectively through Islamic history up to the Ottoman dynasty. T_439_1.c: Young man and woman (recto), and Persian calligraphy (verso), folio from an Ottoman album. Across Iran, India and Turkey, from the sixteenth century at least, albums (or muraqqa`) had become an important way of storing and presenting one's diverse collection of artworks on paper: valuable specimens of calligraphy, single-page paintings or drawings, and even European prints, all re-mounted in a careful sequence. This album was compiled in early seventeenth-century Ottoman Istanbul, probably for a private citizen. T_444.t: Key to the comprehensive divination (Tercüme-i Miftah-ı Cifrü’l-Cami), Turkish translation of the Arabic Miftah al-jafr al-jami`, by Shaykh `Abd al-Rahman al-Bistami (d. 1458)
T_444.c: Key to the comprehensive divination (Tercüme-i Miftah-ı Cifrü’l-Cami), Turkish translation of the Arabic Miftah al-jafr al-jami`, by Shaykh `Abd al-Rahman al-Bistami (d. 1458). This work on cryptic science draws from the divination tradition linked with the Shi`a Imam Ja`far al-Sadiq (d. 765), and discusses places, signs and prophecies of the apocalypse. This copy follows closely a late sixteenth-century manuscript dedicated to an earlier Ottoman sultan, except for the paintings: very unusually, the painter here has omitted figures from many of the landscape scenes, and has replaced the sultans' faces with roses. T_445.c: Calligraphy album, by Mehmed Sa`id Berberzade. This album was created in Ottoman Istanbul, in 1733. The fine calligraphy was written out by a man who had studied under the master-calligrapher Mehmed Efendi (d. 1753), known as Şekerzade ("son of sugar") because his father was a confectioner. Codex, ink, colours and gold on paper, set into gold-flecked card mounts, 4 folios, Arabic text in naskh script, album of calligraphy quoting lines from the Hadith, signed Mehmed Sa`id Berberzade (d. 1774), pupil of Mehmed Shekerzada (Şekerzade Mehmed Efendi, d. 1753), Istanbul, Turkey, dated 1146H, 1733.

T_447.t: Ottoman album (muraqqa'), with calligraphy, views of holy sites, and a world map
a: Mir `Ali Haravi; Dervish `Ali; Hafiz Osman; Unknown
T_447.c: Ottoman album (muraqqa'), with calligraphy, views of the holy sites, and a world map. This album was put together in early eighteenth-century Istanbul, during the reign of Ottoman Sultan Mahmud I. Organised with gold-painted borders throughout, the album combines examples of fine Arabic calligraphy by Ottoman masters of the seventeenth century (such as Dervish `Ali and Hafiz Osman), and (possibly) the older master Mir `Ali Haravi from Iran. These beautiful lines quote from the Qur'an, and from Hadith literature (describing the Prophet's actions). As well as calligraphy, the album preserves four aerial views of famous holy sites: Haram al-Sharif in Jerusalem, the Ka`ba sanctuary in Mecca, the Prophet's mosque in Medina, and the Selimiye mosque of Ottoman Sultan Selim II (r. 1566-74) in Edirne. The final folio is a diagrammatic map of the world, with the continents of Asia, Africa and Europe. Album, ink, colours and gold on paper with leather edging, 9 folios with illuminated floral and

T_474_42.t: Junayd Baghdādī (835-910) invites the Christian youth to accept Islam at the Sufi meeting, witnessed by Saqati, from Breaths of intimacy (Nafaḥāt al-uns), by Jāmī (d. 1492)
T_474_42.c: Junayd Baghdādī (835-910) invites the Christian youth to accept Islam at the Sufi meeting, witnessed by Saqati, from Breaths of intimacy (Nafaḥāt al-uns), by Jāmī (d. 1492). The poet and statesman Jāmī wrote this account of the lives of over six hundred great Sufis in history. In this biographical episode, the Sufi shaykh Junayd Baghdādī (d. 910, seated on the minbar steps in this painting) held a meeting at dawn, and a crowd gathered to hear him speak. Unnoticed, a young Christian man also joined the meeting in the mosque, and asked a searching question. On the insightful shaykh’s invitation, he decided to convert to Islam. T_559_2.t: Arabic calligraphy in bird form: the bismillah
T_559_2.c: Arabic calligraphy in bird form: the bismillah. Bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim (In the Name of God, the Merciful, the Compassionate). This holy phrase in Arabic introduces almost every chapter of the Qur’an. In Muslim life, the bismillah is also spoken or written at the start of all important tasks, to bless the work that follows. Master-calligraphers write out these words with particular attention. Folio, ink on paper, Arabic text, the bismillah in the outline form of a bird, unsigned, possibly Istanbul, Turkey, dated 1250H, 1834-1835.

T_559_4.t: Description of the Prophet (Hilya al-nabi), by Hafiz Osman (d. 1698)
T_559_4.c: Description of the Prophet (Hilya al-nabi), by Ottoman calligrapher Hafiz Osman. Descriptions of the Prophet Muhammad's personal appearance (hilya al-nabi, in Arabic) were recorded by his friends, and carefully preserved ever since in Hadith literature, to remember him. In the early seventeenth century, Ottoman calligraphers designed a new format in which to present one of these simple but resonant pious texts, known in Turkish as the hilye. This is one of the earliest known examples, and the form may have been invented by this master-calligrapher, Hafiz Osman (d. 1698). Tb_1815.o: Object by Function/Ceremonial objects/Religious objects/Thankga; Approved Category 2017/Painting/Hanging Scroll (painting)
Tb_1815.c: Buddhist hanging scroll (thangka) mandala of Hevajra, painted in colours on cotton by an unknown artist in Tibet, 16th century or earlier. This painted mandala (cosmic diagram) is conceived as a four-sided palace-temple with portals to the four quarters. The figure in the centre is a yidam: sometimes defined as a meditational deity, but also a Buddha-figure and practice. The yidam shown here is Hevajra. Hevajra appears in an embrace with his partner Nairatmya. He is depicted with blue skin, five heads and sixteen arms. In each of his hands Hevajra holds a skull cup supporting a ritual object, animal or god. A number of Indian teachers and Tibetan lamas are shown seated in the painting’s upper register.

Tb_1816.o: Object by Function/Ceremonial objects/Religious objects/Thangka; Approved Category 2017/Painting/Hanging Scroll (painting)
Tb_1816.c: Buddhist hanging scroll (thangka) of the wealth deity, Jambhala, made by an unknown artist c. 1800, with colours on cotton in Tibet. Jambhala is shown as a corpulent figure wearing a crown and jewels, and holding a mongoose in his left hand. Tsongkapa, the founder of the Gelug order (Gelugpa) and his two disciples, Gyaltsab Je and Khedrubje, are seated above the main figure, while manifestations of the saviour goddess, Tara, are seated below. There is a short inscription on the reverse in the bottom right corner.

Tb_1817.t: Tsongkapa, founder of the Gelug order (Gelugpa)
Tb_1817.o: Approved Category 2017/Painting/Hanging Scroll (painting); Object by Function/Ceremonial objects/Religious objects/Thankga
Tb_1817.c: Buddhist hanging scroll painting (thangka) of Tsongkapa, founder of the Gelug order (Gelugpa), painted by an unknown artist in colours on cotton, Tibet, 19th century. The central figure, Tsongkapa, is flanked by his two disciples, Gyaltsab Je and Khedrubje. The future Buddha, Maitreya, is seated at the top of the painting, with Atisha, founder of the Kadam order (Kadampa), to the left and Tsongkapa to the right. The saviour goddess Tara, in her white manifestation, is in the centre at the bottom; the bull-headed lord of death, Yama, strikes a fierce pose at bottom left; and the fierce Palden Lhamo rides her wild mule at bottom right.

Tb_1818.o: Object by Function/Ceremonial objects/Religious objects/Thangka; Approved Category 2017/Painting/Hanging Scroll (painting)
Tb_1818.c: Buddhist hanging scroll (thangka) of Avalokiteshvara, bodhisattva of compassion, made by an unknown artist in the late 18th or 19th century, with colours on cotton in Tibet. The central figure is Avalokiteshvara. Above his head in the centre is Akshobhya, Buddha of the east, flanked by green and white forms of the saviour goddess, Tara. In the bottom left corner is Manjushri, bodhisattva of wisdom, and in the bottom right is Vajrapani, bodhisattva of Buddha's power.

Tb_1819.o: Object by Function/Ceremonial objects/Religious objects/Thangka; Approved Category 2017/Painting/Hanging Scroll (painting)
Tb_1819.c: Buddhist hanging scroll (thangka) of Manjushri, bodhisattva of wisdom, made by an unknown artist in the 18th century, with colours on cotton in Tibet. Manjushri is seated in the centre on a lion throne. Tsongkapa, founder of the Gelug order, is shown above and is flanked by Amitayus, Buddha of infinite life, on the left and the saviour goddess, Tara, on the right. Kurukulla dances on a corpse below Manjushri and is flanked by Jambhala on the left and Palden Lhamo riding her mule on the right.

Tb_1820.o: Object by Function/Ceremonial objects/Religious objects/Thangka; Approved Category 2017/Painting/Hanging Scroll (painting)
Tb_1820.c: Buddhist hanging scroll (thangka) of Amitabha, Buddha of infinite light, made by an unknown artist in the 18th or 19th century, with colours on cotton in Tibet. Amitabha is seated in his paradise, Sukhavati (Western Pure Land), along with his entourage of eight bodhisattvas.

Tb_1821.o: Object by Function/Ceremonial objects/Religious objects/Thangka; Approved Category 2017/Painting/Hanging Scroll (painting)
Tb_1821.c: Buddhist hanging scroll (thangka) of Amitabha, Buddha of infinite light, made by an unknown artist in the 18th century, with colours on cotton in Tibet. Enclosed within a large circle, Amitabha is flanked by his chief bodhisattvas, Avalokiteshvara and Vajrasattva, along with the thirty-five Buddhas of confession, including Shakyamuni who sits below Amitabha's throne. Below the circle are the 'protectors of the three families' (wisdom, compassion and power) as represented by Manjushri in the centre, Avalokiteshvara on the left and Vajrapani on the right.

Tb_1822.o: Object by Function/Ceremonial objects/Religious objects/Thangka; Approved Category 2017/Painting/Hanging Scroll (painting)
Tb_1822.c: Buddhist hanging scroll (thangka) of the Medicine Buddha (Bhaisajyaguru) made by an unknown artist in the 18th century, with colours on cotton in Tibet. Bhaisajyaguru is seated in the centre, encircled by the eight buddhas of his entourage and the saviour goddess, Tara, in her green aspect. Tsongkapa, founder of the Gelug order (Gelugpa), is seated above and flanked by his two disciples, Gyaltsab Je and Khedrubje.

Tb_1823.o: Object by Function/Ceremonial objects/Religious objects/Thangka; Approved Category 2017/Painting/Hanging Scroll (painting)
Tb_1823.c: Buddhist hanging scroll (thangka) of Padmasambhava made by an unknown artist in the 18th or 19th century, with colours on cotton in Tibet. The central figure is Padmasambhava (Lotus-born), the eighth-century Indian mystic who is credited with introducing Tantric Buddhism to Tibet and founding the Nyingma order of Tibetan Buddhism. Wearing his customary princely robes and hat with ear-flaps, he holds a vajra in his right hand, and a vajra-topped staff (khatvanga) and skull cup (kapala) containing a jar of elixir in his left hand. Above his head is Amitayus, Buddha of infinite life, flanked by the goddess of long life, Ushnishavijaya, on the left and the saviour goddess, Tara, on the right. Tb_1824.o: Approved Category 2017/Painting/Hanging Scroll (painting); Object by Function/Ceremonial objects/Religious objects/Thangka
Tb_1824.c: Buddhist hanging scroll painting (thangka) of Shakyamuni Buddha painted by an unknown artist in colours on cotton, Tibet, 18th century. The historical Buddha, Shakyamuni, is seated in the centre of the painting surrounded by episodes from his life. Starting at the top left and moving counter-clockwise around the painting, the scenes depicted include his stay in Tushita heaven and descent as a white elephant into his mother's womb; his miraculous birth; and his princely life. Moving up the right side of the painting, depictions include his renunciation and subsequent asceticism; his moment of enlightenment while being tempted by Mara; and his teaching career; before his final nirvana and the enshrining of his relics.

Tb_1860.t: Tsongkapa, founder of the Gelug order (Gelugpa)
Tb_1860.o: Object by Function/Ceremonial objects/Religious objects/Thangka; Approved Category 2017/Painting/Hanging Scroll (painting)
Tb_1860.c: Buddhist hanging scroll (thangka) of Tsongkapa, founder of the Gelug order (Gelugpa) of Tibetan Buddhism, made by an unknown artist in the 18th or 19th century, with colours on cotton in Tibet. The central figure, Tsongkapa, is shown as a mahasiddha (Indian adept) riding a tiger, as seen in a vision by his disciple Khedrub Je. A Sanskrit term meaning ‘great accomplished one’, a mahasiddha is an awakened being who has developed magical powers. Above him is Vajravarahi, shown with eight arms and three faces. At the bottom are Tsongkapa's two main disciples, Khedrub Je on the left and Gyaltsab Je on the right. The painting is framed within a textile mount.

W_022.c: Parchment codex containing the Old Testament books Genesis to Ruth written in Latin in black ink around 1153 for Walsingham Priory, Norfolk (England), around the time the monastery was founded. It is the first (and only extant) volume of a complete Bible. Initial letters are written in red, green or blue ink, some with additional pen flourishes. Important texts, rubrics and introductory words are written in alternating green and red. Marginal notes and corrections were added by a contemporary hand in brown ink. Some rubricator notes are still visible in the margins. Each book (or prefatory text) is illustrated with an historiated or decorated initial (10 in total). The manuscript was purchased by Edith Beatty in 1921 from Fitzroy Fenwick (Phillipps Collection 4769) as a gift for Chester Beatty. W_061.c: Bound parchment codex with leather cover preserving a Latin Psalter written in the 13th century in Flanders. The book includes a calendar, psalter, canticles, and litany. There are 12 calendar illustrations depicting abbreviated versions of the labours of the months, 14 full-page miniatures featuring scenes from the Life of the Virgin and the Passion of Jesus Christ, a full-page historiated Beatus initial with 9 additional historiated initials featuring saints, as well as various decorated initials. Each page has bar borders ending in human and animal heads, with other animals and figures in the margins.

W_080.t: Garden of knowledge (Viridarium), a medieval encyclopaedia
W_080.c: Parchment codex containing Garden of Knowledge (Viridarium), a medieval encyclopaedia, primarily an edited version of Thomas de Cantimpré's On the nature of things (Liber de naturis rerum) with variations and interpolations (including quotations from Gervase of Tilbury), written, edited and illuminated by jurist Jean Reynaud between 1386-1425 probably in Avignon (France). Thomas de Cantimpré (1201-c. 1272) is best known for his encyclopaedia, compiled between 1230-1245, which purported to contain all the natural history knowledge of his time. It included information on anthropology, zoology, botany, mineralogy, astronomy, astrology and meteorology. Jean Reynaud's version took as his model a rare twenty-two book version of Cantimpré's encyclopaedia. The manuscript was purchased in 1924 from the Phillipps Collection.

The Archangel Gabriel delivers the message that she will conceive a child. The main frame contains a view of the cosmos surmounted by God seated on a throne of red seraphim and surrounded by angels. Together with ‘Obsecro te’ this prayer was one of the most popular additions to books of hours. ‘O intermerata’ enumerates the glories of Christ and asks the Virgin to intercede. It is one of a series of twenty-six prayers to the Virgin Mary in this section of the manuscript.

It was commissioned by Prigent de Coëtivy (1399?–1450) on the occasion of his marriage to Marie de Rais (1429–1457). Removed from the bound volume between 1933 and 1960. Beneath rubrics in blue, a prayer to James and Philip opens with the illuminated initial ‘S’ (Si manseritis in me et verba mea in vobis manserint) painted with white, red, blue and gold ivy-leaf ornament (most of the gold is lost). It is one of an unusually large series of forty-seven suffrages, or short prayers to saints, arranged hierarchically. The section opens with a number of prefatory prayers, followed by the Apostles, Martyrs, Confessors and Virgins. It was commissioned by Prigent de Coëtivy (1399?–1450) on the occasion of his marriage to Marie de Rais (1429–1457). The folio was removed from the bound volume between 1933 and 1960. Beneath rubrics in blue, a prayer to St Genevieve opens with the illuminated initial ‘O’ (O felix ancilla dei genovesa nos pondere pressos) painted with white, red, blue and gold ivy-leaf ornament. It is one of an unusually large series of forty-seven suffrages, or short prayers to saints, arranged hierarchically. The section opens with a number of prefatory prayers, followed by the Apostles, Martyrs, Confessors and Virgins. The miniature is painted in demi-grisaille with pigments and gold and depicts St Genevieve. She holds a candle which the devil continually stuffs with a bellows only to be relit by an angel.
